questions.question_text:
Argument 3:

After the city of Navgarh made helmets compulsory for cyclists in 2020, the number of cyclists treated in hospitals for head injuries fell by 35 per cent over three years. The transport commissioner cites this as proof that the helmet law has saved lives, and wants the fine for not wearing a helmet raised from ₹100 to ₹1,000. A cycling association disputes this. It points out that traffic counts show the number of people cycling in the city fell by about a third after the law was introduced, as many occasional cyclists switched to buses rather than buy helmets. Fewer cyclists, it says, would mean fewer injuries of every kind, helmet or no helmet. The association adds that studies in other countries suggest that the more cyclists there are on a road, the more carefully drivers behave around them, so a fall in cycling may make each remaining cyclist less safe. It wants the city to build protected cycle lanes instead of raising fines.

Question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the commissioner's claim that the helmet law caused the fall in head injuries?

options.A: Hospital treatment of cyclists for injuries other than head injuries also fell by about 35 per cent over the same three years.
options.B: Bus fares in Navgarh were unchanged between 2020 and 2023.
options.C: Most cyclists fined for not wearing a helmet in Navgarh paid the ₹100 fine promptly.
options.D: Helmets sold in Navgarh since 2020 have met a stricter national safety standard than those sold before the law came into force.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Helmets protect only the head. If other injuries fell just as much, a general fall in cycling, not the helmets, is the likelier cause.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): This does not bear on why head injuries fell. | Trap (C): Irrelevant to what caused the fall in injuries. | Trap (D): This makes the helmet effect more plausible, so it supports the commissioner.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Weaken – Road safety – cycle helmet law

Question: The cycling association's argument that the fall in cycling explains the fall in head injuries assumes that:

options.A: helmets give no protection at all against head injuries in a road accident involving a car or bus
options.B: those who stopped cycling were not at much lower risk of injury than those who kept cycling
options.C: cyclists who switched to buses are now less likely to be injured in traffic than they were before the law
options.D: drivers in Navgarh behave more carefully than drivers in other countries

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If those who quit were rare, low-risk riders, their leaving would barely cut injuries, and the fall would still need the helmets to explain it. So the argument needs them not to be much safer than average.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Too strong: the association argues the figures do not prove the law's effect, not that helmets are useless. | Trap (C): Their current safety on buses is beside the point; the issue is what their leaving did to cyclist injury numbers. | Trap (D): The association cites foreign studies about driver behaviour but makes no such comparison.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Assumption – Road safety – cycle helmet law
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: Subtle necessary assumption (negation test).

questions.question_text:
Argument 4:

The government of Mithila Pradesh has banned coaching centres from enrolling students below the age of sixteen. The education minister says the ban will reduce the stress that has driven a rise in anxiety among teenagers, since a survey found that 70 per cent of teenagers attending coaching reported feeling anxious, compared with 40 per cent of those who did not. Coaching owners reply that the survey shows only that anxious students are more likely to seek coaching, perhaps because they are already worried about their marks. They add that the ban will not reduce competition for college seats, which is the real source of stress, and that families who can afford it will simply hire private tutors at home, leaving poorer students, who relied on cheaper group coaching, worse off. Some parents agree with the minister, saying that their children spend up to six hours a day travelling to and sitting in coaching classes after school, leaving no time for sleep or play.

Question: The coaching owners' first reply suggests that the minister's reasoning:

options.A: may mistake a result of anxiety for its cause
options.B: relies on a survey whose sample was too small to support any conclusion about the teenagers of Mithila Pradesh
options.C: ignores the views of parents whose children attend coaching
options.D: assumes that all teenagers attend coaching

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The owners argue the link could run the other way: anxious students seek coaching. That is a reversed-causation objection.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The owners say nothing about the survey's size. | Trap (C): The owners' first reply is about the survey, not about parents. | Trap (D): The survey itself compares those who do and do not attend.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Flaw identified – Education – ban on coaching for under-16s

questions.question_text:
Argument 4:

The government of Mithila Pradesh has banned coaching centres from enrolling students below the age of sixteen. The education minister says the ban will reduce the stress that has driven a rise in anxiety among teenagers, since a survey found that 70 per cent of teenagers attending coaching reported feeling anxious, compared with 40 per cent of those who did not. Coaching owners reply that the survey shows only that anxious students are more likely to seek coaching, perhaps because they are already worried about their marks. They add that the ban will not reduce competition for college seats, which is the real source of stress, and that families who can afford it will simply hire private tutors at home, leaving poorer students, who relied on cheaper group coaching, worse off. Some parents agree with the minister, saying that their children spend up to six hours a day travelling to and sitting in coaching classes after school, leaving no time for sleep or play.

Question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the minister's position?

options.A: Many coaching centres in Mithila Pradesh have recently raised their fees.
options.B: Teenagers in states without such a ban report anxiety at rates similar to those found in Mithila Pradesh's survey.
options.C: Most parents of teenagers support the ban.
options.D: Anxiety among students who joined coaching was similar to that of non-attenders before they joined but rose within a year.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Measuring anxiety before and after joining answers the owners' reversed-causation reply: the students were not more anxious to begin with.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Fees do not show that coaching causes anxiety. | Trap (B): This says nothing about whether coaching causes the anxiety. | Trap (C): Popular support is not evidence about cause.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Strengthen – Education – ban on coaching for under-16s

questions.question_text:
Argument 5:

Fifteen years ago, wolves were reintroduced into the Sonmarg Reserve, from which they had been absent for a century. Since then, the reserve's deer population has halved, and saplings of willow and poplar, which deer browse, have spread along the riverbanks. Ecologists credit the wolves, arguing that the predators not only reduced deer numbers but also made the surviving deer avoid open riverbanks, where they are easy to ambush. A neighbouring reserve, which has no wolves, now wants to introduce them to restore its own riverbank forests. Some scientists urge caution. They note that during the same fifteen years, a run of wet years raised the water table along Sonmarg's rivers, which helps willow seedlings take root, and that hunting permits for deer in the reserve were also increased. In the neighbouring reserve, they add, the riverbanks have been badly eroded by sand mining, so even with fewer deer, saplings may find nowhere to root.

Question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the ecologists' explanation?

options.A: Visitors to Sonmarg have increased since the wolves were reintroduced.
options.B: In a riverbank plot fenced off from deer for all fifteen years, willow saplings spread no faster than in unfenced areas.
options.C: Wolves in Sonmarg have also been seen hunting wild boar and hares as well as the reserve's deer.
options.D: Deer in Sonmarg now spend less time on open riverbanks than they did before the wolves returned.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If keeping deer out entirely made no difference, deer browsing was not what held the saplings back, so reducing deer (via wolves) cannot explain the spread.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Irrelevant to sapling growth. | Trap (C): Wolves eating other prey does not challenge their effect on deer. | Trap (D): This supports the ecologists' account.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Weaken – Ecology – wolves and riverbank forests

questions.question_text:
Argument 6:

When Dakshinpur raised its minimum wage for shop workers by 25 per cent in 2022, business groups predicted that shops would cut jobs. Two years later, the number of people employed in shops in the state had actually grown by 4 per cent. Labour activists say this proves that higher minimum wages do not destroy jobs, and are campaigning for a further 25 per cent rise. Economists at the state university are less certain. They point out that in the same two years, a new highway brought a surge of tourists to Dakshinpur's coastal towns, and that shop employment grew by 9 per cent in neighbouring Uttarpur, which did not raise its minimum wage. They also note that many shops in Dakshinpur cut their workers' hours, so that while more people were employed, the total hours worked in shops did not rise at all. A further rise, they argue, would push wages above what many small shops in inland villages, which have seen no tourist boom, can afford.

Question: Which of the following is the conclusion the labour activists draw from the figures?

options.A: Tourism caused the growth in shop jobs.
options.B: The minimum wage for shop workers in Dakshinpur should be raised by a further 25 per cent within two years.
options.C: Business groups exaggerate the costs of regulation.
options.D: Higher minimum wages do not destroy jobs.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The activists say the 4 per cent rise 'proves that higher minimum wages do not destroy jobs'. The campaign follows from that.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): That is the economists' suggestion, not the activists'. | Trap (B): This is what they campaign for, but the conclusion they draw from the figures is the claim about jobs. | Trap (C): Not stated by the activists.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Main point – Economy – minimum wage and jobs

Question: Which of the following shows the same flaw as the activists' reasoning?

options.A: A farmer's yield rose 5 per cent after a new pesticide, so she says it does not harm crops, though the rains were unusually good and neighbours gained 12 per cent.
options.B: A doctor says a drug is safe because its maker says so.
options.C: A cricket captain lost the toss in three matches and his team lost all three matches, so he decided to stop calling heads at the toss in future matches.

questions.question_text:
Argument 7:

When the insurance firm Shubh Assure moved its head office into an open-plan building, removing all private cabins, managers expected staff to collaborate more. A study of the move tracked 150 employees using badges that recorded face-to-face conversations, and also logged their emails and chat messages. In the year after the move, face-to-face conversations fell by about 70 per cent, while emails and chat messages rose by about half. The study's authors concluded that open-plan offices reduce collaboration. Shubh Assure's managers reject this. They say that many face-to-face conversations in the old building were simply people walking to each other's cabins to hand over paper files, a practice that ended in the same year when the firm moved to a digital filing system. They also argue that a rise in electronic messages is itself a sign of more collaboration, not less, and that the number of joint projects between departments rose after the move.

Question: The managers' remark about paper files serves to:

options.A: show that the badges used in the study recorded conversations inaccurately in the new open-plan building
options.B: prove that the open-plan office increased collaboration
options.C: offer another explanation for the fall in face-to-face conversations
options.D: explain why emails and chat messages increased

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If many conversations were file hand-overs that ended with digital filing, the fall need not reflect the open-plan layout.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The managers do not question the badges' accuracy. | Trap (B): It explains a fall; it does not by itself show an increase. | Trap (D): It is about face-to-face talk, not electronic messages.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Role of statement – Workplace – open-plan offices

options.B: Digital filing systems are now used by most insurance firms.
options.C: Badges of the type used in the study sometimes fail to record conversations held in noisy rooms, such as open-plan offices.
options.D: Employees at Shubh Assure said they liked the natural light in the new building.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: It removes the managers' alternative explanation: the fall in talk occurs even where filing did not change.

Argument 8:

Under a proposed law in Rajnagar, every adult would be presumed to have consented to donate their organs after death unless they had registered an objection. Supporters point out that in countries that switched to such 'opt-out' systems, the share of people registered as donors jumped to over 90 per cent, compared with about 20 per cent under 'opt-in' systems, in which people must sign up. They argue that the law would end Rajnagar's long waiting lists for kidneys and livers. Doctors' groups are cautious. They note that in practice, doctors in opt-out countries still ask families before removing organs and usually respect a family's refusal, so the number of actual donations depends heavily on families' attitudes. They add that most organs are lost not for want of consent but because few hospitals in Rajnagar have the intensive-care beds and transplant teams needed to keep a brain-dead donor's organs usable. A legal scholar adds that presuming consent from silence sits uneasily with the principle that consent to interference with one's body must be informed and freely given.

Question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the doctors' groups?

options.A: Opt-out laws are unconstitutional.
options.B: Switching to opt-out alone may not much increase actual organ donations in Rajnagar.
options.C: Families in Rajnagar should be given the final say over organ donation, whatever the deceased person had registered in life.
options.D: Rajnagar should build more hospitals.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Both of the doctors' points (family refusals and lack of ICU capacity) show that registered consent is not what limits donations.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): That concern is the legal scholar's, and it is about principle. | Trap (C): The doctors describe practice in opt-out countries; they do not propose this rule. | Trap (D): A possible implication, but not their main point.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Main point – Law – opt-out organ donation

questions.question_text:
Argument 9:

In 2015, the state of Vindhyagiri made the rape of a minor punishable by death. Since then, the number of such cases registered by the police has risen every year, and by 2024 it was 60 per cent higher than in 2014. A columnist argues that this shows the death penalty does not deter such crimes and should be abolished for them. A former police chief disputes the columnist's reading of the figures. He points out that in 2015 the state also opened special police desks for children and launched a campaign urging families to report abuse, so many cases that would once have gone unrecorded are now registered. Child-rights groups, while also opposing the death penalty for these crimes, give a different reason: because most such crimes are committed by relatives or neighbours, the threat of a death sentence makes families more reluctant to report them and puts pressure on victims to withdraw complaints.

Question: The former police chief challenges the columnist mainly by:

options.A: questioning the accuracy of police records before 2015
options.B: suggesting that the rise in registered cases may reflect more reporting rather than more crimes
options.C: pointing out that most offenders are relatives or neighbours
options.D: arguing that the death penalty does deter such crimes and should be kept for rape of a minor in Vindhyagiri

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The special desks and the reporting campaign offer another explanation for the rise in registered cases.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): He says cases went unrecorded, not that records were inaccurate. | Trap (C): That is the child-rights groups' point. | Trap (D): He questions the columnist's reading of the figures; he does not argue for the penalty.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Method – Criminal law – death penalty and deterrence

Argument 10:

In a study at a college in Pune, 200 students were randomly assigned to read the same 2,000-word article either on paper or on a tablet, and then answered questions about it. Those who read on paper scored on average 12 per cent higher on questions about the article's main argument, though the two groups scored about the same on questions about specific facts. The college's principal has cited the study to justify withdrawing the tablets given to first-year students and returning to printed textbooks. Some teachers question the decision. They point out that the students in the study were given only fifteen minutes, and that earlier research suggests readers skim faster on screens when they are under time pressure. They also note that the tablets are used mainly for watching recorded lectures and doing practice tests, not for reading long texts, and that printed textbooks would cost the college three times as much each year.

Question: If the statements in the passage are true, which of the following must also be true?

options.A: First-year students use their tablets mainly for reading.
options.B: Tablet readers in the study scored about as well on factual questions as paper readers.
options.C: Reading on tablets harms students' understanding of a text's main argument whatever the time limit they are given.
options.D: Printed textbooks improve students' examination results.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says the two groups scored about the same on questions about specific facts.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The teachers say the opposite. | Trap (C): Overgeneralised: the study used a fifteen-minute limit, and the teachers doubt the result holds without it. | Trap (D): The study did not measure examination results.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Inference – Education – reading on screens

questions.question_text:
Argument 1:

In January last year, the state of Varunpur installed forty speed cameras along a 120-km stretch of the National Highway that had recorded 85 deaths in road accidents the year before. In the twelve months after installation, deaths on the stretch fell to 51. The transport secretary has called the cameras "the single most effective road-safety measure the state has ever taken" and announced that cameras will be installed on every highway in the state. A road-safety researcher at the state university is less certain. She points out that the 85 deaths in the year before installation were the highest the stretch had recorded in a decade, and that in an average year the stretch records about 60 deaths. She also notes that in the middle of last year the highway authority repaired a long section of the road that had been badly damaged by floods, and added crash barriers on the sharpest bends.

Question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the road-safety researcher?

options.A: Speed cameras have no effect at all on the number of road deaths on any highway in the state.
options.B: Installing speed cameras on every highway in the state would cost far more than it would save.
options.C: The highway authority's road repairs were the only reason that deaths on the stretch fell last year.
options.D: The fall in deaths does not clearly show that the cameras were the cause.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Both of her points, the unusually bad base year and the road repairs, attack the claim that the cameras explain the fall.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Overstated: she questions the size of the cameras' effect, not whether they have any effect. | Trap (B): Cost is never mentioned in the passage. | Trap (C): She offers the repairs as a rival factor, not as the proven sole cause.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Main point – Road safety – speed cameras on a highway

A road-safety researcher at the state university is less certain. She points out that the 85 deaths in the year before installation were the highest the stretch had recorded in a decade, and that in an average year the stretch records about 60 deaths. She also notes that in the middle of last year the highway authority repaired a long section of the road that had been badly damaged by floods, and added crash barriers on the sharpest bends.

Question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the transport secretary's claim about the cameras?

options.A: Most drivers interviewed on the stretch said that they now drive more slowly when they see a camera.
options.B: On a nearby stretch with the same repairs and barriers but no cameras, deaths fell by a similar proportion.
options.C: The cameras issued more than two lakh speeding fines on the stretch in the first year.
options.D: Accident deaths on the state's other highways rose slightly over the same twelve months.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A similar fall where only the repairs and barriers were added points to those changes, not the cameras, as the cause.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): This supports the cameras having some effect. | Trap (C): Fines show the cameras operated, not that they reduced deaths. | Trap (D): If anything this makes the camera stretch look better by comparison.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Weaken – Road safety – speed cameras on a highway

Argument 1:

In January last year, the state of Varunpur installed forty speed cameras along a 120-km stretch of the National Highway that had recorded 85 deaths in road accidents the year before. In the twelve months after installation, deaths on the stretch fell to 51. The transport secretary has called the cameras "the single most effective road-safety measure the state has ever taken" and announced that cameras will be installed on every highway in the state. A road-safety researcher at the state university is less certain. She points out that the 85 deaths in the year before installation were the highest the stretch had recorded in a decade, and that in an average year the stretch records about 60 deaths. She also notes that in the middle of last year the highway authority repaired a long section of the road that had been badly damaged by floods, and added crash barriers on the sharpest bends.

Question: The secretary's decision to install cameras on every highway assumes which of the following?

options.A: The road-safety researcher at the state university has no expertise in the study of speed cameras.
options.B: The other highways in the state have each recorded at least 85 deaths in a single year.
options.C: Other highways have the kind of speed-related deaths that cameras are able to reduce.
options.D: Flood damage on other highways in the state will be repaired before the cameras are installed.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If deaths on other highways had little to do with speeding, cameras could not be expected to cut them, so extending the scheme presupposes this.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The secretary's plan does not depend on discrediting the researcher. | Trap (B): Too strong: the plan does not require every highway to be as dangerous as this stretch. | Trap (D): Repairs are the researcher's rival explanation, not a premise of the secretary's plan.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Assumption – Road safety – speed cameras on a highway

questions.question_text:
Argument 2:

A survey of 200 private schools in Nandgarh found that schools requiring a uniform reported, on average, 30 per cent fewer disciplinary incidents per pupil than schools with no uniform. A parents' association has used this finding to demand that the state make uniforms compulsory in all government schools, arguing that uniforms "create a sense of discipline and belonging". The education department's statistician has urged caution. Most of the schools with uniforms, she notes, are older institutions with long waiting lists, which can select the pupils they admit and expel those who misbehave repeatedly. Schools without uniforms are mostly new schools, many opened in the last five years, that admit every applicant. She adds that schools differ in what they record as a "disciplinary incident": some log every late arrival, while others record only serious misconduct.

Question: The parents' association's demand rests on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Every government school in Nandgarh currently reports more disciplinary incidents than any private school in the state.
options.B: Pupils in Nandgarh's government schools would prefer to wear a uniform than their own clothes.
options.C: Uniforms themselves, not other differences between the schools, explain part of the gap.
options.D: Uniforms are cheaper for parents than the clothes pupils would otherwise wear to school.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The survey shows a correlation. To demand uniforms as a remedy, the association must take the uniform to be at least partly causal.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Too strong: the demand needs no claim that every government school is worse than every private one. | Trap (B): Pupils' preferences are irrelevant to whether uniforms reduce incidents. | Trap (D): Cost plays no part in the argument.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Assumption – Education – school uniforms and discipline

options.A: presenting a different survey which shows that uniforms increase the number of disciplinary incidents
options.B: arguing that a sense of discipline and belonging is not worth creating in schools
options.C: naming other differences between the schools and inconsistent recording
options.D: disputing that the survey of 200 private schools was ever actually carried out by anyone

options.A: Among schools of similar age and admissions policy, uniforms make no difference to incident rates.
options.B: Several newer schools without uniforms have recently begun to record every late arrival as a disciplinary incident.
options.C: Government schools in Nandgarh already require pupils to wear a badge showing the school's name.
options.D: Some pupils in schools with uniforms say that they dislike the uniform and would rather not wear it.

questions.trap_type: Trap (B): This is consistent with the statistician's point but is weaker than a like-for-like comparison. | Trap (C): A badge is not a uniform, and this says nothing about incident rates. | Trap (D): Dislike of uniforms does not show that uniforms fail to reduce incidents.

options.B: Newer schools in Nandgarh are poorly managed compared with older, established schools that have waiting lists.
options.C: Schools with uniforms in Nandgarh have fewer serious cases of misconduct than schools without uniforms.

Argument 2:

She adds that schools differ in what they record as a "disciplinary incident": some log every late arrival, while others record only serious misconduct.

Question: Which of the following arguments contains reasoning most similar to the parents' association's?

options.A: A school found that pupils who took extra mathematics classes improved their scores, so it extended the classes to all pupils in the same school.
options.B: Because a famous coach recommends early-morning practice, all teams in the league should practise early in the morning.
options.C: Members of an exclusive club that screens and expels applicants live longer than non-members, so club membership should be made compulsory to raise life expectancy.
options.D: A survey found that towns with more doctors have more hospital admissions, so the number of doctors in towns should be reduced to cut admissions.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Both arguments draw a causal conclusion from a group that selects and removes members, then propose imposing the group's feature on everyone.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Same population and an intervention given to pupils directly; there is no selection by the institution. | Trap (B): This is an appeal to authority, not a correlation affected by selection. | Trap (D): This reverses cause and effect; it lacks the element of a selective group that screens out problem cases.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Parallel flaw – Education – school uniforms and discipline

questions.question_text:
Argument 3:

A technology company gave standing desks to 150 volunteers among its office staff. After six months, 62 per cent of them reported less lower-back pain than before, compared with 35 per cent of 150 colleagues who kept ordinary desks. The company's wellness head now proposes buying standing desks for all 3,000 office staff, saying that this will halve the number of days lost to back pain. A physiotherapist consulted by the company points out that the volunteers were people who had asked for standing desks, many of them because they already suffered from back pain and were keen to try something new. She adds that the improvement was self-reported, that the volunteers knew they were part of a trial, and that standing for long periods causes problems of its own, such as varicose veins and foot pain.

Question: Which of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?

options.A: Standing for long periods causes more health problems than sitting for long periods.
options.B: Standing desks will halve the number of working days that the company's 3,000 staff lose to back pain.
options.C: More of the standing-desk group than of the comparison group reported less back pain.
options.D: Most of the volunteers who received standing desks had suffered from back pain before the trial began.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 62 per cent versus 35 per cent of equal-sized groups is stated directly.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The physiotherapist names some problems of standing but makes no comparison of this kind. | Trap (B): This is the wellness head's forecast, not something the evidence establishes. | Trap (D): She says 'many', not most.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Inference – Health – standing desks and back pain

Question: The wellness head's proposal assumes that:

options.A: standing desks are cheaper to buy and maintain than ordinary office desks
options.B: all 3,000 office staff currently suffer from lower-back pain that keeps them away from work
options.C: the physiotherapist was not consulted before the trial was designed
options.D: staff who did not volunteer would benefit about as much as the volunteers did

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The trial used self-selected volunteers. Extending the result to all staff requires assuming non-volunteers would respond similarly.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Cost is not part of the argument. | Trap (B): Too strong: halving lost days does not require every employee to have back pain. | Trap (C): Irrelevant to whether the desks would work for all staff.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Assumption – Health – standing desks and back pain

options.A: The standing desks used in the trial were made by a well-known manufacturer of office furniture.
options.B: A randomised trial with doctor-assessed pain found no difference between the groups.
options.C: Some of the volunteers said that their standing desks took up more space than their old desks had.
options.D: Days lost to back pain at the company have risen slightly in each of the last three years.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A randomised trial with objective measurement removes the self-selection, self-reporting and expectation effects the physiotherapist raised, and it finds no benefit.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The maker's reputation says nothing about the desks' effect. | Trap (C): Space is irrelevant to back pain. | Trap (D): This shows a problem exists, not that the desks would fix it.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Weaken – Health – standing desks and back pain

options.A: suggest that any benefit must be weighed against new harms
options.B: show that the volunteers did not in fact experience any reduction in their lower-back pain during the trial
options.C: prove that the trial was not designed by a qualified medical professional
options.D: explain why the comparison group reported less improvement than the standing-desk group did

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Her other points question the evidence for the benefit; this one adds that even a real benefit may come with costs.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): It concerns other harms, not whether back pain fell. | Trap (C): It says nothing about who designed the trial. | Trap (D): It does not address the comparison group.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Role of statement – Health – standing desks and back pain
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: 'Weighed against new harms' is an interpretive key.

Argument 3:

A technology company gave standing desks to 150 volunteers among its office staff. After six months, 62 per cent of them reported less lower-back pain than before, compared with 35 per cent of 150 colleagues who kept ordinary desks. The company's wellness head now proposes buying standing desks for all 3,000 office staff, saying that this will halve the number of days lost to back pain. A physiotherapist consulted by the company points out that the volunteers were people who had asked for standing desks, many of them because they already suffered from back pain and were keen to try something new. She adds that the improvement was self-reported, that the volunteers knew they were part of a trial, and that standing for long periods causes problems of its own, such as varicose veins and foot pain.

Question: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating whether the trial supports the wellness head's proposal?

options.A: Whether the company's competitors have also bought standing desks for their own office staff
options.B: Whether the standing desks used in the trial could be adjusted to different heights for different employees
options.C: Whether the wellness head has personally used a standing desk at work for some period of time
options.D: Whether volunteers and non-volunteers had similar back pain at the start of the trial

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If the volunteers started with more pain, they had more room to improve (and more motivation to report improvement), which would inflate the gap.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): What competitors do does not show whether the desks work. | Trap (B): Relevant to comfort, but it does not test whether the comparison was fair. | Trap (C): Her personal use is irrelevant to the evidence.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Evaluate – Health – standing desks and back pain

questions.question_text:
Argument 4:

The government of Meghpur paid 40 per cent of the cost of rooftop solar panels for households that installed them over the past three years. About 90,000 households took up the subsidy, and the state's energy minister reports that they now generate enough electricity to save the state's power utility the equivalent of one small coal plant. She proposes doubling the subsidy budget, predicting that this will double the number of households with panels and allow the state to cancel a planned new coal plant. An economist argues that the minister's prediction is too optimistic. Most of the households that took the subsidy, he notes, were well-off homeowners with large, sunny roofs who might have installed panels even without help. The remaining households are mostly tenants, who cannot install panels on roofs they do not own, or residents of apartment blocks with shared roofs, where every owner must agree before anything is installed.

Question: Which of the following best states the economist's main conclusion?

options.A: Doubling the subsidy is unlikely to double the number of households with panels.
options.B: The state should build the planned coal plant rather than spend more money on any rooftop solar subsidy.
options.C: The subsidy over the past three years was wasted, because none of the 90,000 households needed any help at all.
options.D: Tenants should be given legal rights to install solar panels on the roofs of the buildings they live in.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: His points about who took the subsidy and who remains explain why more money will not bring a proportional rise in uptake.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): He criticises the forecast; he does not recommend the coal plant. | Trap (C): Overstated: he says many 'might have' installed anyway, not that none needed help. | Trap (D): He identifies a barrier but proposes no remedy.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Main point – Energy – rooftop solar subsidy

About 90,000 households took up the subsidy, and the state's energy minister reports that they now generate enough electricity to save the state's power utility the equivalent of one small coal plant. options.A: Many well-off homeowners who installed panels say they would have done so even without the subsidy.
options.B: The state's demand for electricity is forecast to rise steadily over the next decade as incomes increase.
options.C: A new law lets apartment blocks install panels by majority vote and gives landlords the subsidy.
options.D: Households with rooftop panels have lower monthly electricity bills than households without them.

questions.question_text:
Argument 5:

A study of 600 ten-year-olds in the city of Dharampur found that children who spoke two languages at home scored, on average, 12 per cent higher on a test of attention control than children who spoke only one. A newspaper reported the study under the headline "Learning a second language sharpens children's minds" and urged parents to send their children to weekend language classes. One of the researchers wrote to the newspaper to object. In Dharampur, she explained, the bilingual children came mostly from families of teachers and civil servants who had moved to the city from other states, while the monolingual children came from a wider range of backgrounds, including many families in which neither parent had finished school. Moreover, the bilingual children in the study had spoken both languages from birth; the study included no children who had learnt a second language in weekend classes.

Question: The researcher's letter mainly argues that:

options.A: the study does not justify the newspaper's headline or its advice
options.B: the attention-control test used in the study was badly designed and should not be used again
options.C: bilingual children in Dharampur have poorer attention control than monolingual children once family background is considered
options.D: weekend language classes are harmful to the development of ten-year-old children

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Both her points (the families differ, and no child learnt a language in weekend classes) undercut the step from the finding to the headline and advice.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): She does not criticise the test itself. | Trap (C): She suggests family background may explain the gap, not that it reverses it. | Trap (D): She does not say the classes do harm.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Main point – Science – bilingual children and attention

Argument 5:

A study of 600 ten-year-olds in the city of Dharampur found that children who spoke two languages at home scored, on average, 12 per cent higher on a test of attention control than children who spoke only one. A newspaper reported the study under the headline "Learning a second language sharpens children's minds" and urged parents to send their children to weekend language classes. One of the researchers wrote to the newspaper to object. In Dharampur, she explained, the bilingual children came mostly from families of teachers and civil servants who had moved to the city from other states, while the monolingual children came from a wider range of backgrounds, including many families in which neither parent had finished school. Moreover, the bilingual children in the study had spoken both languages from birth; the study included no children who had learnt a second language in weekend classes.

Question: The newspaper's advice to parents assumes that:

options.A: the children in the study were representative of all ten-year-old children throughout the whole country
options.B: learning a language in weekend classes brings the same benefit as growing up bilingual
options.C: attention control is the most important skill a ten-year-old child can have
options.D: parents in Dharampur can afford weekend language classes for their children

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The study covered only children bilingual from birth; recommending weekend classes assumes the effect carries over to that very different route.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Too broad: the advice needs a transfer to weekend learners, not national representativeness. | Trap (C): The advice needs only that it is a benefit, not the most important one. | Trap (D): Affordability is not required for the claim that the classes would help.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Assumption – Science – bilingual children and attention

questions.question_text:
Argument 5:

A study of 600 ten-year-olds in the city of Dharampur found that children who spoke two languages at home scored, on average, 12 per cent higher on a test of attention control than children who spoke only one. A newspaper reported the study under the headline "Learning a second language sharpens children's minds" and urged parents to send their children to weekend language classes. One of the researchers wrote to the newspaper to object. In Dharampur, she explained, the bilingual children came mostly from families of teachers and civil servants who had moved to the city from other states, while the monolingual children came from a wider range of backgrounds, including many families in which neither parent had finished school. Moreover, the bilingual children in the study had spoken both languages from birth; the study included no children who had learnt a second language in weekend classes.

Question: The newspaper's headline is most vulnerable to which criticism?

options.A: It infers a causal effect from a difference that other factors may explain
options.B: It relies on a sample of 600 children, which is far too small to show any difference at all between two groups
options.C: It treats a 12 per cent difference as if it were a difference of more than 50 per cent
options.D: It assumes that the researchers were biased in favour of bilingual families when choosing whom to test

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Family background differs systematically between the groups, so the correlation does not show that speaking two languages caused better attention.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): 600 is not a tiny sample; the problem is confounding, not size. | Trap (C): The headline does not misstate the size. | Trap (D): The passage gives no hint of researcher bias.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Flaw – Science – bilingual children and attention

options.A: The number of weekend language classes in Dharampur has doubled over the past five years
options.B: Many teachers in Dharampur believe that bilingual children are better behaved in class than monolingual ones

options.A: Trees grown from seed in a park are healthy, but none was transplanted when mature, so the park's record cannot support transplanting mature trees.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Her second point is that the study included no one who acquired the trait by the route being recommended. The tree argument has exactly that structure.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): This is an appeal to popular belief, with no study at all. | Trap (C): This parallels her first objection (a confounder), not the second. | Trap (D): Again a confounding factor, which is her first objection.

questions.question_text:
Argument 6:

During the monsoon last year, ride-hailing fares in the city of Pravalgarh sometimes rose to four times the normal rate when heavy rain increased demand. After complaints from commuters, the city council capped fares at one and a half times the normal rate. A councillor who supported the cap says that it has been a success: since it took effect, the average fare paid by riders during rainstorms has fallen by more than half. An economist disagrees. Surge pricing, he says, exists to persuade more drivers to come out in bad weather, and to ration rides to those who need them most. Since the cap, he reports, the number of drivers on the road during rainstorms has fallen by 30 per cent and the average waiting time for a ride has risen from eight minutes to thirty-five. Many riders, he adds, now cannot get a ride at all during storms and walk or wait in the rain.

Question: The economist challenges the councillor's claim of success mainly by:

options.A: pointing to costs the councillor's measure of success leaves out
options.B: arguing that commuters had no real reason to complain about fares during last year's monsoon
options.C: showing that the cap was introduced without a proper vote in the city council
options.D: disputing that the average fare paid by riders during rainstorms has actually fallen since the cap took effect

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Fewer drivers, longer waits and riders unable to get a ride are costs that the average fare paid does not capture.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): He does not address whether the complaints were justified. | Trap (C): Procedure is never mentioned. | Trap (D): He does not dispute the fall in fares.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Method – Economics – cap on surge pricing

options.B: ride-hailing companies will eventually stop operating in Pravalgarh if the cap stays in place
options.C: drivers in Pravalgarh were earning too much money before the cap was introduced by the council

options.A: Prices should always be set so that companies earn the largest profit possible from each ride

options.C: A price rule should be judged by its effect on all who need the service, including those it leaves unserved.

questions.concept_tag: LR – Principle – Economics – cap on surge pricing

questions.question_text:
Argument 7:

Two years ago, the state of Aranya made it compulsory for parties in property and family disputes to attempt mediation before filing a civil suit. Since then, the number of such suits filed in the state's courts has fallen by 45 per cent. The state's law minister cites this as proof that compulsory mediation resolves most disputes without litigation and proposes extending it to all civil disputes, including commercial contracts and claims against the government. A senior advocate questions the minister's reasoning. Filing fees for civil suits in Aranya were tripled in the same year that mediation became compulsory, she points out, and many litigants who cannot afford to go to court now simply abandon their claims. She adds that in claims against the government, the government is itself a party, and its officials rarely have the authority to agree to a settlement in mediation.

Question: The law minister's conclusion that mediation 'resolves most disputes' assumes that:

options.A: all disputes resolved through mediation in Aranya have been resolved fairly to both of the parties involved
options.B: commercial contract disputes are more common in Aranya than property and family disputes
options.C: the fall in suits mostly reflects disputes settled in mediation, not claims dropped
options.D: the filing fees for civil suits in Aranya were not changed at any point in the last two years

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A fall in suits shows resolution through mediation only if the missing suits were settled rather than abandoned.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Fairness is not part of the minister's claim about numbers. | Trap (B): Relative frequency does not bear on whether mediation resolved the disputes. | Trap (D): Too strong: the minister needs only that settlements, not fees, explain most of the fall.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Assumption – Law – compulsory mediation before civil suits

options.B: Records show that fewer than a fifth of mediations in property and family disputes ended in a settlement.

questions.question_text:
Argument 8:

After the municipal corporation of Sitapur replaced old street lamps with bright LED lights in fifty of the city's wards, the police recorded 22 per cent fewer night-time thefts in those wards over the next year, while thefts in the city's other wards fell by only 3 per cent. A corporation official argues that better lighting deters thieves and wants LED lights installed in every ward. A criminologist agrees that lighting may deter some crime but warns against drawing firm conclusions. The fifty wards, she notes, were chosen for the first phase because their residents' welfare associations had petitioned the corporation, and many of those associations also hired private night guards that year. She also notes that police recorded thefts only when victims reported them, and that reporting rates differ between wards.

Question: The criminologist's main point is that:

options.A: the police in Sitapur deliberately under-record thefts in the city's poorer wards
options.B: residents' welfare associations should not hire private night guards to protect their neighbourhoods
options.C: better street lighting has no effect whatever on the number of thefts committed at night in any ward
options.D: the drop in thefts may not be due mainly to the new lights

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Guards, selection by petition and uneven reporting are all reasons why the gap may not be caused by the lights.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): She notes reporting rates differ, not deliberate under-recording. | Trap (B): She mentions the guards only as an alternative explanation. | Trap (C): She accepts that lighting 'may deter some crime'.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Main point – Urban safety – street lighting and crime

options.A: the police recording more thefts in the city's other wards than actually took place in them
options.B: thieves moving from the fifty wards into neighbouring wards where the lights had not yet been installed
options.C: the corporation installing lights of a lower quality in some of the fifty wards than in the others
options.D: differences between the wards that sought the lights and those that did not

questions.question_text:
Argument 9:

A ten-year study followed 50,000 adults in the country of Kesaria and found that those who drank three or more cups of coffee a day were 15 per cent less likely to die during the study period than those who drank none. A popular health website reported the study under the headline "Three cups a day keep the doctor away" and advised readers to increase their coffee intake. The study's lead author has cautioned against this advice. People who drank no coffee at all, she points out, included many who had given it up on their doctors' advice because they already had heart problems, high blood pressure or stomach disorders. She also notes that the study recorded coffee drinking only once, at the start, and did not track whether participants changed their habits during the ten years.

Question: The website's advice to drink more coffee assumes that:

options.A: the study's lead author does not herself drink any coffee at all
options.B: the coffee drinkers' lower death rate was caused at least in part by the coffee
options.C: everyone who drinks three cups of coffee a day will live longer than everyone who drinks none

Argument 9:

A ten-year study followed 50,000 adults in the country of Kesaria and found that those who drank three or more cups of coffee a day were 15 per cent less likely to die during the study period than those who drank none. A popular health website reported the study under the headline "Three cups a day keep the doctor away" and advised readers to increase their coffee intake. The study's lead author has cautioned against this advice. People who drank no coffee at all, she points out, included many who had given it up on their doctors' advice because they already had heart problems, high blood pressure or stomach disorders. She also notes that the study recorded coffee drinking only once, at the start, and did not track whether participants changed their habits during the ten years.

Question: The lead author's first point suggests that the comparison may be distorted because:

options.A: coffee drinkers in Kesaria tend to be wealthier than people who drink only tea instead
options.B: some non-drinkers avoided coffee because they were already ill
options.C: people who drink coffee tend to sleep less than those who do not drink any coffee at all
options.D: the study included too few people who drank more than three cups of coffee a day to be useful

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If the no-coffee group contains people who quit because of illness, their higher death rate reflects that illness, not the absence of coffee: reverse causation.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Wealth is not mentioned, and tea drinkers are not the comparison group. | Trap (C): Sleep is never mentioned. | Trap (D): Sample size for heavy drinkers is not her point.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Flaw – Health – coffee and longevity

options.A: Coffee is the second most widely consumed drink in Kesaria after tea
options.B: Excluding those who quit on medical advice, the groups' death rates were nearly equal.
options.C: The study was paid for by a government health research council rather than by a coffee company

Question: Which of the following arguments contains the flaw most similar to the website's?

options.A: A survey found that people who exercise sleep better, so the survey's authors plan to study whether exercise improves sleep.
options.B: Doctors recommend regular exercise, so everyone in the town should begin to exercise regularly every single morning.
options.C: A school's results improved after it hired new teachers, so the school will keep the new teachers next year.

questions.review_note: Faculty flag: Parallel rests on reverse causation; faculty may want it explicit in the stem.

Argument 10:

When the government of Rajmahal abolished entry fees at its five state museums, the number of visits rose by 70 per cent in the first year. The culture minister hailed the policy as a success in "bringing art to people who could never afford it" and proposes extending free entry to state-run monuments and archaeological sites. A museum economist questions this claim. Visitor surveys at the museums, he says, show that the share of visitors from low-income households is almost unchanged since entry became free; most of the extra visits were made by people who already visited the museums regularly and now come more often. He also notes that the museums used to earn 18 per cent of their budget from entry fees, and that since the fees were abolished two museums have shortened their opening hours and one has closed a gallery.

Question: The museum economist's main conclusion is that:

options.A: the rise in visits does not show that free entry reached people who could not afford it
options.B: the number of museum visits in Rajmahal has not actually risen since the entry fees were abolished
options.C: low-income households in Rajmahal have no interest in art or museums
options.D: entry fees should immediately be restored at all five state museums in Rajmahal to protect their budgets

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Surveys show the low-income share unchanged and the extra visits made by regular visitors, which undercuts the minister's claim.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): He accepts the rise and explains who made the extra visits. | Trap (C): He reports their share is unchanged, not that they lack interest. | Trap (D): He reports the budget effects but recommends nothing.
questions.concept_tag: LR – Main point – Culture – free entry to museums

questions.question_text:
Passage 1: Constitutional morality is one of those phrases that sounds grand in a courtroom and evaporates the moment one tries to pin it down. Its champions describe it as the spirit behind the text: a commitment to liberty, equality and dignity that should guide judges when the words of the document run out. Its critics reply that a spirit, unlike a text, can be summoned by anyone, and that judges who invoke it are often simply announcing their own preferences in a more respectable vocabulary.

Both camps tend to forget where the idea came from. When it entered Indian constitutional debate, constitutional morality was not a licence for judges at all. It described a habit expected of citizens and officials: a willingness to obey the forms of the constitution even when those forms produced results one disliked, to criticise those in power without seeking to overthrow them, and to accept that one's opponents were entitled to govern if they won. It was, in short, a discipline of restraint, and its chief audience was the political class, not the bench. The worry of the time was that a population newly freed from colonial rule, and divided by caste, language and religion, might treat the constitution as a set of rules to be honoured only when convenient.

Over the last two decades, the phrase has migrated. Courts now use it to test whether laws and social practices conform to the deeper values of the constitution, and in several notable cases it has been deployed against popular morality, the prevailing views of a majority, to protect individuals whose choices the majority condemned. There is something admirable in this. A constitution that protected only those whom the majority already tolerated would protect very little. The rights of the unpopular are precisely the rights that need a guardian.

Yet the migration carries a cost that its admirers rarely acknowledge. When constitutional morality becomes primarily a tool of judicial review, the original audience is let off the hook. Legislators come to believe that protecting minorities is the court's job rather than theirs; executives learn that they can pass doubtful measures and leave the cleaning up to judges; citizens learn to think of constitutional values as something handed down in judgments rather than practised in daily public life. A court can strike down a discriminatory law, but it cannot make a legislature want to write fair ones.

Nor is the judiciary well placed to carry the whole burden. Judges are few, unelected, and dependent for their authority on public acceptance of their rulings. The more often they are asked to substitute their reading of the constitution's spirit for the choices of elected bodies, the more their decisions will be seen as political, and the more fragile that acceptance becomes.

None of this means the courts should abandon the idea. It means the idea should be restored to its full scope. Constitutional morality is at its strongest when it is a shared expectation binding every institution, and at its weakest when it is a weapon wielded by one institution against the others. The aim should be a polity in which judges rarely need to invoke it, because everyone else already does.

Question: Which of the following best captures the primary purpose of the passage?

options.A: To argue that courts should stop using constitutional morality as a ground for striking down laws.
options.B: To trace how the meaning of constitutional morality has changed over the decades, without evaluating that change.
options.C: To argue that constitutional morality, now used mainly by courts, should again be understood as a discipline binding all institutions and citizens.
options.D: To defend popular morality against judicial attempts to override the views of the majority.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage moves from the idea's original meaning ('a discipline of restraint, and its chief audience was the political class, not the bench') to its 'migration' into the courts, names the cost of that shift, and ends: 'the idea should be restored to its full scope... a shared expectation binding every institution.' Only C captures this complete arc of describe, evaluate and recommend.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Too extreme – the last paragraph says 'None of this means the courts should abandon the idea.' | Trap (B): Partially true but incomplete – the passage does trace the shift, but it clearly evaluates it ('carries a cost') and proposes a remedy. | Trap (D): Reverses the author's view – the author calls judicial protection of the unpopular 'admirable' and never defends popular morality.

options.A: political actors and citizens might respect the constitution's rules only when those rules served their interests.
options.B: judges would use vague constitutional values to override elected legislatures.
options.C: majority opinion would be used to condemn the private choices of unpopular individuals.
options.D: the constitution's text would prove too detailed to adapt to changing circumstances.

Nor is the judiciary well placed to carry the whole burden. Judges are few, unelected, and dependent for their authority on public acceptance of their rulings. The more often they are asked to substitute their reading of the constitution's spirit for the choices of elected bodies, the more their decisions will be seen as political, and the more fragile that acceptance becomes.

None of this means the courts should abandon the idea. It means the idea should be restored to its full scope. Constitutional morality is at its strongest when it is a shared expectation binding every institution, and at its weakest when it is a weapon wielded by one institution against the others. The aim should be a polity in which judges rarely need to invoke it, because everyone else already does.

Question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument about the cost of the phrase's 'migration'?

options.A: In states where courts frequently struck down discriminatory laws, legislators became less likely to debate the constitutionality of bills before passing them.
options.B: Most citizens say in surveys that they trust the judiciary more than the legislature.
options.C: Several judgments invoking constitutional morality were later praised by legal scholars for protecting minorities.
options.D: In countries where courts rarely invoke constitutional values, legislatures pass laws protecting minorities at about the same rate as in countries where courts invoke them often.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The cost is described in paragraph 4: 'Legislators come to believe that protecting minorities is the court's job rather than theirs... A court can strike down a discriminatory law, but it cannot make a legislature want to write fair ones.' Paragraph 5 adds that judges cannot 'carry the whole burden.' Option A gives direct evidence that frequent judicial correction makes legislators less careful, which is exactly the predicted abdication. D is the close trap, but it points the other way.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Irrelevant, or mildly weakening – high trust in the judiciary cuts against the paragraph 5 worry that judicial authority is 'fragile'; it does not show any cost. | Trap (C): Supports the wrong half – it confirms the 'admirable' side (paragraph 3), not the cost the question asks about. | Trap (D): Weakens – if legislatures behave the same whether or not courts are active, judicial activism is not making them abdicate responsibility.

questions.question_text:
Passage 2: Every round of climate negotiations rehearses the same quarrel. Industrialised countries, having burned through most of the atmosphere's safe carbon budget during two centuries of growth, ask developing economies to grow differently. Developing economies answer that they are being asked to climb a ladder whose rungs have been sawn off by the very people who used it. The quarrel is usually staged as a contest between justice and survival, and each side accuses the other of choosing the wrong one.

This framing, though emotionally powerful, has become an obstacle. It assumes that development and decarbonisation are locked in a fixed trade-off, so that every tonne of emissions avoided is a unit of prosperity forgone. That assumption was broadly true when coal was the cheapest way to light a city. It is far less true now. In much of the tropical world, new solar capacity is cheaper to build than new coal plants, and a factory powered by sunlight is not obviously poorer than one powered by smoke. The question facing a developing country today is less whether it can afford clean energy than whether it can afford the financing to build it quickly.

Here the old quarrel returns, but in a more useful form. Clean energy is cheap to run and expensive to install; nearly all of its cost is paid upfront. A coal plant, by contrast, spreads its cost over decades of fuel purchases. This means that the price of capital, the interest rate a country must pay to borrow, matters enormously. A solar farm in a country that borrows at three per cent may produce power at half the cost of an identical farm in a country that borrows at twelve. Poorer nations, judged riskier by lenders, pay the higher rates. The effect is perverse: the countries with the strongest sunlight and the greatest need for new power face the steepest barriers to using it.

Seen this way, the duty of wealthy nations is not mainly to donate money or to lecture others about restraint. It is to reduce the cost of capital for clean investment in poorer regions, through guarantees, shared risk and reforms to the lending institutions they control. Such measures cost far less than outright grants, and they align the interests of lenders, governments and the climate in a way that appeals to virtue rarely achieve.

None of this dissolves the moral debt that historical emitters owe. But a debt is best repaid in the currency the creditor actually needs. Developing countries do not need permission to grow, nor sermons about the planet; they need the same access to cheap finance that allowed today's rich countries to build their infrastructure in the first place. A negotiation that focused on interest rates rather than blame would be less dramatic. It might also, for the first time, be productive.

The cruel irony of the present arrangement is that it punishes the very countries best positioned to leapfrog fossil fuels altogether. Correcting it requires less moral exhortation and more attention to the unglamorous plumbing of global finance.

Question: The central argument of the passage is that:

options.A: developing countries should be exempt from emission-reduction obligations until they reach the income levels of industrialised nations.
options.B: the conflict between climate action and development is best addressed by lowering the cost of finance for clean energy in poorer countries rather than by arguing over blame.
options.C: solar power has made fossil fuels obsolete in every part of the world.
options.D: industrialised countries owe no moral debt for their historical emissions.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author says the duty of wealthy nations 'is to reduce the cost of capital for clean investment in poorer regions' and that 'A negotiation that focused on interest rates rather than blame would be less dramatic. It might also, for the first time, be productive.' B states this thesis.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Out of scope – the author never proposes exemptions; the argument is about financing clean growth. | Trap (C): Too extreme – the passage says solar is cheaper 'in much of the tropical world', not everywhere. | Trap (D): Reverses the author's view – 'None of this dissolves the moral debt that historical emitters owe.'

Question: Based on the passage, which of the following can most reasonably be inferred about a coal plant and a solar farm built in a country that must borrow at a high interest rate?

options.A: The coal plant will always cost more to operate over its lifetime than the solar farm.
options.B: The high interest rate affects both projects equally, since both must be financed.
options.C: The solar farm will have higher running costs than the coal plant.
options.D: The high interest rate erodes the solar farm's cost advantage more than the coal plant's, because a far larger share of the solar farm's cost must be paid upfront.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Combine paragraph 2 ('new solar capacity is cheaper to build than new coal plants') with paragraph 3 ('nearly all of its cost is paid upfront... the price of capital... matters enormously. A solar farm in a country that borrows at three per cent may produce power at half the cost of an identical farm in a country that borrows at twelve'). A high rate therefore hurts the upfront-heavy solar farm most, eroding its advantage. A is the close trap because it overstates solar's edge with 'always'.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Too absolute – the passage makes no 'always' claim, and paragraph 3 implies high interest can make solar power much costlier. | Trap (B): Ignores the key contrast – paragraph 3 says a coal plant 'spreads its cost over decades of fuel purchases', so capital costs weigh far less on it. | Trap (C): Reverses a stated fact – 'Clean energy is cheap to run and expensive to install.'

Question: The author's attitude towards the conventional 'justice versus survival' framing of climate negotiations is best described as:

options.A: critical but understanding: the author acknowledges its emotional force while arguing that it has become an obstacle.
options.B: contemptuous, treating it as dishonest posturing by both sides.
options.C: nostalgic, wishing negotiations could return to it.
options.D: wholly approving, seeing it as the moral core of the debate.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 2 opens: 'This framing, though emotionally powerful, has become an obstacle.' The concession ('emotionally powerful') together with the criticism ('obstacle') shows critical but understanding disapproval, so A is correct.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Too extreme – the author never calls either side dishonest and grants that the framing is 'emotionally powerful.' | Trap (C): Reverses the author's view – the author wants to move beyond the framing, not back to it. | Trap (D): Reverses the author's view – the author says the framing 'has become an obstacle.'

Question: According to the passage, why do poorer nations pay higher interest rates on borrowing for clean energy?

options.A: Because solar technology works less efficiently in tropical climates.
options.B: Because wealthy nations deliberately bar them from international lending institutions.
options.C: Because lenders judge them to be riskier borrowers.
options.D: Because clean energy projects take longer to build than coal plants.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 3 states directly: 'Poorer nations, judged riskier by lenders, pay the higher rates.' C restates this.

Question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's proposed solution?

options.A: Some wealthy nations have already offered grants for clean energy projects in developing countries.
options.B: The price of solar panels is expected to fall further over the next decade.
options.C: In many developing countries, the main obstacle to clean energy is not the cost of finance but the lack of transmission grids and land approvals, which cheaper loans would not address.
options.D: Coal plants in developing countries also depend on borrowed money for their initial construction.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author's remedy rests on the claim that the binding constraint is 'whether it can afford the financing to build it quickly' (paragraph 2) and that the duty of wealthy nations is 'to reduce the cost of capital' (paragraph 4). If the real bottleneck is grids and approvals, cheaper capital would not unlock clean energy, which undercuts the core of the proposal. D looks relevant but leaves the upfront-cost asymmetry intact.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Irrelevant – existing grants say nothing about whether lowering capital costs would work; the author already treats grants as a costlier, separate route. | Trap (B): Strengthens or is neutral – cheaper panels make clean energy more attractive and do not undermine the finance argument. | Trap (D): Close but insufficient – the passage already accepts that coal involves capital; its point is that coal 'spreads its cost over decades of fuel purchases', so solar remains far more sensitive to interest rates.

questions.question_text:
Passage 3: We are often told that privacy is dead, and that those who mourn it are nostalgic for a world that never really existed. The argument runs as follows: people freely hand over their locations, purchases and conversations in exchange for convenient services; they rarely read the terms they accept; and when offered a paid version of a product that collects less data, most decline. If people valued privacy as much as they claim, the argument concludes, their behaviour would show it.

This reasoning has the appeal of hard-headed realism, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what choice means. A choice is meaningful only when the person making it understands the options and has a realistic alternative. Neither condition is met in most digital transactions. The terms of service for a typical app run to thousands of words of legal prose, and a person who tried to read every agreement presented to them in a year would spend weeks doing nothing else. The alternative to accepting, meanwhile, is often exclusion from services that have become necessities: messaging platforms through which employers send instructions, maps without which a delivery worker cannot do her job, payment apps that small shops now prefer to cash.

More fundamentally, the 'people don't really care' argument treats privacy as a private good, something each individual trades for herself. But much of the data we surrender describes other people. When I upload my contacts, I disclose the phone numbers of friends who never consented. When I submit my genetic sample to a testing service, I reveal information about relatives who may not wish it known. And when millions of individuals each surrender a little information, companies can draw inferences about whole populations that no single disclosure would permit, predicting, for instance, which neighbourhoods are likely to default on loans or which groups are likely to protest. Privacy, in this sense, behaves less like a personal possession and more like clean air: its loss is shared, and no single person's decision to protect it is sufficient.

If this is right, then relying on individual consent as the main safeguard is a category error. We do not ask each citizen to negotiate the level of pollution a factory may emit; we set limits collectively, through law. Data protection deserves similar treatment. Rules limiting what may be collected, how long it may be kept, and for what purposes it may be used would protect people regardless of whether they had read the fine print. They would also relieve individuals of a burden that no one can realistically carry.

Critics warn that such rules would stifle innovation. Perhaps some business models would become unviable. But a business model that depends on people not understanding what is being done to them is not one a society is obliged to preserve. The real question is not whether privacy survives, but whether we continue to pretend that its fate rests on choices no one is truly in a position to make.

Question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Technology companies deliberately deceive users by writing lengthy terms of service.
options.B: Privacy is already dead, and efforts to protect it are merely nostalgic.
options.C: Individuals should read terms of service more carefully before accepting them.
options.D: Because individual consent cannot meaningfully protect privacy, which is partly a shared good, privacy should be safeguarded through collective legal limits.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author argues that consent fails because choices are not meaningful (paragraph 2) and that privacy 'behaves less like a personal possession and more like clean air' (paragraph 3), and concludes that 'relying on individual consent as the main safeguard is a category error... Data protection deserves similar treatment' to collective pollution limits (paragraph 4). D captures this.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Out of scope – the passage notes that the terms are long but makes no claim about deliberate deception. | Trap (B): Reverses the author's view – this is the position the author sets out to refute in paragraph 1. | Trap (C): Contradicts the passage – reading every agreement would take 'weeks', and the author wants to relieve individuals of 'a burden that no one can realistically carry.'
