Question: It can be inferred that the author regards a person's refusal to pay for a less data-hungry version of an app as weak evidence that the person is indifferent to privacy, primarily because:

options.A: paid versions of apps are usually of lower quality than free versions.
options.B: guarding one's own data achieves little when other people's disclosures can reveal information about one anyway, and when the terms involved are too complex to evaluate meaningfully.
options.C: people who refuse data collection are excluded from services that have become necessities.
options.D: most companies do not in fact offer paid, less data-hungry versions of their products.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Two strands must be combined. Paragraph 2 says a meaningful choice requires that the person 'understands the options', but terms 'run to thousands of words of legal prose.' Paragraph 3 says 'much of the data we surrender describes other people... no single person's decision to protect it is sufficient.' Together these explain why declining to pay for one's own privacy says little about how much one values privacy. C is the close trap: it is drawn from the passage, but it explains a different situation.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Out of scope – the passage never compares the quality of paid and free versions. | Trap (C): True but does not answer the question – exclusion explains why people accept data collection when there is no alternative; the scenario here offers an alternative (the paid version), so exclusion does not explain the refusal. | Trap (D): Contradicts the premise – the passage accepts that such versions are offered and that 'most decline.'

Question: The author's attitude towards critics who warn that data-protection rules would stifle innovation is best described as:

options.A: persuaded, conceding that such rules should be abandoned.
options.B: indifferent, treating their concern as irrelevant to the debate.
options.C: sceptical yet concessive: granting that some business models may fail while denying that such models deserve protection.
options.D: alarmed, fearing the economic damage such rules would cause.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 5: 'Perhaps some business models would become unviable' (a concession). 'But a business model that depends on people not understanding what is being done to them is not one a society is obliged to preserve' (a rejection of the critics' conclusion). This matches C.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Reverses the author's view – the author still calls for collective rules. | Trap (B): Wrong – the author engages with the concern directly and concedes part of it. | Trap (D): Reverses the author's view – the author accepts the possible loss of some business models with equanimity.

questions.question_text:
Passage 3: We are often told that privacy is dead, and that those who mourn it are nostalgic for a world that never really existed. The argument runs as follows: people freely hand over their locations, purchases and conversations in exchange for convenient services; they rarely read the terms they accept; and when offered a paid version of a product that collects less data, most decline. If people valued privacy as much as they claim, the argument concludes, their behaviour would show it.

This reasoning has the appeal of hard-headed realism, but it rests on a misunderstanding of what choice means. A choice is meaningful only when the person making it understands the options and has a realistic alternative. Neither condition is met in most digital transactions. The terms of service for a typical app run to thousands of words of legal prose, and a person who tried to read every agreement presented to them in a year would spend weeks doing nothing else. The alternative to accepting, meanwhile, is often exclusion from services that have become necessities: messaging platforms through which employers send instructions, maps without which a delivery worker cannot do her job, payment apps that small shops now prefer to cash.

More fundamentally, the 'people don't really care' argument treats privacy as a private good, something each individual trades for herself. But much of the data we surrender describes other people. When I upload my contacts, I disclose the phone numbers of friends who never consented. When I submit my genetic sample to a testing service, I reveal information about relatives who may not wish it known. And when millions of individuals each surrender a little information, companies can draw inferences about whole populations that no single disclosure would permit, predicting, for instance, which neighbourhoods are likely to default on loans or which groups are likely to protest. Privacy, in this sense, behaves less like a personal possession and more like clean air: its loss is shared, and no single person's decision to protect it is sufficient.

If this is right, then relying on individual consent as the main safeguard is a category error. We do not ask each citizen to negotiate the level of pollution a factory may emit; we set limits collectively, through law. Data protection deserves similar treatment. Rules limiting what may be collected, how long it may be kept, and for what purposes it may be used would protect people regardless of whether they had read the fine print. They would also relieve individuals of a burden that no one can realistically carry.

Critics warn that such rules would stifle innovation. Perhaps some business models would become unviable. But a business model that depends on people not understanding what is being done to them is not one a society is obliged to preserve. The real question is not whether privacy survives, but whether we continue to pretend that its fate rests on choices no one is truly in a position to make.

Question: In the passage, describing reliance on individual consent as a 'category error' suggests that this approach:

options.A: treats a collective problem as if it were a purely individual one.
options.B: is a minor procedural slip that can easily be corrected.
options.C: was originally designed for a different category of technology.
options.D: sorts consumers into categories for targeted advertising.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sentence follows the argument that privacy is shared 'like clean air' and continues: 'We do not ask each citizen to negotiate the level of pollution a factory may emit; we set limits collectively, through law.' The error is to treat a collective good as an individual one, so A is correct.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Understates the claim – a category error is a fundamental mistake of classification, not a minor slip. | Trap (C): Literal misreading – nothing suggests consent was designed for another technology. | Trap (D): Word-association trap – plays on 'category' but has nothing to do with the author's point.

Question: The author's comparison between data protection and limits on factory pollution depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.A: Factories and technology companies cause the same amount of harm to society.
options.B: Like pollution, the harms of data collection fall on people collectively in ways that individual decisions cannot adequately control.
options.C: Pollution laws have completely eliminated environmental harm.
options.D: Citizens prefer collective rules to individual choice in every area of life.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The analogy works only if data harms share pollution's key feature: 'its loss is shared, and no single person's decision to protect it is sufficient' (paragraph 3). That is why the author argues that 'we set limits collectively, through law' (paragraph 4). B states this necessary premise.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Too strong – the analogy needs the two harms to be similar in structure, not equal in size. | Trap (C): Too extreme – the analogy does not require pollution laws to be perfectly effective. | Trap (D): Too broad – the argument concerns only shared harms, not every area of life.

questions.question_text:
Passage 4: Few institutions in South Asia have proved as durable as the ones built to govern it from outside. The district, with its collector at the apex, the police thana, the revenue record, and the elaborate rules governing government service were designed in the nineteenth century to extract revenue and keep order in a territory whose people had no say in how they were ruled. More than seven decades after independence, they remain the skeleton of administration across much of the region.

The usual explanation for this persistence is inertia. New governments, the argument goes, had more urgent priorities than redesigning the machinery they inherited, and once a system is running, the cost of replacing it always seems greater than the cost of tolerating its defects. There is truth in this, but it is incomplete. Inertia explains why institutions are not abolished; it does not explain why they are so often actively defended.

A fuller account must recognise that colonial institutions, whatever their origins, created constituencies. The officers who staffed them acquired prestige and security; the procedures they followed became forms of expertise that only insiders could navigate; the records they kept became the basis on which property was claimed and inherited. By the time the colonial power departed, a large number of people had a stake in the system's survival, not because they admired the empire, but because their own positions depended on the machinery it had left behind. The nationalist elite that took power was itself drawn heavily from those trained in colonial schools and services. Dismantling the system would have meant dismantling much of its own authority.

This does not make the inherited institutions illegitimate, any more than a road is illegitimate because it was built by forced labour. Institutions acquire new meanings as new people use them for new purposes. The courts that once enforced imperial rule became, in time, forums where citizens challenged their own governments. The census, devised partly to classify and control, became a tool for directing welfare to the poor. To treat every inherited structure as a colonial relic to be swept away is to ignore how thoroughly it has been reworked.

Yet the opposite error is equally tempting. Some features of colonial administration were not neutral tools awaiting better users; they were designed around a basic distrust of the governed. The citizen approaching a government office as a supplicant, the official who answers upward to superiors rather than outward to the public, the presumption that every application is suspect until proven otherwise: these habits were written into procedures meant for a population that was to be managed rather than served. Changing who sits at the desk does not by itself change the logic of the desk.

The task, then, is neither to celebrate continuity nor to denounce it, but to sort the inheritance: to ask of each institution what it was built to do, what it now does, and whether the gap between the two has been genuinely closed.

Question: The primary purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: argue that colonial-era institutions should be judged neither as wholly illegitimate nor as wholly benign, but examined one by one for what they now do.
options.B: show that colonial institutions survived independence mainly because new governments were too busy to replace them.
options.C: call for the immediate abolition of colonial administrative structures in South Asia.
options.D: praise the colonial administration for building institutions that have stood the test of time.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The final paragraph states the purpose: 'The task, then, is neither to celebrate continuity nor to denounce it, but to sort the inheritance: to ask of each institution what it was built to do, what it now does...' Paragraphs 4 and 5 warn against the two opposite errors. A summarises this.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Partially true but rejected as incomplete – the author says the inertia explanation has 'truth in this, but it is incomplete.' | Trap (C): Too extreme – the author warns against treating 'every inherited structure as a colonial relic to be swept away.' | Trap (D): Reverses the author's view – the author says the task is 'neither to celebrate continuity nor to denounce it.'

Question: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about the nationalist elite that took power at independence?

options.A: It preserved colonial institutions because it admired the way the empire had governed.
options.B: It lacked the administrative skill needed to design an alternative system.
options.C: Its own authority was bound up with the inherited institutions, which helps explain why those institutions were actively defended rather than merely tolerated.
options.D: It was chiefly responsible for turning the courts into forums where citizens could challenge the government.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 2 sets the puzzle: inertia 'does not explain why they are so often actively defended.' Paragraph 3 answers it: 'The nationalist elite that took power was itself drawn heavily from those trained in colonial schools and services. Dismantling the system would have meant dismantling much of its own authority.' Linking the two gives C. A is the close trap because it confuses having a stake in the system with admiring the empire.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Contradicts the passage – people had a stake in the system's survival 'not because they admired the empire, but because their own positions depended on the machinery.' | Trap (B): Out of scope – the passage says nothing about any lack of skill; if anything, the elite was trained in colonial services. | Trap (D): Unsupported attribution – the passage says the courts became such forums 'in time', without crediting the elite.

Question: According to the passage, which of the following is an example of an inherited institution that came to serve a new purpose?

options.A: The police thana, which became a centre for community welfare.
options.B: The census, which came to be used to direct welfare to the poor.
options.C: The revenue record, which was abolished soon after independence.
options.D: The district collector's office, which began answering to the public rather than to superiors.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 4: 'The census, devised partly to classify and control, became a tool for directing welfare to the poor.' B is the only option the passage states.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Not stated – the thana is listed as a colonial institution, but no new purpose is given for it. | Trap (C): Contradicts the passage – the records 'became the basis on which property was claimed and inherited'; no abolition is mentioned. | Trap (D): Not stated, and contrary to paragraph 5 – the passage criticises officials who still answer 'upward to superiors.'

Question: The author's tone in the last three paragraphs of the passage is best described as:

options.A: celebratory of the achievements of colonial administration.
options.B: indignant and accusatory towards present-day officials.
options.C: resigned to the impossibility of institutional reform.
options.D: balanced and analytical, cautioning against both wholesale rejection and uncritical continuity.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 4 warns against treating every structure 'as a colonial relic to be swept away'; paragraph 5 says 'the opposite error is equally tempting'; paragraph 6 concludes 'neither to celebrate continuity nor to denounce it.' This even-handed weighing is balanced and analytical, so D is correct.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Reverses the author's view – the author says plainly that we should not 'celebrate continuity.' | Trap (B): Too extreme – the author criticises procedures and inherited habits, not individuals, and does so in measured terms. | Trap (C): Wrong – the author sets out a constructive task ('sort the inheritance'), which implies reform is possible.

Question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's claim that 'changing who sits at the desk does not by itself change the logic of the desk'?

options.A: Decades after independence, officials in offices that still follow unchanged colonial-era procedures treat applicants with the same presumption of suspicion, whatever the officials' own social backgrounds.
options.B: Many officials in post-independence administrations had been trained in colonial schools and services.
options.C: Courts in several former colonies have struck down laws dating from the colonial period.
options.D: Offices that recruited officials from more diverse social backgrounds became markedly more responsive to the public, even though their procedures were unchanged.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 5 says these habits of distrust 'were written into procedures' and concludes that new personnel alone will not change outcomes. A isolates the variable: the people differ, the procedures are the same, and the suspicion persists. That supports the claim. B is the close trap because it does not vary the personnel at all.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Close but off-target – it suggests the people at the desk did not change much, so it cannot show that changing the people fails to change the logic; it relates to the paragraph 3 point about constituencies. | Trap (C): Wrong direction – it illustrates institutions being reworked (paragraph 4), not procedural habits persisting. | Trap (D): Weakens – it shows that changing who sits at the desk did change behaviour.

questions.question_text:
Passage 5: Debates about inequality tend to circle a single number. Whether it is the share of national income captured by the richest one per cent or a coefficient summarising the whole distribution, the number rises or falls, and commentators draw conclusions about the health of the economy. This fixation is understandable, since numbers travel well, but it obscures the questions that actually matter to people living within the distribution.

Consider two societies with identical measured inequality. In the first, the children of poor parents have a reasonable chance of ending up in the middle or at the top; a gifted student from a village can become a surgeon, and the son of a factory owner may well end up driving a taxi. In the second, positions are effectively inherited: those born at the bottom stay there, and so do their grandchildren. A snapshot of income would show the two societies as equally unequal. Yet almost no one would regard them as morally equivalent, and few would choose to be born into the second without knowing where they would land.

This suggests that what troubles us about inequality is not merely the gap between rich and poor at a given moment but the rigidity of that gap over time. Static inequality can coexist with a sense of fairness if people believe that effort and talent are rewarded. Inequality that hardens into hereditary advantage corrodes that belief, and with it the willingness of citizens to accept the outcomes of markets at all.

The mechanisms by which advantage hardens are, for the most part, unglamorous. Wealthy families buy homes in neighbourhoods with good schools, and schools in turn raise the value of the homes. They pay for coaching that converts modest talent into high examination scores. They provide the unpaid internships, family contacts and financial cushions that allow their children to take risks, such as starting a business or switching careers, that poorer children cannot afford. None of these acts is sinister; each is simply what a loving parent with means would do. But their cumulative effect is to turn temporary advantage into a durable inheritance.

This has implications for policy. Measures aimed solely at narrowing the income gap in a given year, such as higher taxes on top earners or larger transfers to the poor, are valuable, but they may do little to loosen the grip of inherited position if the channels through which advantage passes remain open. A society concerned with mobility would pay at least as much attention to early childhood education, to the funding of schools in poor areas, to access to credit for first-generation entrepreneurs, and perhaps to the taxation of large inheritances, which convert one generation's success into the next generation's head start.

There is no formula that will produce perfect mobility, and no society has achieved it. But the choice of what to measure shapes the choice of what to fix. As long as debate remains fixed on a single annual figure, the slower and more consequential story of how fortunes pass from parents to children will go largely untold.

Question: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Income inequality is not a serious concern as long as markets reward effort.
options.B: Higher taxes on top earners are the most effective way of tackling inequality.
options.C: Debates about inequality should attend to how advantage persists across generations, not only to a single annual measure of income distribution.
options.D: Wealthy parents act unethically when they secure advantages for their children.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage opens by criticising the focus on 'a single number' and closes: 'As long as debate remains fixed on a single annual figure, the slower and more consequential story of how fortunes pass from parents to children will go largely untold.' C captures this.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Distortion – the author says static inequality 'can coexist with a sense of fairness', but does not dismiss inequality as unimportant. | Trap (B): Contradicts the passage – such measures 'may do little to loosen the grip of inherited position.' | Trap (D): Reverses the author's view – 'None of these acts is sinister; each is simply what a loving parent with means would do.'

questions.question_text:
Passage 5: Debates about inequality tend to circle a single number. Whether it is the share of national income captured by the richest one per cent or a coefficient summarising the whole distribution, the number rises or falls, and commentators draw conclusions about the health of the economy. This fixation is understandable, since numbers travel well, but it obscures the questions that actually matter to people living within the distribution.

Consider two societies with identical measured inequality. In the first, the children of poor parents have a reasonable chance of ending up in the middle or at the top; a gifted student from a village can become a surgeon, and the son of a factory owner may well end up driving a taxi. In the second, positions are effectively inherited: those born at the bottom stay there, and so do their grandchildren. A snapshot of income would show the two societies as equally unequal. Yet almost no one would regard them as morally equivalent, and few would choose to be born into the second without knowing where they would land.

This suggests that what troubles us about inequality is not merely the gap between rich and poor at a given moment but the rigidity of that gap over time. Static inequality can coexist with a sense of fairness if people believe that effort and talent are rewarded. Inequality that hardens into hereditary advantage corrodes that belief, and with it the willingness of citizens to accept the outcomes of markets at all.

The mechanisms by which advantage hardens are, for the most part, unglamorous. Wealthy families buy homes in neighbourhoods with good schools, and schools in turn raise the value of the homes. They pay for coaching that converts modest talent into high examination scores. They provide the unpaid internships, family contacts and financial cushions that allow their children to take risks, such as starting a business or switching careers, that poorer children cannot afford. None of these acts is sinister; each is simply what a loving parent with means would do. But their cumulative effect is to turn temporary advantage into a durable inheritance.

This has implications for policy. Measures aimed solely at narrowing the income gap in a given year, such as higher taxes on top earners or larger transfers to the poor, are valuable, but they may do little to loosen the grip of inherited position if the channels through which advantage passes remain open. A society concerned with mobility would pay at least as much attention to early childhood education, to the funding of schools in poor areas, to access to credit for first-generation entrepreneurs, and perhaps to the taxation of large inheritances, which convert one generation's success into the next generation's head start.

There is no formula that will produce perfect mobility, and no society has achieved it. But the choice of what to measure shapes the choice of what to fix. As long as debate remains fixed on a single annual figure, the slower and more consequential story of how fortunes pass from parents to children will go largely untold.

Question: The author's attitude towards wealthy parents who invest in their children's advantages can best be described as:

options.A: non-judgmental about their motives but concerned about the combined consequences of their actions.
options.B: openly condemnatory of their selfishness.
options.C: admiring, holding them up as a model for other parents.
options.D: indifferent, since their actions have no bearing on inequality.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 4: 'None of these acts is sinister; each is simply what a loving parent with means would do. But their cumulative effect is to turn temporary advantage into a durable inheritance.' The author excuses the motives but worries about the cumulative effect, so A is correct.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Too extreme – the author explicitly says their acts are not 'sinister.' | Trap (C): Out of scope – the author does not recommend their behaviour as a model. | Trap (D): Reverses the author's view – their acts 'turn temporary advantage into a durable inheritance.'

Question: Based on the passage, which of the following would the author most likely conclude from a report that a country's top one per cent income share has fallen over a decade?

options.A: That the country has become fairer in every morally relevant respect.
options.B: That the report, taken alone, cannot show whether children born poor in that country now have better prospects than before.
options.C: That the country's tax system must have become more progressive.
options.D: That inherited advantage in the country must have increased.

Question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author's suggestion that policies targeting the channels of inherited advantage are needed in addition to annual income redistribution?

options.A: Some wealthy families choose not to pay for coaching or internships for their children.
options.B: School-funding reforms in poor areas have sometimes failed to raise students' examination results.
options.C: Early childhood education programmes are expensive to administer.
options.D: In countries that sharply narrowed annual income gaps, intergenerational mobility rose by a comparable amount, with no change to schooling, credit or inheritance rules.

B is tempting but attacks only one example policy.

questions.question_text:
Passage 6: It has become fashionable to defend literature by its usefulness. Novels, we are told, build empathy; reading fiction makes people kinder, more tolerant, better at understanding minds unlike their own. Schools cite such claims when justifying literature in crowded syllabuses, and publishers print them on the covers of books. The defence is well meant, and it may even be partly true. But it concedes too much, and it may end by harming the thing it sets out to protect.

The difficulty begins with the evidence. Studies that claim to show fiction increasing empathy typically measure changes over hours or days, using tests that ask participants to identify emotions in photographs or to report how much they care about strangers. Whether such effects last, or translate into kinder conduct, is far less certain. History offers sobering counterexamples: some of the most cultivated readers of their age were also capable of great cruelty, and a deep familiarity with the literary canon has never been a reliable guide to moral character.

More troubling is what the empathy defence does to our expectations of books themselves. If the purpose of a novel is to make readers kinder, then the best novels will be those that most efficiently produce that effect: books with sympathetic protagonists, clear moral arcs, and suffering that invites pity without demanding much thought. Works that are difficult, ambiguous or unsettling, that invite us to inhabit the minds of the cruel or the indifferent, will seem less useful and therefore less worth reading. A theory meant to celebrate literature becomes a filter that excludes much of its most demanding achievement.

There is also something faintly insulting in the idea that we read in order to become better people, as though a novel were a vitamin to be swallowed for its benefits. Most serious readers would describe the experience differently. They read because a book offers a way of seeing that they could not have reached alone: a sentence that captures a feeling they had never named, a structure that rearranges their sense of time, a voice that is strange and yet persuasive. Such experiences may make them wiser, or they may not. Their value does not depend on the outcome.

None of this means literature has no social role. Books have shaped how societies understand themselves, given voice to people excluded from public life, and preserved memories that official histories preferred to forget. But these effects arise because literature is free to pursue truth as it finds it, not because it has been enlisted to produce a desired attitude. A literature required to justify itself by its moral results will soon learn to supply them, and in doing so will lose the very independence that made it worth defending.

The better defence is harder to print on a book cover. It is simply that literature is one of the ways human beings think, and that a society which stops reading difficult books has narrowed the range of what it is able to think at all.

Question: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to:

options.A: prove that reading fiction has no effect whatever on empathy.
options.B: argue that defending literature mainly by its capacity to build empathy is weakly supported and harmful to literature itself.
options.C: recommend that schools remove literature from their crowded syllabuses.
options.D: show that cultivated readers are generally crueller than those who do not read.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 1 states the thesis: the empathy defence 'concedes too much, and it may end by harming the thing it sets out to protect.' Paragraph 2 questions the evidence and paragraph 3 shows the harm ('becomes a filter that excludes much of its most demanding achievement'). B summarises this.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Too extreme – the author concedes the claim 'may even be partly true.' | Trap (C): Reverses the author's view – the author defends literature, only on different grounds. | Trap (D): Distortion – the author says only that cultivation 'has never been a reliable guide to moral character', not that readers are crueller.
questions.concept_tag: RC – Primary Purpose – Literature and Society

options.B: would be especially favoured by those who defend literature on grounds of empathy.
options.C: may have considerable literary value even if it does not make readers kinder, and risks being undervalued under the empathy defence.

questions.question_text:
Passage 7: When a new technology arrives that can alter the human body at its foundations, the first public reaction is usually to draw a line. Somatic gene editing, which changes the cells of a single patient and dies with that patient, is placed on the permitted side. Germline editing, which alters embryos, eggs or sperm so that the change passes to future generations, is placed on the forbidden side. The line is tidy, easy to explain, and reflects an intuition that most people share: it is one thing to treat a person who has consented, another to rewrite the inheritance of people who do not yet exist.

The intuition deserves respect, but the line it produces is less stable than it looks. Consider a couple who both carry a gene for a severe hereditary disease. Today they may use embryo screening to select an embryo that does not carry the condition, a practice widely accepted in many countries. If editing could correct the faulty gene in an embryo instead, the outcome for the child would be similar, and arguably the process would discard fewer embryos. It is not obvious why one procedure should be lawful and the other criminal, when both are aimed at the same end and affect future generations in the same way.

Opponents of germline editing usually respond with two arguments. The first concerns safety: editing tools remain imprecise, and changes intended for one gene can produce unintended effects elsewhere, effects that would then be inherited. This is a serious objection, but it is an objection to present techniques rather than to the principle. If the tools became reliably precise, the safety argument would weaken accordingly.

The second argument concerns the slope from therapy to enhancement. Once society accepts editing to prevent disease, the fear goes, it will soon accept editing to raise intelligence, height or athletic ability, producing a world in which advantage is engineered into the genome and inequality becomes biological. This objection is weightier, because it does not depend on technical progress; indeed, better tools would make it more pressing. Yet even here, the distinction between therapy and enhancement is not self-executing. A condition counts as a disease partly by social agreement, and that agreement shifts. The real question is not where the line falls but who is entitled to draw it, and through what process.

This suggests that the ethics of gene editing cannot be settled by scientists alone, or by a single dramatic prohibition. It requires institutions capable of deliberating case by case, with public participation and the power to revise their judgments as knowledge changes. Such institutions are slower and messier than a bright line. They are also more honest about the fact that the hardest questions here are not technical but political: questions about what kinds of people a society wishes to make possible, and who gets to decide.

A ban offers the comfort of certainty. What it cannot offer is a reason that will survive the next scientific advance.

Question: Which of the following best captures the main argument of the passage?

options.A: A fixed prohibition on germline editing rests on distinctions less stable than they appear, so the issue calls for ongoing, participatory deliberation.
options.B: Germline editing should be permitted immediately because it is equivalent to embryo screening.
options.C: Somatic gene editing is more dangerous than germline editing.

questions.question_text:
Passage 7: When a new technology arrives that can alter the human body at its foundations, the first public reaction is usually to draw a line. Somatic gene editing, which changes the cells of a single patient and dies with that patient, is placed on the permitted side. Germline editing, which alters embryos, eggs or sperm so that the change passes to future generations, is placed on the forbidden side. The line is tidy, easy to explain, and reflects an intuition that most people share: it is one thing to treat a person who has consented, another to rewrite the inheritance of people who do not yet exist.

The intuition deserves respect, but the line it produces is less stable than it looks. Consider a couple who both carry a gene for a severe hereditary disease. Today they may use embryo screening to select an embryo that does not carry the condition, a practice widely accepted in many countries. If editing could correct the faulty gene in an embryo instead, the outcome for the child would be similar, and arguably the process would discard fewer embryos. It is not obvious why one procedure should be lawful and the other criminal, when both are aimed at the same end and affect future generations in the same way.

Opponents of germline editing usually respond with two arguments. The first concerns safety: editing tools remain imprecise, and changes intended for one gene can produce unintended effects elsewhere, effects that would then be inherited. This is a serious objection, but it is an objection to present techniques rather than to the principle. If the tools became reliably precise, the safety argument would weaken accordingly.

The second argument concerns the slope from therapy to enhancement. Once society accepts editing to prevent disease, the fear goes, it will soon accept editing to raise intelligence, height or athletic ability, producing a world in which advantage is engineered into the genome and inequality becomes biological. This objection is weightier, because it does not depend on technical progress; indeed, better tools would make it more pressing. Yet even here, the distinction between therapy and enhancement is not self-executing. A condition counts as a disease partly by social agreement, and that agreement shifts. The real question is not where the line falls but who is entitled to draw it, and through what process.

This suggests that the ethics of gene editing cannot be settled by scientists alone, or by a single dramatic prohibition. It requires institutions capable of deliberating case by case, with public participation and the power to revise their judgments as knowledge changes. Such institutions are slower and messier than a bright line. They are also more honest about the fact that the hardest questions here are not technical but political: questions about what kinds of people a society wishes to make possible, and who gets to decide.

A ban offers the comfort of certainty. What it cannot offer is a reason that will survive the next scientific advance.

Question: According to the passage, why does the author regard the safety objection as less fundamental than the enhancement objection?

options.A: Because the safety concerns about editing tools have already been fully resolved.
options.B: Because the public does not care about the safety of new technologies.
options.C: Because unintended changes from editing are never inherited.
options.D: Because the safety objection targets present techniques and would weaken as tools improve, whereas the enhancement objection would grow more pressing with better tools.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 3: the safety objection 'is an objection to present techniques rather than to the principle. If the tools became reliably precise, the safety argument would weaken.' Paragraph 4: the enhancement objection 'is weightier, because it does not depend on technical progress; indeed, better tools would make it more pressing.' D combines the two.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Too extreme – the passage says the tools 'remain imprecise.' | Trap (B): Out of scope – public attitudes to safety are never discussed. | Trap (C): Contradicts the passage – unintended effects 'would then be inherited.'

Question: It can be inferred that the author discusses embryo screening primarily in order to:

options.A: recommend that embryo screening be banned along with germline editing.

questions.question_text:
Passage 8: India's cities are usually described as bursting at the seams. Images of crowded trains, flooded streets and sprawling informal settlements reinforce the impression that the country is urbanising too fast for its institutions to cope. The impression is half right. Indian cities are indeed straining, but the deeper problem may be that the country is not urbanising fast enough or, more precisely, that it refuses to recognise much of the urbanisation that has already happened.

Official statistics classify a settlement as urban only if it meets certain administrative or demographic criteria. Thousands of large villages on the edges of metropolitan regions have populations, densities and economies that look unmistakably urban: most residents work outside agriculture, commute to nearby cities, and live in multi-storey buildings. Yet because these settlements remain governed as villages, they lack the municipal institutions that cities possess: no planning authority, no sewerage system worth the name, no power to levy the property taxes that pay for roads and drains. Their growth is real; their governance is fictional.

This mismatch has consequences that extend well beyond the settlements themselves. Because they are unplanned, construction proceeds plot by plot, with no space reserved for future roads, parks or schools. When the city eventually expands to absorb them, retrofitting infrastructure costs many times what it would have cost to plan in advance. Floods worsen because natural drainage channels have been built over. Commutes lengthen because no one designed a network. The chaos so often blamed on urban growth is, in large part, the price of growth that was allowed to happen without being acknowledged.

Why does the classification persist? Part of the answer lies in incentives. Rural status brings access to certain subsidies and programmes, and lower taxes; local leaders may prefer to keep it. Part lies in an older political imagination, in which the village is the authentic heart of the nation and the city a necessary evil to be contained. Policies shaped by that imagination have often treated migration to cities as a problem to be slowed rather than a transition to be managed.

The alternative is not to romanticise cities. Urban life brings its own forms of exclusion, and the poorest migrants often bear the heaviest costs of congestion and pollution. But cities are also where productivity rises fastest, where rigid social hierarchies loosen most readily, and where public services can be delivered most cheaply per person. A country that wishes to reap these benefits must stop treating urbanisation as an accident and begin governing it as a certainty.

That would mean recognising urban areas where they actually exist, giving them elected governments with real powers and revenues, and planning infrastructure ahead of settlement rather than in pursuit of it. It would mean, in short, abandoning the pretence that the country is still essentially rural. The cities are coming whether or not they are counted. The only choice is whether they arrive planned or improvised.

Question: The main point of the passage is that:

options.A: India is urbanising too fast and should slow migration into its cities.
options.B: villages are the authentic heart of the nation and must be protected from urban growth.
options.C: urban life is superior to rural life in every respect.
options.D: much of the chaos in India's cities stems from a failure to recognise and govern urbanisation that has already occurred.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 1: the country 'refuses to recognise much of the urbanisation that has already happened.' Paragraph 3: 'The chaos so often blamed on urban growth is, in large part, the price of growth that was allowed to happen without being acknowledged.' D captures this.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Reverses the author's view – the author says the problem may be that the country 'is not urbanising fast enough' in recognised terms. | Trap (B): Reverses the author's view – this is the 'older political imagination' the author criticises. | Trap (C): Too extreme – 'The alternative is not to romanticise cities. Urban life brings its own forms of exclusion.'

Question: It can be inferred from the passage that if a large village on a city's edge were officially reclassified as urban early in its growth, the author would expect:

options.A: its residents to lose their jobs in agriculture at once.
options.B: the subsidies it receives to increase.
options.C: the eventual cost of providing it with roads and drainage to be lower than if reclassification came only after unplanned construction.
options.D: flooding in the area to stop altogether.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 2 says unrecognised settlements lack 'a planning authority' and taxing powers. Paragraph 3 says 'retrofitting infrastructure costs many times what it would have cost to plan in advance.' Paragraph 6 calls for 'planning infrastructure ahead of settlement.' Early reclassification brings planning sooner and therefore lower costs, which gives C. D is the close trap because its 'altogether' overreaches.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Out of scope – most residents of such villages already 'work outside agriculture'; reclassification changes governance, not jobs. | Trap (B): Reverses the passage – 'Rural status brings access to certain subsidies', so reclassification would more likely reduce them. | Trap (D): Too extreme – planning would reduce flooding caused by built-over drainage channels, but the passage supports no claim that floods would stop entirely.

Question: In the passage, the statement 'their governance is fictional' most nearly means that these settlements:

options.A: are formally governed as villages, a status that does not match their actual urban character.

options.B: Giving elected municipal governments real revenue powers in areas that are already urban in practice would help address problems usually blamed on urban growth itself.
options.C: The poorest migrants benefit most from congestion in cities.
options.D: Keeping rural status for villages on the edges of cities is justified because it keeps residents' taxes low.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 3 says chaos 'blamed on urban growth' is really the price of unrecognised growth; paragraph 2 says such places lack the 'power to levy the property taxes that pay for roads and drains'; paragraph 6 calls for 'elected governments with real powers and revenues.' Combining these supports B. D is the close trap: the author describes the tax incentive in paragraph 4 but does not endorse it.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Reverses the author's view – the author criticises treating migration as 'a problem to be slowed.' | Trap (C): Contradicts the passage – the poorest migrants 'often bear the heaviest costs of congestion and pollution.' | Trap (D): Close but wrong – the author mentions lower taxes as an incentive that explains why the classification persists, not as a justification; the author wants recognition and taxing powers.

questions.question_text:
Passage 9: For most of the twentieth century, the gravest threat to a free press was thought to be the censor. Governments that wished to control what citizens knew would ban newspapers, imprison editors and seize printing presses. Democracies defined themselves in opposition to such practices, and the measure of press freedom was largely the absence of state interference.

That measure now looks incomplete. In many democracies today, few journalists are jailed and no newspapers are banned, yet public understanding of shared facts appears to be fraying. The cause is not a shortage of information but an excess of it, distributed through platforms whose business depends on capturing attention. Content that provokes outrage, fear or tribal loyalty spreads faster and further than content that informs, and the systems that rank what people see learn to reward whatever keeps them scrolling. No censor is needed when careful reporting is simply drowned out.

This shift has weakened the economic foundation of serious journalism. Advertising revenue that once supported newsrooms has migrated to platforms that do not produce news but profit from distributing it. Local newspapers, which once reported on municipal budgets, court cases and school boards, have closed in large numbers. Where they disappear, studies suggest, fewer candidates contest local elections, public officials face less scrutiny, and the costs of government borrowing rise. A democracy can survive without a particular newspaper; it is far less clear that it can survive without the routine, unglamorous work of watching those in power.

The tempting response is to demand that platforms remove false or harmful content. Some moderation is necessary, but this remedy carries its own danger. It hands to private companies, or to governments directing them, the power to decide what counts as true, the very power that the older idea of press freedom was meant to deny. A rule written to suppress dangerous falsehoods today may be used to suppress inconvenient truths tomorrow, depending on who holds office.

A more durable approach would focus less on policing speech and more on rebuilding the conditions in which reliable information can compete. That might include public funding for local journalism, distributed at arm's length from government to protect editorial independence; transparency requirements obliging platforms to disclose how their ranking systems work; and investment in teaching citizens how to evaluate sources. None of these measures is dramatic, and none promises to restore a lost golden age, which, in truth, never existed, since the older press had its own biases and exclusions.

But democracy has never depended on citizens agreeing about everything. It depends on their sharing enough facts to disagree productively, and on institutions that make it costly for the powerful to lie. Protecting those conditions requires seeing that the threat has changed shape. The censor has not disappeared, but he has been joined by a subtler adversary: a marketplace that rewards attention over accuracy, and that can silence the truth without ever forbidding it.

Question: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of the passage?

options.A: To argue that governments should take control of social media platforms.
options.B: To celebrate the press of the twentieth century as a golden age.
options.C: To argue that threats to democratic information now come largely from attention-driven markets, calling for remedies beyond the traditional focus on state censorship.
options.D: To show that state censorship no longer exists anywhere.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage says the old measure of press freedom 'now looks incomplete' and ends: 'The censor has not disappeared, but he has been joined by a subtler adversary: a marketplace that rewards attention over accuracy.' It proposes remedies focused on 'rebuilding the conditions in which reliable information can compete.' C captures this.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Reverses the author's view – the author warns against handing governments 'the power to decide what counts as true.' | Trap (B): Contradicts the passage – the golden age 'never existed, since the older press had its own biases and exclusions.' | Trap (D): Too extreme – 'The censor has not disappeared.'

options.A: Some platforms have recently adjusted their ranking systems to promote news from established outlets.
options.B: Some local newspapers have reopened with funding from philanthropists.
options.C: In democracies where public understanding of shared facts has declined, investigations reveal that governments have been quietly pressuring platforms and media owners to suppress critical reporting.
options.D: Content that provokes outrage spreads faster than informative content on most platforms.

questions.question_text:
Passage 10: Commentators who announce the end of the international order have rarely been short of evidence. Great powers ignore rulings they dislike, trade agreements unravel, and multilateral bodies seem paralysed whenever their most powerful members disagree. From this, many conclude that the rules-based order built after the Second World War is collapsing, and that the world is returning to a condition in which the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.

The diagnosis is dramatic, but it confuses the visible failures of the system with its everyday functioning. Most of what international rules accomplish happens quietly. Ships pass through crowded straits according to agreed conventions; aircraft cross dozens of jurisdictions under common safety standards; postal services, telecommunications and the allocation of radio frequencies depend on cooperation so routine that it goes unnoticed. These arrangements survive great-power rivalry because every state, including the most powerful, benefits from their continuation. An order that is failing at the top may still be thriving underneath.

It is also worth asking what the supposed golden age actually looked like. The post-war institutions were designed by a handful of victorious states and reflected their interests. For decades, much of the world was represented in them only through colonial powers, and many of the rules that newly independent states inherited had been written without them. When such states now demand a larger voice, or decline to follow rules they had no part in making, their behaviour is often described as a threat to order. It might more accurately be described as a contest over whose order it is to be.

This reframing matters, because it changes what a sensible response looks like. If the problem is simply that rules are being broken, the remedy is enforcement: punish violators and restore discipline. But if the problem is that a large share of the world regards the existing rules as unrepresentative, enforcement may deepen the very resentment that weakens the system. A more durable order would require reforms to the institutions themselves: redistributing voting power, opening leadership positions, and allowing the rules to be revised by those now expected to obey them.

Such reforms would cost established powers some of their privileges, and they will resist them. Yet the alternative is not the preservation of the present arrangement; it is its gradual hollowing out, as rising states build parallel institutions in which they have the influence they are denied elsewhere. Some of that is already happening. The question is whether the old institutions adapt quickly enough to remain the main forum for cooperation, or whether they survive merely as formalities while real decisions move elsewhere.

The international order, in other words, is neither collapsing nor secure. It is being renegotiated. Those who insist on describing every challenge as a breakdown may find that, by refusing to negotiate, they bring about the very collapse they fear.

Question: The primary purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: challenge the view that the international order is collapsing, arguing instead that it is being renegotiated and needs institutional reform.
options.B: show that great powers routinely ignore international rulings they dislike.
options.C: argue that rising states should build parallel international institutions of their own.
options.D: defend the post-war international order as fair and representative.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The author says the collapse diagnosis 'confuses the visible failures of the system with its everyday functioning', calls for 'reforms to the institutions themselves', and concludes: 'The international order... is neither collapsing nor secure. It is being renegotiated.' A captures this.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): True but not the purpose – this is evidence cited by the commentators the author argues against (paragraph 1). | Trap (C): Out of scope – the author describes parallel institutions as a risk of failing to reform ('hollowing out'), not as a recommendation. | Trap (D): Reverses the author's view – the post-war institutions 'were designed by a handful of victorious states and reflected their interests.'

questions.question_text:
Passage 10: Commentators who announce the end of the international order have rarely been short of evidence. Great powers ignore rulings they dislike, trade agreements unravel, and multilateral bodies seem paralysed whenever their most powerful members disagree. From this, many conclude that the rules-based order built after the Second World War is collapsing, and that the world is returning to a condition in which the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.

The diagnosis is dramatic, but it confuses the visible failures of the system with its everyday functioning. Most of what international rules accomplish happens quietly. Ships pass through crowded straits according to agreed conventions; aircraft cross dozens of jurisdictions under common safety standards; postal services, telecommunications and the allocation of radio frequencies depend on cooperation so routine that it goes unnoticed. These arrangements survive great-power rivalry because every state, including the most powerful, benefits from their continuation. An order that is failing at the top may still be thriving underneath.

It is also worth asking what the supposed golden age actually looked like. The post-war institutions were designed by a handful of victorious states and reflected their interests. For decades, much of the world was represented in them only through colonial powers, and many of the rules that newly independent states inherited had been written without them. When such states now demand a larger voice, or decline to follow rules they had no part in making, their behaviour is often described as a threat to order. It might more accurately be described as a contest over whose order it is to be.

This reframing matters, because it changes what a sensible response looks like. If the problem is simply that rules are being broken, the remedy is enforcement: punish violators and restore discipline. But if the problem is that a large share of the world regards the existing rules as unrepresentative, enforcement may deepen the very resentment that weakens the system. A more durable order would require reforms to the institutions themselves: redistributing voting power, opening leadership positions, and allowing the rules to be revised by those now expected to obey them.

Such reforms would cost established powers some of their privileges, and they will resist them. Yet the alternative is not the preservation of the present arrangement; it is its gradual hollowing out, as rising states build parallel institutions in which they have the influence they are denied elsewhere. Some of that is already happening. The question is whether the old institutions adapt quickly enough to remain the main forum for cooperation, or whether they survive merely as formalities while real decisions move elsewhere.

The international order, in other words, is neither collapsing nor secure. It is being renegotiated. Those who insist on describing every challenge as a breakdown may find that, by refusing to negotiate, they bring about the very collapse they fear.

Question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's explanation of why some states decline to follow existing international rules?

options.A: Great powers frequently disagree with one another within multilateral bodies.
options.B: International conventions on shipping and aviation continue to function despite great-power rivalry.
options.C: Some states defy international rules because doing so brings them short-term economic gains, regardless of who wrote the rules.
options.D: States that were given a greater role in revising particular international rules subsequently complied with those rules at markedly higher rates.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Paragraph 3 explains non-compliance by representation: states 'decline to follow rules they had no part in making.' Paragraph 4 proposes 'allowing the rules to be revised by those now expected to obey them.' D shows that giving states a voice raises compliance, which supports the representation explanation across both paragraphs.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): True but does not answer the question – great-power quarrels concern paralysis at the top, not why newer states decline to follow rules. | Trap (B): Supports a different claim – it backs paragraph 2's point that the order is 'thriving underneath', not the explanation for non-compliance. | Trap (C): Weakens – it offers an alternative explanation (self-interest) that has nothing to do with representation.

questions.question_text:
Passage 1: It is one of the most quoted sentences in Indian criminal law, and one of the least obeyed: bail is the rule and jail the exception. Judges repeat it in judgment after judgment. Yet roughly three out of every four prisoners in Indian jails are undertrials, people who have not been convicted of anything. Many of them will eventually be acquitted. Some will have spent longer in prison waiting for trial than they would have served had they been found guilty.

The gap between the maxim and the practice is not mainly a story of harsh judges. It is a story of small, ordinary frictions. An accused who is granted bail must often produce sureties, people of standing willing to vouch for him, and pay a bond he cannot afford. A migrant labourer arrested far from home may know no one who qualifies. A court may grant bail on conditions that are, for a poor person, as good as a refusal. The order looks generous on paper; the prison gate stays shut.

There is also the matter of incentives. A magistrate who grants bail to an accused who later absconds or reoffends will be blamed, sometimes publicly. A magistrate who refuses bail to a hundred people who would have appeared faithfully for trial will never be blamed at all, because their harmless conduct leaves no record. Caution is rewarded; liberty has no constituency.

Reformers have proposed many remedies: personal bonds instead of cash sureties for the poor, automatic review of every case in which an undertrial has served half the maximum sentence, legal aid lawyers stationed in every police station. Each is sensible. But none will work fully unless the system begins to count the cost of detention as carefully as it counts the risk of release. A wrongful detention is not a neutral outcome; it is a harm, borne by a person the law still presumes to be innocent.

The presumption of innocence is usually discussed as a rule about the trial: the prosecution must prove guilt. It is also, or ought to be, a rule about the time before trial. A society that detains first and asks questions later has not abandoned the presumption in theory. It has simply arranged matters so that the presumption arrives too late to help.

Question: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.A: The presumption of innocence applies only to the trial and not to the period before it.
options.B: The maxim that bail is the rule fails in practice because of everyday frictions and skewed incentives.
options.C: Indian judges are harsh and routinely refuse bail to poor accused persons out of prejudice against them and their communities.
options.D: Bail should be granted automatically to every accused person regardless of the offence charged.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage contrasts the maxim with practice, explains frictions (sureties, conditions) and incentives (asymmetric blame), and ends by urging that detention be counted as a harm.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Reverses the author's view: he says it ought to apply before trial too. | Trap (C): The author says the gap is 'not mainly a story of harsh judges'. | Trap (D): Too extreme: the author proposes counting costs and targeted reforms, not automatic bail.

questions.question_text:
Passage 2: Every few months a new statistic about pending cases makes the headlines: tens of millions of matters waiting in the courts, some for decades. The usual response is to demand more judges, more courtrooms, more days of work. These demands are reasonable. But they rest on an assumption worth questioning, namely that every dispute which reaches a court ought to be decided by one.

Many disputes are not really about legal rights at all. A quarrel between brothers over a family house, a falling-out between business partners, a fight between neighbours over a wall: these are often disagreements about respect, memory or trust, dressed up in the language of title deeds and contracts. A judgment can declare who owns the wall. It cannot make the neighbours speak to each other again. Frequently the winner of such a case feels hardly better than the loser, because the thing he actually wanted was never on offer.

Mediation offers something different. A trained mediator does not decide; she helps the parties understand what each actually needs, and invites them to design a solution themselves. Because the outcome belongs to the parties, it tends to be obeyed. Because the process is confidential, people can say things they would never say in open court. And because it is quicker, the relationship has a chance of surviving the dispute.

None of this means mediation is a cure for everything. Where one party is far more powerful than the other, as with a large company and a single consumer, or an abusive spouse and a frightened partner, a private negotiation may simply allow the strong to dictate terms in a gentler voice. Some disputes also matter beyond the parties: a case that settles an important point of law protects thousands of others who will never see a courtroom. Such cases need judges, and the public reasons that judges must give.

The sensible conclusion is not that courts should give way to mediation, but that the two should be matched to the disputes they suit. A system that sent every quarrel to a judge would be as foolish as one that sent every quarrel to a mediator. The task is to know the difference, and to build the institutions that can tell.

Question: The primary purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: criticise the demand for more judges as unreasonable
options.B: argue that disputes should be matched to mediation or to courts according to their nature
options.C: explain the training that mediators receive before they are allowed to handle disputes between parties
options.D: argue that mediation should replace courts for most civil disputes

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The last paragraph states the thesis: match the method to the dispute.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The author calls these demands 'reasonable'. | Trap (C): Training is mentioned in passing only. | Trap (D): The author says the conclusion is 'not that courts should give way to mediation'.

questions.question_text:
Passage 3: Groundwater is India's invisible reservoir. It supplies most of the water used for irrigation and a large share of drinking water in towns and villages alike. It is also falling. In large parts of the north-west and the peninsula, wells that once struck water at a few metres must now go down several hundred. The water that farmers lift today was in many places stored over centuries; it is being spent like an inheritance.

Economists have a familiar diagnosis. In many States, electricity for farm pumps is free or nearly free, and charged at a flat rate unrelated to how much is used. A farmer who pumps for twelve hours pays no more than one who pumps for two. The extra water, and the extra power, cost him nothing at the margin. Predictably, the pumps run long and the water table falls. The remedy, on this view, is to meter power and price it.

Passage 4: Courts around the world are experimenting with artificial intelligence. Some use it to translate judgments into regional languages, a genuine service to litigants who cannot read English. Others use it to transcribe hearings, sort case files or flag cases that raise the same question so that they can be heard together. Few would object to any of this. The harder question arrives when software is asked not to assist judges but to advise them: to predict whether an accused is likely to reoffend, or to suggest how a case ought to be decided.

The case for such tools is easy to make. Human judges are inconsistent. Studies in several countries have found that sentences vary with the judge's mood, the time of day, even the result of a local football match. A well-built model, it is said, would at least be consistent: like cases treated alike, every time.

But consistency is not the same as fairness. A model learns from past decisions, and past decisions carry the patterns of the society that produced them. If certain communities were policed more heavily, they will appear more often in the records of arrest, and a model trained on those records will judge their members riskier. The software does not invent the bias. It inherits it, launders it through mathematics, and returns it with an air of objectivity that a human prejudice could never claim.

There is a further difficulty. A judge must give reasons, and the reasons can be examined, criticised and overturned on appeal. Many modern models cannot explain their outputs in terms a court can review. To accept a recommendation that no one can explain is to replace a reasoned decision with an oracle.

None of this argues for banning technology from courtrooms. It argues for a clear line. Machines can carry the files, translate the words and find the precedents. The act of judgment, weighing a person's liberty against the claims of society and explaining why, should remain with someone who can be asked to account for it.

Question: The primary purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: distinguish acceptable from unacceptable uses of AI in courts, keeping judgment with humans
options.B: show that AI tools are more consistent than human judges and are therefore fairer to every accused person
options.C: argue that all uses of AI should be banned from courtrooms
options.D: describe how AI translation tools work

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage separates assistance (translation, transcription) from advice on decisions, and draws a line at the act of judgment.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The author says consistency is not the same as fairness. | Trap (C): The author says 'none of this argues for banning technology'. | Trap (D): Translation is only one example of acceptable use.
questions.concept_tag: RC – Primary Purpose – Artificial Intelligence in Courts

questions.question_text:
Passage 5: Indian federalism is often discussed in the vocabulary of power: who may legislate on what, which government controls the police, whether a Governor may sit on a Bill. Less noticed, but no less important, is the vocabulary of money. States in India are responsible for most of the spending that touches citizens' daily lives, from schools and hospitals to roads and policing. Yet the Union collects a larger share of the most buoyant taxes. The gap is bridged by transfers, and how those transfers are made shapes the relationship more than any constitutional clause.

The Constitution's answer is the Finance Commission, appointed every five years to recommend how the divisible pool of central taxes should be shared. Its formula weighs population, area, income distance and other factors, and the resulting shares are largely untied: States may spend the money as they choose. Over time, however, a growing portion of central support has flowed through centrally sponsored schemes, which come with conditions, matching contributions and the Union's priorities attached.

There is a case for conditions. The Union may legitimately want national goals pursued everywhere, and money without conditions can be wasted. But conditions carry a cost that is easy to miss. A State that must match central funds for a dozen schemes may find its own budget committed before it has decided anything. Its elected government becomes, in part, an implementing agency for decisions taken elsewhere.

Another strain arises from cesses and surcharges, which the Union may levy outside the divisible pool. When these grow, the share that States receive under the Finance Commission's formula can fall in real terms, even if the formula itself is unchanged. The States notice; trust erodes.

A federation is not only a division of powers. It is a relationship that depends on each side believing the other will play fair. Money is where that belief is most often tested, and where it is most quietly lost.

Question: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.A: States should collect all taxes themselves
options.B: Centrally sponsored schemes are always wasteful
options.C: How money flows between the Union and the States shapes federalism as much as the division of powers
options.D: The Finance Commission should be abolished because its formula is unfair to the more populous States

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The first and last paragraphs frame money as central to the federal relationship.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): No such proposal is made. | Trap (B): The author concedes there is a case for conditions. | Trap (D): The author does not call for abolition.

options.A: triumphant and celebratory
options.B: detached and purely technical
options.C: reflective and cautionary

Passage 6: In March 2017, within days of each other, New Zealand's Parliament and an Indian High Court made rivers into legal persons. The Whanganui River gained that status through an Act of Parliament negotiated with the Maori people for whom it was an ancestor; the Ganga and Yamuna were declared persons by a judgment that the Supreme Court soon stayed. Since then, courts and legislatures in several countries have extended similar recognition to forests, lakes and, in a few cases, individual animals.

To many lawyers this sounds like poetry rather than law. A river cannot sue, sign a contract or appear in court. But legal personhood has never required a human body. Companies, trusts and temples are legal persons in Indian law. Personhood is a device: it allows the law to recognise that an entity has interests, and to appoint someone to speak for those interests. A company speaks through its directors; a minor through a guardian. A river might speak through guardians charged with its protection.

The device is attractive because ordinary environmental law protects nature only indirectly. A polluted river can usually be defended only by showing harm to people who use it. If no person with standing complains, or if their losses are small, the river has no voice. Personhood changes the question from 'whose property was damaged?' to 'was the river harmed?'

Yet the device has limits. Rights mean little without guardians who are independent, funded and willing to act, and without courts prepared to enforce their claims against powerful interests. A river declared a person but left in the care of the very authorities that permit its pollution has gained a title, not a protector. There is also the awkward question of liability. If a river is a person, may it be sued when it floods?

Rights of nature, then, are neither a fairy tale nor a solution in themselves. They are a tool, and like every legal tool they are only as good as the institutions that use them.

Question: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to:

options.A: show that legal personhood for nature is pure poetry that has no basis in the law
options.B: argue that rivers should be worshipped as ancestors
options.C: assess personhood for nature as a tool whose value depends on institutions
options.D: explain the history of company law in India

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The final paragraph calls these rights 'a tool' that is 'only as good as the institutions that use them'.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The author rebuts this view in the second paragraph. | Trap (B): The Maori view is reported, not urged on readers. | Trap (D): Companies are an analogy, not the subject.
questions.concept_tag: RC – Primary Purpose – Rights of Nature

Passage 7: The delivery rider who brings dinner to the door in twenty minutes occupies a strange place in law. He wears the company's colours, follows the company's app, and can be 'deactivated' if his ratings fall. Yet in most contracts he is described as an independent partner, not an employee. He has no fixed wage, no paid leave, and often no protection if he is injured on the road.

The platforms defend this arrangement as freedom. Riders choose when to log in and for how long; many combine the work with studies or another job; a rigid employment contract would destroy the flexibility that attracts them. There is truth in this. Surveys find that a large number of gig workers value the ability to set their own hours.

But flexibility in choosing hours is not the same as independence. A genuinely independent contractor sets his own prices, chooses his clients and bears the profit of his own skill. The rider does none of these. The app sets the fare, assigns the order and adjusts his pay through incentives he cannot negotiate. The algorithm, not the rider, controls almost everything except the moment he switches it on.

Some countries have responded by presuming that platform workers are employees unless the company proves otherwise. India's labour codes have taken a different path. The Code on Social Security, 2020 recognises gig and platform workers as a separate category and provides for social security schemes funded partly by contributions from aggregators, without making them employees. Supporters call this a pragmatic middle way; critics fear that a separate category may become a permanent second class.

The deeper question is whether labour law should continue to depend on a single yes-or-no test, employee or not, at all. Protection against injury, a floor on earnings and a fair process before deactivation could be attached to the work itself rather than to the label on the contract. The label, after all, is written by the party with more power.

Question: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Gig work should be banned because it exploits workers
options.B: Gig workers are happier than regular employees
options.C: Flexibility is not independence, and protection could attach to the work itself
options.D: India's approach is identical to that of the countries that presume platform workers to be employees

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage separates flexibility from independence and ends by questioning the employee/non-employee test.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): No ban is proposed. | Trap (B): No such comparison is made. | Trap (D): The passage says India took 'a different path'.
questions.concept_tag: RC – Main Idea – Gig Work and Labour Law
