questions.question_text:
Passage 8: For most of independent India's history, a student who wanted to become an engineer or a doctor had to do so in English. Bright students from villages, fluent in Tamil or Marathi or Bengali, often arrived at college to find that the subject was not the hardest thing to learn; the language was. Many struggled, some dropped out, and a few succeeded only by spending years mastering a vocabulary before they could master a discipline.

In recent years, several States and national institutions have begun offering technical and professional courses in Indian languages. Textbooks are being translated; entrance examinations are being offered in more languages. Supporters argue that students understand concepts more deeply when they learn in the language they think in, and that a country which wants talent from everywhere cannot keep a linguistic gate at the entrance.

The critics are not all snobs. They point out that most research is published in English, that employers in many sectors expect it, and that a student trained only in her mother tongue may find the world of work narrower than she hoped. They fear, too, that hurried translations will produce textbooks that are technically accurate and pedagogically useless, filled with coined terms no one uses.

Both sides have a point, and the conflict between them is less sharp than it seems. The choice is not between English and Indian languages but between two ways of combining them. A student may learn thermodynamics in Kannada and still learn to read a paper in English; indeed, a firm grasp of the concept may make the foreign vocabulary easier, not harder, to acquire. What matters is that language should be a bridge into knowledge and not a toll gate before it.

The real test of the new policy will be quality. A course in an Indian language that is taught well will attract students and earn respect. One that is taught badly will confirm every prejudice against it, and do lasting harm to the cause it was meant to serve.

Question: The primary purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: show that translated textbooks are always useless and should be replaced by English textbooks
options.B: describe the history of English education in British India
options.C: argue that English should be abolished from Indian universities
options.D: weigh the arguments on teaching in Indian languages and suggest a reconciliation

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage presents both sides and concludes that the choice is between ways of combining languages.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The critics fear hurried translations; the author does not call all translations useless. | Trap (B): The passage is about independent India and current policy. | Trap (C): The author wants languages combined, not English abolished.
questions.concept_tag: RC – Primary Purpose – Languages of Higher Education

Passage 8: For most of independent India's history, a student who wanted to become an engineer or a doctor had to do so in English. Bright students from villages, fluent in Tamil or Marathi or Bengali, often arrived at college to find that the subject was not the hardest thing to learn; the language was. Many struggled, some dropped out, and a few succeeded only by spending years mastering a vocabulary before they could master a discipline.

In recent years, several States and national institutions have begun offering technical and professional courses in Indian languages. Textbooks are being translated; entrance examinations are being offered in more languages. Supporters argue that students understand concepts more deeply when they learn in the language they think in, and that a country which wants talent from everywhere cannot keep a linguistic gate at the entrance.

The critics are not all snobs. They point out that most research is published in English, that employers in many sectors expect it, and that a student trained only in her mother tongue may find the world of work narrower than she hoped. They fear, too, that hurried translations will produce textbooks that are technically accurate and pedagogically useless, filled with coined terms no one uses.

Both sides have a point, and the conflict between them is less sharp than it seems. The choice is not between English and Indian languages but between two ways of combining them. A student may learn thermodynamics in Kannada and still learn to read a paper in English; indeed, a firm grasp of the concept may make the foreign vocabulary easier, not harder, to acquire. What matters is that language should be a bridge into knowledge and not a toll gate before it.

The real test of the new policy will be quality. A course in an Indian language that is taught well will attract students and earn respect. One that is taught badly will confirm every prejudice against it, and do lasting harm to the cause it was meant to serve.

options.A: some objections rest on practical concerns rather than prejudice
options.B: snobbery has no role at all in the debate about the language of higher education
options.C: the critics are mostly from villages
options.D: all critics of the policy are snobs

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The paragraph lists practical concerns: research in English, employer expectations, poor translations.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): 'Not all' implies some may be. | Trap (C): No claim about their origin. | Trap (D): Reverses the remark.

Passage 9: A public library is one of the few places in a modern city where a person may stay as long as she likes without being expected to buy anything. That simple fact makes it more radical than it looks. In a café, a mall or a cinema, time is rented; in a library, it is given away.

For a long time, libraries justified themselves by their books. They were the places where people without money could read what people with money owned. The internet seemed to threaten that role. Why walk to a building for a book when a phone holds a thousand? Many city governments drew the obvious conclusion and cut library budgets. Some branches closed; others shrank to a few shelves and a tired reading room.

Yet those who still use libraries tell a different story. Students come because their homes are crowded and noisy. Job-seekers come to use computers and printers they do not own. Elderly people come for company as much as for reading. Children come because a librarian once handed them a book they had not known they wanted. None of these needs is met by a phone, and some of them grow sharper as more of life moves online, because the people without good devices or quiet rooms fall further behind.

Seen this way, the library is less a warehouse of books than a piece of social infrastructure, like a park or a bus stop: a shared space that makes other things possible. The value of such infrastructure is easy to miss, because it is spread thinly across many lives and rarely appears in a balance sheet. Its loss is felt only slowly, as a city becomes a little more lonely and a little more unequal.

Cities that want to measure what their libraries are worth might start by asking not how many books were borrowed, but how many people had nowhere else to go.

Question: Which of the following best captures the main argument of the passage?

options.A: Phones are harmful to children's reading
options.B: Libraries should charge a fee to cover their costs
options.C: Libraries should close because the internet has replaced books for most readers
options.D: Libraries are valuable social spaces whose worth goes well beyond lending books

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage reframes libraries as 'social infrastructure' and urges a different measure of value.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Not the author's argument. | Trap (B): The author praises their being free. | Trap (C): The author argues against this conclusion.

Passage 10: Low Earth orbit is getting crowded. Thousands of active satellites now circle the planet, and many thousands more are planned as companies race to build networks that will beam the internet to every corner of the globe. Around them swirl fragments of older satellites, spent rocket stages and the debris of collisions and weapons tests, travelling at speeds at which even a fleck of paint can damage a spacecraft.

The danger is not only to individual satellites. Scientists have long warned of a cascade: one collision produces fragments that cause further collisions, until some orbits become too dangerous to use. Such a cascade would not respect national boundaries. A country that never launched a satellite would still lose weather forecasts, navigation and communications that depend on space.

The law has not kept pace. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 declared that space is free for exploration and use by all States and is not subject to national appropriation. It made States responsible for their national activities in space, including those of private companies, and liable for damage caused by their space objects. But it was drafted when only a handful of countries could reach orbit, and it says almost nothing about debris. Later guidelines on reducing debris are voluntary.

Orbit, in other words, is a commons, a shared resource open to all and owned by none. Economists have a name for what tends to happen to such resources: each user, acting reasonably for himself, takes a little more than is wise, and the sum of these reasonable choices is ruin. Pastures are overgrazed; fisheries collapse. The orbits of Earth may be next.

Commons are not doomed, however. Where users agree on rules, monitor one another and accept sanctions, shared resources can be managed for generations. The question is whether the nations and companies now crowding into orbit can agree on such rules before the cascade makes the question irrelevant.

Question: The primary purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: explain how satellites provide weather forecasts
options.B: celebrate the growth of satellite internet networks
options.C: warn that orbital debris is a commons problem that the law does not yet address
options.D: argue that the Outer Space Treaty should be abolished and replaced by national space laws

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage describes the danger, the gaps in law, and frames orbit as a commons needing rules.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): This is a passing example. | Trap (B): Growth is described as a source of crowding. | Trap (D): The author says the law has not kept pace, not that it should be abolished.
questions.concept_tag: RC – Primary Purpose – Space Debris and the Commons

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The all-India CPI (Rural, Urban, Combined) is compiled by the National Statistics Office, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation. The WPI is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry. CPI-IW is compiled by the Labour Bureau (MoSPI/DPIIT/PIB releases).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The RBI uses CPI for inflation targeting but does not compile it; the NSO does not compile WPI. | Trap (B): The Labour Bureau compiles CPI-Industrial Workers, a different series; the RBI does not compile WPI. | Trap (C): CPI part is right, but WPI comes from the Office of the Economic Adviser under DPIIT (Ministry of Commerce and Industry).
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Economy – CPI and WPI compilers

questions.question_text:
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described this functionary as probably the most important officer under the Constitution of India. The officer is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal and holds office for six years or until the age of sixty-five, whichever is earlier. The officer can be removed only in the manner and on the grounds on which a judge of the Supreme Court is removed, and is not eligible for any further office under the Union or a State after ceasing to hold office. Salary and other conditions of service are determined by Parliament and cannot be varied to the officer's disadvantage after appointment. The officer audits all receipts and expenditure of the Union and the States. Reports relating to Union accounts are submitted to the President, who causes them to be laid before each House of Parliament, where they are examined in detail by the Public Accounts Committee.

Under which Article of the Constitution is this office established?

options.A: Article 149
options.B: Article 151
options.C: Article 148
options.D: Article 76

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The passage describes the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, established by Article 148 (Constitution text); duties are in Article 149 and audit reports in Article 151. Tenure (six years or age 65) comes from the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 149 sets out the CAG's duties and powers; it is the next Article, not the one that creates the office. | Trap (B): Article 151 deals with the CAG's audit reports being laid before the legislature. | Trap (D): Article 76 establishes the Attorney-General for India, another constitutional office appointed by the President.
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: Passage takes the six-year/65 tenure from the 1971 Act, not the Article (explanation says so).

questions.question_text: The right to free and compulsory education for all children aged 6 to 14 years is a Fundamental Right under which Article of the Constitution of India?

options.A: Article 45
options.B: Article 51A(k)
options.C: Article 24
options.D: Article 21A

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 21A was inserted by the Constitution (86th Amendment) Act, 2002 (Constitution text). The same amendment substituted Article 45 and added Fundamental Duty 51A(k). The right is given effect by the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, in force from 1 April 2010.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 45 was the original DPSP on free education; after 2002 it covers early childhood care for children below six. | Trap (B): Article 51A(k) is the Fundamental Duty of parents/guardians to provide opportunities for education, not the right itself. | Trap (C): Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in hazardous work; same age group, different right.

questions.question_text: Mahatma Gandhi began the Dandi March from Sabarmati Ashram on:

options.A: 6 April 1930
options.B: 26 January 1930
options.C: 12 March 1930
options.D: 8 August 1942

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Dandi March began from Sabarmati Ashram on 12 March 1930 with 78 followers and ended at Dandi on 6 April 1930, when Gandhi broke the salt law, launching the Civil Disobedience Movement (NCERT history).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 6 April 1930 is when Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi, at the end of the march. | Trap (B): 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Purna Swaraj Day, weeks before the march. | Trap (D): 8 August 1942 is when the Quit India resolution was passed in Bombay.

questions.question_text:
In 2016, Parliament amended the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 to give statutory backing to a flexible inflation targeting framework. Under this framework, the Central Government, in consultation with the Reserve Bank, sets an inflation target once every five years; the current target is 4 per cent consumer price inflation with a tolerance band of 2 percentage points on either side. If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the central bank must send a report to the Government explaining the reasons for the failure and the remedial action proposed. Decisions on the policy repo rate are taken by a statutory committee that must meet at least four times a year and publish its resolution after each meeting, along with the voting pattern of its members. Some of its members are drawn from the central bank, while others are external experts appointed by the Government for four-year terms who are not eligible for reappointment.

How many members does the committee that decides the policy repo rate have, and who has the casting vote in case of a tie?

options.A: Six members; the Union Finance Minister
options.B: Five members; the Governor of the RBI
options.C: Six members; the Governor of the RBI
options.D: Seven members; the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act, 1934 (inserted by the Finance Act, 2016) (Act text/RBI), the MPC has six members: the Governor (chair), the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer nominated by the Central Board, and three external members appointed by the Government. The Governor has a second or casting vote in a tie.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Right size, but the Finance Minister is not a member; the Governor chairs the MPC. | Trap (B): An odd number is assumed so that no casting vote would be needed; the MPC actually has six members. | Trap (D): The Deputy Governor is a member but has no casting vote, and the size is wrong.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Economy – Monetary Policy Committee
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Retained by Gazette S.O. 1580(E), 25 Mar 2026, for 1 Apr 2026–31 Mar 2031. Re-check after the next five-year review. (valid until 2031-03-31)

questions.question_text:
On 5 November 2013, ISRO launched the Mars Orbiter Mission, popularly called Mangalyaan, aboard a PSLV-XL rocket from Sriharikota. Because the PSLV was not powerful enough to send the spacecraft directly towards Mars, ISRO used a series of orbit-raising manoeuvres around Earth before performing the trans-Mars injection on 1 December 2013. After a journey of about ten months, the spacecraft was inserted into an elliptical orbit around Mars on 24 September 2014. Built at a reported cost of about 450 crore rupees, the mission was widely noted for its low budget compared with similar missions of other space agencies. Designed for a life of six months, the orbiter continued to work for about eight years until ground contact was lost in 2022. It carried five scientific instruments, including a methane sensor and a colour camera that produced a full-disc image of the planet.

This mission made India:

options.A: The first country to soft-land a rover on Mars
options.B: The first country ever to send a spacecraft towards Mars
options.C: The only Asian country ever to attempt a Mars mission
options.D: The first country to reach Mars orbit in its maiden attempt

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Mars Orbiter Mission, launched on PSLV-C25 on 5 November 2013 and inserted into Mars orbit on 24 September 2014 (ISRO), made India the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt and the first Asian nation to reach Mars orbit.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Mangalyaan was only an orbiter; it carried no lander or rover. | Trap (B): The USSR and the USA had sent Mars missions decades earlier. | Trap (C): Japan (Nozomi, 1998) and China (Yinghuo-1, 2011) had attempted missions earlier, though both failed.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Science & tech – Mars Orbiter Mission

questions.question_text: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam came into force on:

options.A: 25 December 2023
options.B: 26 January 2024
options.C: 1 July 2024
options.D: 1 April 2024

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The three Acts received Presidential assent on 25 December 2023 and were brought into force from 1 July 2024 by Gazette notifications of the Ministry of Home Affairs (PIB/Gazette). They replaced the IPC 1860, the CrPC 1973 and the Indian Evidence Act 1872 respectively.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): This is the date the three Acts received Presidential assent, not the date they came into force. | Trap (B): Republic Day is a guess based on symbolism; no law came into force then. | Trap (D): Start of the financial year; a common guess for the date a law takes effect.

questions.question_text: India won the ICC Champions Trophy 2025 by defeating which team in the final in Dubai?

options.A: New Zealand
options.B: South Africa
options.C: Australia
options.D: Pakistan

questions.pedagogical_explanation: On 9 March 2025, India beat New Zealand by four wickets in the final at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium to win their third Champions Trophy title (ICC). Rohit Sharma was Player of the Match.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): South Africa was India's opponent in the 2024 T20 World Cup final. | Trap (C): India beat Australia in the 2025 semi-final, not the final. | Trap (D): Pakistan were the 2025 hosts and beat India in the 2017 Champions Trophy final.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Sports – ICC Champions Trophy 2025

questions.question_text: The GST Council, constituted under Article 279A of the Constitution, is chaired by:

options.A: The Prime Minister
options.B: The Union Finance Minister
options.C: The Union Revenue Secretary
options.D: The Governor of the RBI

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 279A, inserted by the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016 (Constitution text), provides for a GST Council chaired by the Union Finance Minister, with the Union Minister of State for Finance and the State Finance/Taxation Ministers as members. GST was rolled out on 1 July 2017.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Prime Minister chairs NITI Aayog's Governing Council, not the GST Council. | Trap (C): The Revenue Secretary is the ex-officio Secretary to the Council, not its chair. | Trap (D): The RBI Governor has no role in the GST Council.

questions.question_text: Which is the longest river of peninsular India, often called the 'Dakshin Ganga'?

options.A: Godavari
options.B: Krishna
options.C: Narmada
options.D: Mahanadi

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Godavari, rising at Trimbakeshwar near Nashik in Maharashtra and draining into the Bay of Bengal, is the largest peninsular river system and about 1,465 km long (NCERT Geography).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Krishna is the second-longest peninsular river. | Trap (C): The Narmada is the largest west-flowing river of the peninsula, not the longest overall. | Trap (D): The Mahanadi is a major east-flowing river, but it is shorter than the Godavari.

questions.question_text:
Launched on an LVM3 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, on 14 July 2023, Chandrayaan-3 was ISRO's follow-up to a 2019 mission whose lander had crashed during its final descent. The new mission consisted of a propulsion module, the lander Vikram and the six-wheeled rover Pragyan, and was designed specifically to demonstrate safe soft landing and roving on the lunar surface. After a series of orbit-raising manoeuvres, lunar orbit insertion and careful lowering of its orbit, the lander touched down in the high-latitude region near the Moon's south pole. This made India the first country to land in that region and the fourth country to achieve a soft landing on the Moon. The landing site was later named 'Shiv Shakti Point'. In the days that followed, Pragyan's instruments confirmed the presence of sulphur in the lunar soil near the landing site.

The date of Vikram's soft landing is now observed every year as National Space Day. What is that date?

options.A: 23 August
options.B: 14 July
options.C: 7 September
options.D: 22 July

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander soft-landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, and the Government of India declared 23 August as National Space Day (PIB/ISRO). India was the first country to land in that region and the fourth to soft-land on the Moon.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): 14 July 2023 was the launch date of Chandrayaan-3, not the landing. | Trap (C): 7 September 2019 is when the Chandrayaan-2 lander lost contact during descent. | Trap (D): 22 July 2019 was the launch date of Chandrayaan-2.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Science & tech – Chandrayaan-3 / National Space Day

questions.question_text: The permanent secretariat of BIMSTEC is located in:

options.A: Kathmandu
options.B: Dhaka
options.C: Jakarta
options.D: Colombo

questions.pedagogical_explanation: BIMSTEC (Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation), formed in 1997 by the Bangkok Declaration, set up its permanent secretariat in Dhaka in 2014 (BIMSTEC official site/MEA). The Charter was adopted at the Colombo Summit in March 2022.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Kathmandu hosts the SAARC Secretariat, a similar South Asian body. | Trap (C): Jakarta hosts the ASEAN Secretariat; BIMSTEC links South and South-East Asia. | Trap (D): Colombo hosted the 5th BIMSTEC Summit (2022), where the BIMSTEC Charter was adopted, but it is not the secretariat.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Regional organisations – BIMSTEC secretariat

questions.question_text:
When the two Houses of Parliament disagree on an ordinary bill, because one House rejects a bill passed by the other, disagrees with amendments made to it, or allows more than six months to pass without acting on it, the Constitution provides a mechanism to break the deadlock. The President may summon both Houses to meet together, and the bill is then passed by a majority of the total number of members of both Houses present and voting. Because the Lok Sabha has more than twice as many members as the Rajya Sabha, the mechanism usually favours the lower House. It cannot be used for Money Bills, on which the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations, or for constitutional amendment bills, which must be passed by each House separately. Since independence, the procedure has been used only three times: for the Dowry Prohibition Bill in 1961, the Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill in 1978 and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill in 2002.

Who ordinarily presides over such a sitting?

options.A: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
options.B: The President of India
options.C: The Vice-President, as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
options.D: The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Under Article 108 and Article 118(4) (Constitution text), the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting; in the Speaker's absence the Deputy Speaker, and failing both, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The President summons the joint sitting but does not preside over it. | Trap (C): The Chairman presides over the Rajya Sabha, not over joint sittings. | Trap (D): The Deputy Chairman presides only if both the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker are absent.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Polity – Joint sitting of Parliament
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: Passage is the author's wording; facts (joint sittings 1961, 1978, 2002) are correct.

questions.question_text:
On 30 December 2024, ISRO launched its Space Docking Experiment, or SpaDeX, aboard PSLV-C60 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota. The mission placed two small satellites of about 220 kilograms each, named SDX01 (the 'Chaser') and SDX02 (the 'Target'), into a low Earth orbit. Over the following two weeks the spacecraft were gradually brought closer together, with planned attempts deferred more than once while engineers analysed the drift between the two satellites. The docking was finally achieved on 16 January 2025 using an indigenously developed docking mechanism and a suite of sensors, and the satellites were later separated in a controlled undocking. ISRO has described in-space docking as essential for its future plans, including Chandrayaan-4, which is to bring lunar samples back to Earth, and the Bharatiya Antariksh Station, India's planned space station.

With this achievement, India became:

options.A: The third country to achieve in-space docking, after the USA and Russia
options.B: The fourth country to achieve in-space docking, after the USA, Russia and China
options.C: The first Asian country to achieve in-space docking
options.D: The fourth country to achieve in-space docking, after the USA, Russia and the United Kingdom

questions.pedagogical_explanation: ISRO's SpaDeX mission was launched on PSLV-C60 on 30 December 2024, and the two satellites docked on 16 January 2025 (ISRO/PIB). India became the fourth country, after the USA, Russia and China, to demonstrate space docking.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Leaves out China, which first docked spacecraft in 2011 (Shenzhou-8 with Tiangong-1). | Trap (C): China docked spacecraft more than a decade earlier. | Trap (D): The UK has no independent docking capability; China is the third country.

questions.question_text: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), the Supreme Court upheld reservation for Other Backward Classes in central government posts, subject to a 50% ceiling and exclusion of the creamy layer. Under which provision was this reservation made, and which commission's report did it implement?

options.A: Article 15(4); the Mandal Commission
options.B: Article 16(4); the Kaka Kalelkar Commission
options.C: Article 335; the Sachar Committee
options.D: Article 16(4); the Mandal Commission

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), a nine-judge bench (Supreme Court judgment), upheld the 1990 office memorandum implementing the Second Backward Classes (Mandal) Commission report (1980) under Article 16(4). It imposed a 50% ceiling, excluded the creamy layer and barred reservation in promotions (later altered by the 77th Amendment, 1995).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 15(4) allows special provisions (e.g. in education), not reservation in public posts. | Trap (B): Kalelkar headed the First Backward Classes Commission (1953); its report was not implemented. | Trap (C): Article 335 deals with claims of SCs/STs to services, and the Sachar Committee (2006) studied Muslims' status.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – Indra Sawhney (1992) and Article 16(4)

questions.question_text: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court held that:

options.A: Articles 14, 19 and 21 operate in separate, mutually exclusive compartments
options.B: The 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable, not arbitrary
options.C: Parliament cannot amend the basic structure of the Constitution
options.D: The right to travel abroad is not part of personal liberty

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), a seven-judge bench decision (Supreme Court judgment) arising from impounding of a passport, held that Articles 14, 19 and 21 are interlinked and that any procedure depriving personal liberty must be fair, just and reasonable, overruling the narrow A.K. Gopalan (1950) reading.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): This was the A.K. Gopalan (1950) approach, which Maneka Gandhi rejected. | Trap (C): This is the Kesavananda Bharati (1973) holding. | Trap (D): Wrong: the right to travel abroad was held part of personal liberty (Satwant Singh Sawhney, 1967), and Maneka built on it.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – Maneka Gandhi (1978)

questions.question_text: India won the ICC Men's T20 World Cup 2024 by defeating which team in the final at Kensington Oval, Barbados?

options.A: Australia
options.B: England
options.C: New Zealand
options.D: South Africa

questions.pedagogical_explanation: On 29 June 2024, India beat South Africa by 7 runs in the final at Barbados to win their second T20 World Cup title (ICC). Virat Kohli was Player of the Match and Jasprit Bumrah Player of the Tournament.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Australia beat India in the 2023 ODI World Cup final; it is a recent final confused with this one. | Trap (B): England were the 2022 T20 World Cup champions; India beat them in the 2024 semi-final, not the final. | Trap (C): India beat New Zealand in the 2025 Champions Trophy final, a different tournament.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Sports – T20 World Cup 2024
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: True for 2024; don't reuse as 'how many titles' without re-checking after the 2026 edition (valid until stable)

questions.question_text:
Introduced through the Finance Act, 2017 and notified in January 2018, the Electoral Bond Scheme allowed individuals and companies to buy interest-free bearer instruments from authorised branches of the State Bank of India and donate them to eligible political parties, which had to encash them within fifteen days. To make the scheme work, amendments were made to the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the Companies Act, 2013 and the Income Tax Act, 1961. These removed the earlier cap on corporate donations and exempted parties from disclosing contributions received through bonds. Critics argued that donor identities were hidden from citizens but not necessarily from the government, because the issuing bank was State-owned. On 15 February 2024, a five-judge Constitution Bench headed by Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud unanimously struck down the scheme, directed the bank to stop issuing bonds, and ordered purchase and redemption details to be shared with the Election Commission for publication.

On which primary ground did the Court strike down the scheme?

options.A: It violated voters' right to information, which the Court located in Article 21
options.B: It violated voters' right to information about political funding under Article 19(1)(a)
options.C: It violated the right to adult suffrage under Article 326
options.D: It violated political parties' right to form associations under Article 19(1)(c)

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India, decided on 15 February 2024 by a five-judge Constitution Bench (Supreme Court judgment), held that the anonymous Electoral Bond Scheme violated the voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a). The Court also held the amendment removing the cap on corporate donations (Section 182, Companies Act) manifestly arbitrary under Article 14.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Close option: information/privacy rights are often linked to Article 21, but the Court grounded this right in Article 19(1)(a). | Trap (C): Article 326 provides for adult suffrage; it is not a Fundamental Right and was not the basis of the ruling. | Trap (D): Parties are associations, but the ruling protected voters' information, not parties' association rights.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – Electoral Bonds (2024) and Article 19(1)(a)

questions.question_text:
The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 2024 Nobel Peace Prize to a grassroots movement founded in 1956 by survivors of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, known in Japanese as hibakusha. For decades its members have travelled the world sharing personal testimonies of the suffering caused by nuclear weapons, campaigning for their abolition and seeking support for victims. In announcing the prize in October 2024, the Committee said the movement had helped build and sustain a powerful international norm stigmatising the use of nuclear weapons, often described as the nuclear taboo. The Committee noted with concern that this taboo was under pressure, with nuclear-armed states modernising and expanding their arsenals and threats of nuclear use being made in ongoing conflicts. The prize was presented at a ceremony in Oslo on 10 December 2024, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death, and the survivors' representatives used the occasion to urge younger generations to carry their message forward.

Which organisation is described in the passage?

options.A: International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN)
options.B: Nihon Hidankyo
options.C: Mayors for Peace
options.D: Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 2024 Nobel Peace Prize was announced on 11 October 2024 for Nihon Hidankyo, the Japan Confederation of A- and H-Bomb Sufferers Organizations (founded 1956) (NobelPrize.org). It was presented in Oslo on 10 December 2024.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): ICAN, an anti-nuclear coalition, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2017, not 2024. | Trap (C): Mayors for Peace is a Hiroshima-led network of cities against nuclear weapons, but it has not won the prize. | Trap (D): Pugwash, also anti-nuclear, shared the 1995 Nobel Peace Prize with Joseph Rotblat.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Awards – Nobel Peace Prize 2024
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: Passage gives the answer away; faculty may want to drop 'known in Japanese as hibakusha'.

questions.question_text:
On 25 June 2025, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida carrying the Axiom Mission 4 crew aboard a Crew Dragon spacecraft. The commercial mission, organised by the US company Axiom Space, docked with the International Space Station the next day. Commanded by veteran astronaut Peggy Whitson, the four-member crew included astronauts from Poland and Hungary, both countries returning to human spaceflight after more than four decades. India's representative, an officer of the Indian Air Force, served as the mission pilot and conducted experiments developed by Indian institutions, including studies on microalgae and the sprouting of seeds in microgravity. He became the first Indian to visit the space station and the second Indian citizen to travel to space, four decades after the first. After about two weeks aboard the station, the crew splashed down off the coast of California on 15 July 2025.

Who was India's astronaut on this mission?

options.A: Group Captain Prasanth Balakrishnan Nair
options.B: Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla
options.C: Group Captain Angad Pratap
options.D: Sunita Williams

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Axiom Mission 4 launched on 25 June 2025 from Kennedy Space Center and docked with the ISS on 26 June 2025 (NASA/ISRO/PIB). Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla became the first Indian aboard the ISS and the second Indian in space after Rakesh Sharma (1984). The crew splashed down on 15 July 2025.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Nair was the backup for this mission and is a Gaganyaan astronaut-designate. | Trap (C): Angad Pratap is a Gaganyaan astronaut-designate who did not fly on Ax-4. | Trap (D): Sunita Williams is an Indian-origin NASA astronaut, not India's representative.

questions.question_text: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368. These clauses had been inserted by which amendment?

options.A: 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
options.B: 44th Amendment Act, 1978
options.C: 24th Amendment Act, 1971
options.D: 39th Amendment Act, 1975

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) (Supreme Court judgment) invalidated Sections 4 and 55 of the Constitution (42nd Amendment) Act, 1976. Section 55 had inserted clauses (4) and (5) into Article 368 to bar judicial review of amendments. The Court held limited amending power and the balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs to be part of the basic structure.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The 44th Amendment undid many 42nd Amendment changes and removed the right to property, but it did not insert these clauses. | Trap (C): The 24th Amendment affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights, but did not add clauses (4) and (5). | Trap (D): The 39th Amendment shielded the PM's election from judicial review, struck down in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975).
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – Minerva Mills (1980) and 42nd Amendment

questions.question_text:
In the early 1970s, the head of a Hindu mutt in Kerala approached the Supreme Court challenging the State's land reform laws, which restricted how the mutt could manage its property. The petition soon became a much larger contest over the limits of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution, especially after the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments were passed in 1971–72 to expand that power and to protect land reform and nationalisation measures from judicial challenge. The matter was heard by the largest bench ever assembled in the Court's history, thirteen judges, over sixty-eight working days. On 24 April 1973, the judges delivered eleven separate opinions and decided the central question by a narrow 7:6 majority. The ruling has since been invoked to test constitutional amendments on issues ranging from judicial appointments to elections, and it remains among the most cited constitutional judgments in India.

Which principle did the majority lay down in this case?

options.A: Parliament has no power to amend Fundamental Rights
options.B: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule are completely immune from judicial review
options.C: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter or destroy its basic structure
options.D: Any 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The case is Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, decided on 24 April 1973 by a 13-judge bench (7:6) (Supreme Court judgment). It upheld the 24th Amendment but held that the amending power under Article 368 does not extend to altering the basic structure, overruling I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): This was the Golaknath (1967) view, which this case overruled. | Trap (B): Opposite of the law: I.R. Coelho (2007) held Ninth Schedule laws inserted after 24 April 1973 are open to basic-structure review. | Trap (D): This is Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), a different landmark case.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – Kesavananda Bharati (1973)

questions.question_text: Who presided over the first session of the Indian National Congress held in Bombay in 1885?

options.A: A.O. Hume
options.B: Dadabhai Naoroji
options.C: W.C. Bonnerjee
options.D: Badruddin Tyabji

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The first session of the INC was held at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, in December 1885 with 72 delegates and was presided over by Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee (NCERT history/INC records).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Hume is credited with founding the Congress, but he did not preside. | Trap (B): Naoroji presided over the second session (Calcutta, 1886). | Trap (D): Tyabji presided over the third session (Madras, 1887) as the first Muslim president.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – History – First INC session

questions.question_text: The maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha permitted by the Constitution is:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 80 (Constitution text) fixes the Rajya Sabha's maximum at 250: up to 238 representatives of States and UTs plus 12 members nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art and social service. The current strength is 245.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 245 is the present actual strength (233 elected + 12 nominated), not the maximum. | Trap (C): 238 is the maximum number of elected representatives of States and UTs, without the 12 nominated members. | Trap (D): 552 was the former maximum strength of the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Polity – Rajya Sabha strength
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: 'Former maximum 552' trap refers to the pre-104th Amendment Lok Sabha maximum. | Time-sensitive: Changes only if Fourth Schedule seats are altered (e.g. a new State/UT) (valid until review yearly)

questions.question_text: Who took charge as the 26th Governor of the Reserve Bank of India in December 2024?

options.A: Sanjay Malhotra
options.B: Michael Debabrata Patra
options.C: T. Rabi Sankar
options.D: Ajay Seth

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Sanjay Malhotra, an IAS officer who was serving as Union Revenue Secretary, took charge as the 26th RBI Governor on 11 December 2024, succeeding Shaktikanta Das (RBI press release/PIB).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Patra was a Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, not the new Governor. | Trap (C): T. Rabi Sankar is a Deputy Governor of the RBI. | Trap (D): Ajay Seth was a senior Finance Ministry secretary, like Malhotra, but he did not become Governor.
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Question is dated ('took charge in Dec 2024'), so it stays correct; any 'current Governor' rewording would expire at the end of the 3-year term (valid until 2027-12-10)

questions.question_text:
Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) came into wide use in refrigerators, air conditioners and foam products as replacements for chlorofluorocarbons, which damage the stratospheric ozone layer. Although HFCs do not deplete ozone, many of them are extremely powerful greenhouse gases, with global warming potentials hundreds to thousands of times that of carbon dioxide. Meeting in Kigali, Rwanda, in October 2016, the parties to an existing environmental treaty agreed to add HFCs to the list of substances it controls and to phase down their production and consumption by more than 80 per cent over the coming decades. Countries were placed in groups with different timelines; India, in a later group, is to freeze HFC use in 2028 and complete most of its phase-down by 2047. The Union Cabinet approved India's ratification in August 2021, and the agreement is expected to avoid up to 0.4 degrees Celsius of global warming by the end of the century.

The Kigali Amendment was made to which international treaty?

options.A: Kyoto Protocol
options.B: Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer
options.C: Paris Agreement
options.D: Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Kigali Amendment (October 2016) to the Montreal Protocol (1987) added HFCs to the controlled substances (UNEP Ozone Secretariat). India's Cabinet approved ratification in August 2021 (PIB). India is to freeze HFC use in 2028 and reach an 85% reduction by 2047.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Kyoto Protocol (1997) set greenhouse gas targets under the UNFCCC; HFCs being greenhouse gases makes this tempting. | Trap (B): The Vienna Convention (1985) is the parent framework; the control measures and the Kigali Amendment are under the Protocol made under it. | Trap (C): The Paris Agreement (2015) is the UNFCCC climate treaty adopted a year before Kigali.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Environment treaties – Kigali Amendment

questions.question_text:
One of the three criminal-law statutes that came into force on 1 July 2024 overhauls the way crimes are investigated and tried in India. It formally recognises the 'Zero FIR', allowing information about a cognizable offence to be recorded at any police station regardless of where the offence took place, and it permits FIRs to be lodged electronically. Audio-video recording of search and seizure is made mandatory, and a forensic expert must visit the crime scene for offences punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more. The law allows trial in absentia of proclaimed offenders who have absconded, prescribes time limits for steps such as framing charges and pronouncing judgments, and permits trials, inquiries and other proceedings to be held in electronic mode. With 531 sections, it is the longest of the three new statutes, and it retains much of the structure of the code it replaced.

Which earlier statute has this law replaced?

options.A: Indian Penal Code, 1860
options.B: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898
options.C: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
options.D: Indian Evidence Act, 1872

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The law described is the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (531 sections), in force from 1 July 2024, which repealed and replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Gazette of India/MHA). Zero FIR, e-FIR, mandatory videography of search and seizure, and forensic visits for offences punishable with seven years or more are among its features.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The IPC, a substantive law defining offences, was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, not by this procedural law. | Trap (B): Wrong year: the 1898 Code had already been repealed and replaced by the 1973 Code. | Trap (D): Electronic records and proceedings suggest evidence law, but the Evidence Act was replaced by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam.

questions.question_text:
In July 2025, the sitting Vice-President of India resigned from office citing health reasons, more than two years before the end of his five-year term. Under Article 68 of the Constitution, an election to fill a vacancy caused by resignation must be held as soon as possible after it occurs, and the person elected holds office for a full term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office. The Vice-President is elected by an electoral college consisting of the members of both Houses of Parliament, including nominated members, in accordance with proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and voting is by secret ballot. The election was held on 9 September 2025. The ruling alliance fielded the then Governor of Maharashtra, while the opposition parties jointly nominated a former judge of the Supreme Court. Until the new office-holder took oath, the Rajya Sabha was presided over by its Deputy Chairman.

Who was elected as the 15th Vice-President of India in this election, and whom did he defeat?

options.A: B. Sudershan Reddy, who defeated C.P. Radhakrishnan
options.B: C.P. Radhakrishnan, who defeated Margaret Alva
options.C: Harivansh Narayan Singh, who defeated B. Sudershan Reddy
options.D: C.P. Radhakrishnan, who defeated B. Sudershan Reddy

questions.pedagogical_explanation: After Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned on 21 July 2025, the Vice-Presidential election was held on 9 September 2025. C.P. Radhakrishnan, then Governor of Maharashtra, defeated former Supreme Court judge B. Sudershan Reddy and was sworn in as the 15th Vice-President on 12 September 2025 (Election Commission/PIB). The electoral college is set by Article 66.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Right candidates, wrong winner: Reddy was the opposition nominee who lost. | Trap (B): Right winner, but Margaret Alva was the opposition candidate in 2022, against Jagdeep Dhankhar. | Trap (C): Harivansh, Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, presided in the Chairman's absence, but he was not the candidate.
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Dated question; stable (valid until 2030-09-11)

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is correct?

options.A: It sits in the Palais des Nations, Geneva
options.B: It has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms by the UN General Assembly and the Security Council
options.C: It was created by the Rome Statute of 1998
options.D: Only states that separately ratify its Statute are parties, and India is not one of them

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Under the Statute of the ICJ and the UN Charter (UN/ICJ official sources), the ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the UN, seated at the Peace Palace in The Hague. Its 15 judges serve nine-year terms and are elected by absolute majorities in both the General Assembly and the Security Council.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Palais des Nations houses the UN Office at Geneva; the ICJ sits in the Peace Palace, The Hague. | Trap (C): The Rome Statute created the International Criminal Court (ICC), a separate body that tries individuals. | Trap (D): All UN members, including India, are automatically parties to the ICJ Statute (Article 93, UN Charter).
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – International law – International Court of Justice

questions.question_text:
India's framework for safeguarding rights and ensuring accountable governance relies on many national bodies. Some draw their existence directly from the Constitution, so their composition and core functions can be changed only through a constitutional amendment. Others are created by ordinary Acts of Parliament or by executive resolutions and can be restructured through simple legislation or government orders. The distinction is not merely technical: a constitutional body enjoys greater permanence and independence, and laying its reports before Parliament is often a constitutional obligation rather than a statutory one. The line between the two categories can also shift over time. In 2018, for instance, one prominent national commission was raised from statutory to constitutional status through an amendment, after which it could inquire into complaints with the powers of a civil court. Students of polity are therefore expected to know not only what a body does but also the source from which its authority is derived.

Which of the following is a statutory body and NOT a constitutional body?

options.A: National Commission for Scheduled Castes
options.B: National Commission for Backward Classes
options.C: National Commission for Scheduled Tribes
options.D: National Human Rights Commission

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The National Human Rights Commission is a statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (Act text). The NCSC (Article 338), NCST (Article 338A, 89th Amendment 2003) and NCBC (Article 338B, 102nd Amendment 2018) are constitutional bodies.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The NCSC is constitutional, under Article 338. | Trap (B): The NCBC was statutory until 2018; the 102nd Amendment made it constitutional under Article 338B. | Trap (C): The NCST is constitutional, under Article 338A, inserted by the 89th Amendment, 2003.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Constitutional vs statutory bodies – NHRC

questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs of organisation and headquarters is INCORRECTLY matched?

options.A: UNESCO – Paris
options.B: International Labour Organization – Geneva
options.C: Food and Agriculture Organization – Rome
options.D: International Atomic Energy Agency – Nairobi

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The IAEA is headquartered in Vienna (IAEA official site); Nairobi hosts UNEP and UN-Habitat. UNESCO is in Paris, the ILO in Geneva and the FAO in Rome (official UN agency sites).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Correctly matched; it can be confused with UNICEF (New York). | Trap (B): Correctly matched; Geneva hosts many UN agencies, so it can look like a guess. | Trap (C): Correctly matched; Rome also hosts WFP and IFAD, so it can feel uncertain.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – International organisations – headquarters matching

questions.question_text: Who was sworn in as the 51st Chief Justice of India on 11 November 2024, succeeding Justice D.Y. Chandrachud?

options.A: Justice Sanjiv Khanna
options.B: Justice B.R. Gavai
options.C: Justice Surya Kant
options.D: Justice U.U. Lalit

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Justice Sanjiv Khanna took oath as the 51st Chief Justice of India on 11 November 2024 (Supreme Court/PIB) and retired on 13 May 2025. Justice B.R. Gavai succeeded him as the 52nd CJI on 14 May 2025.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Justice Gavai became the 52nd CJI in May 2025, after Justice Khanna. | Trap (C): Justice Surya Kant became CJI in November 2025, later in the line of succession. | Trap (D): Justice Lalit was the 49th CJI (2022), Justice Chandrachud's predecessor.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Judiciary – 51st Chief Justice of India
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Surya Kant retires 9 Feb 2027; the trap text stays true (valid until 2027-02-09)

questions.question_text:
In the first decade of the twentieth century, the British government introduced a package of constitutional reforms in India, partly to rally moderate opinion in the Indian National Congress after the agitation against the partition of Bengal. The size of the central and provincial legislative councils was enlarged considerably, and members were allowed to discuss the budget, move resolutions and ask supplementary questions, though the councils remained largely advisory. For the first time, an Indian, Satyendra Prasanna Sinha, was appointed to the Viceroy's Executive Council as Law Member. The most controversial feature was a provision under which members of one community would be elected only by voters belonging to that community. Nationalist leaders criticised this as an attempt to divide Indians on religious lines, and later historians saw it as a step that sharpened communal politics in the decades that followed.

Which enactment introduced these reforms?

options.A: Indian Councils Act, 1892
options.B: Government of India Act, 1919
options.C: Indian Councils Act, 1909
options.D: Government of India Act, 1935

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The reforms are the Morley–Minto Reforms, enacted as the Indian Councils Act, 1909 (NCERT/modern Indian history). The Act introduced separate electorates for Muslims, and Satyendra Prasanna Sinha became the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The 1892 Act also enlarged councils and allowed budget discussion, but it had no separate electorates. | Trap (B): The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy and extended communal representation to other groups; it did not introduce it. | Trap (D): The 1935 Act provided provincial autonomy and a proposed federation, much later.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – History – Indian Councils Act 1909

questions.question_text:
Article 356 empowers the President to assume the functions of a State government if satisfied, on the Governor's report or otherwise, that the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar hoped the provision would remain a dead letter, but it was invoked more than a hundred times in the following decades, often to dismiss elected governments run by parties opposed to the ruling party at the Centre. In April 1989, the Karnataka government was dismissed on the Governor's report that it had lost its majority after defections, without being given a chance to prove its strength in the Assembly. The resulting challenge, heard together with petitions concerning other States, was decided by a nine-judge bench in March 1994. The Court held that the floor of the House is the proper place to test a majority, that the proclamation is open to judicial review, and that secularism is part of the basic structure.

In which case was this ruling delivered?

options.A: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
options.B: State of Rajasthan v. Union of India
options.C: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
options.D: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu

questions.pedagogical_explanation: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), a nine-judge bench decision (Supreme Court judgment), arose from the 1989 dismissal of the Bommai government in Karnataka. It held that Article 356 proclamations are subject to judicial review, that majority must be tested on the floor of the House, and that secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): An earlier (1977) Article 356 case, about dissolving nine State Assemblies, that treated the President's satisfaction as largely non-justiciable. | Trap (C): A later (2006) case that held the 2005 dissolution of the Bihar Assembly unconstitutional; same subject, different case. | Trap (D): A 1992 case on the validity of the Tenth Schedule; defections link it to the facts here.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – S.R. Bommai (1994) and Article 356

questions.question_text: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described which Article of the Constitution as its 'very soul' and 'very heart'?

options.A: Article 32
options.B: Article 226
options.C: Article 21
options.D: Article 14

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 32, the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, was described by Dr. Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly (Constituent Assembly Debates, December 1948) as the very soul and heart of the Constitution.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Article 226 also gives writ jurisdiction, but to High Courts, and it is not a Fundamental Right. | Trap (C): Article 21 is the most widely interpreted right, but it is not the one Ambedkar described this way. | Trap (D): Article 14 (equality) is basic to the Constitution, but the description refers to the remedy, Article 32.

questions.question_text:
The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution lists the languages of India recognised for specific constitutional purposes. Under Article 344, the Official Language Commission is to include members representing these languages, and Article 351 directs the Union to promote the spread of Hindi and to enrich it by drawing on the forms, style and expressions of Hindustani and of the other languages specified in the Schedule. When the Constitution came into force, the Schedule contained fourteen languages. It has since been expanded through three constitutional amendments, passed in 1967, 1992 and 2003, taking the total to twenty-two. Demands for inclusion continue to be raised on behalf of several more languages, and the Union government has stated in Parliament that there are no fixed criteria for deciding such claims. Inclusion carries practical benefits: candidates may write certain all-India competitive examinations in these languages, and the languages receive institutional support for literature and education.

Which group of languages was added to the Schedule by the Constitution (92nd Amendment) Act, 2003?

options.A: Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali and Sindhi
options.B: Sindhi, Konkani, Bodo and Dogri
options.C: Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali
options.D: Maithili, Santhali, Bhojpuri and Rajasthani

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Eighth Schedule (Constitution text) now lists 22 languages: Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment (1967), Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali by the 71st Amendment (1992), and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali by the 92nd Amendment (2003).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Mixes the 71st Amendment, 1992 (Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali) with the 21st Amendment, 1967 (Sindhi). | Trap (B): Mixes languages from all three amendments; only Bodo and Dogri came in 2003. | Trap (D): Bhojpuri and Rajasthani are long-standing demands that have not been included.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Constitution – Eighth Schedule (92nd Amendment)

questions.question_text: Which of the following was NOT among the recipients of the Bharat Ratna announced in 2024?

options.A: Karpoori Thakur
options.B: P.V. Narasimha Rao
options.C: Pranab Mukherjee
options.D: M.S. Swaminathan

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Bharat Ratna was announced for five persons in 2024: Karpoori Thakur (23 January), L.K. Advani (3 February), and P.V. Narasimha Rao, Chaudhary Charan Singh and M.S. Swaminathan (9 February) (PIB/Rashtrapati Bhavan). Pranab Mukherjee received the award in 2019.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Karpoori Thakur was announced on 23 January 2024, the eve of his birth centenary. | Trap (B): P.V. Narasimha Rao was announced on 9 February 2024, along with two others. | Trap (D): M.S. Swaminathan, the agricultural scientist, was announced on 9 February 2024.

questions.question_text: In Tibet, the river Brahmaputra is known as:

options.A: Jamuna
options.B: Tsangpo (Yarlung Tsangpo)
options.C: Siang (Dihang)
options.D: Padma

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Brahmaputra rises near Mansarovar in the Chemayungdung glacier of Tibet, where it is called the Tsangpo. It enters India in Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang/Dihang and flows into Bangladesh as the Jamuna (NCERT Geography).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Jamuna is the Brahmaputra's main channel in Bangladesh, not Tibet. | Trap (C): Siang/Dihang is its name in Arunachal Pradesh, after it enters India. | Trap (D): Padma is the name of the Ganga in Bangladesh.

questions.question_text: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that the right to privacy is:

options.A: Not a fundamental right, as held in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh
options.B: A fundamental right flowing only from Article 19(1)(a)
options.C: A constitutional right under Article 300A
options.D: A fundamental right protected as an intrinsic part of Article 21 and the freedoms in Part III

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, decided on 24 August 2017 by a nine-judge bench (Supreme Court judgment), unanimously held privacy to be a fundamental right intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and part of Part III, overruling contrary observations in M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) observations were overruled by this bench. | Trap (B): Too narrow: the Court rooted privacy mainly in Article 21, not only in free speech. | Trap (C): Article 300A is the right to property, a constitutional but not a fundamental right.

questions.question_text: The Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, which deals with disqualification on the ground of defection, was added by which amendment?

options.A: 52nd Amendment Act, 1985
options.B: 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
options.C: 91st Amendment Act, 2003
options.D: 61st Amendment Act, 1988

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the Constitution (52nd Amendment) Act, 1985 (Constitution text). Its validity was upheld in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992). The 91st Amendment Act, 2003 later removed the split exception.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The 42nd Amendment ('mini-Constitution') made sweeping changes but did not add the anti-defection law. | Trap (C): The 91st Amendment only modified the Tenth Schedule, deleting the one-third 'split' exception and capping ministry size. | Trap (D): The 61st Amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18; close in time to 1985.

questions.question_text: The superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President is vested in the Election Commission by:

options.A: Article 324
options.B: Article 326
options.C: Article 243K
options.D: Article 329

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 324 (Part XV, Constitution text) vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission. Local body elections fall under State Election Commissions (Articles 243K and 243ZA).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Article 326 provides for elections on the basis of adult suffrage; it is in the same Part XV. | Trap (C): Article 243K creates the State Election Commissions for panchayat elections. | Trap (D): Article 329 bars courts from interfering in electoral matters except through election petitions.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Constitutional body – Election Commission (Article 324)

questions.question_text: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 replaced which law?

options.A: Indian Penal Code, 1860
options.B: Indian Evidence Act, 1872
options.C: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
options.D: Information Technology Act, 2000

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (170 sections), in force from 1 July 2024, repealed and replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (Gazette of India/MHA). It treats electronic and digital records as documents with the same legal standing as paper records.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The IPC was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. | Trap (C): The CrPC was replaced by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. | Trap (D): The BSA expands the treatment of electronic records, but the IT Act remains in force.

questions.question_text:
In May 1998, India conducted a series of five nuclear tests at the Indian Army's Pokhran test range in the Thar Desert of Rajasthan. Three devices, including a thermonuclear device, were detonated on the first day and two low-yield devices two days later, after which the Prime Minister declared that India had become a nuclear weapon state. The operation, codenamed Operation Shakti, was carried out jointly by the Defence Research and Development Organisation and the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre under great secrecy, avoiding detection by foreign surveillance satellites. The tests came twenty-four years after India's first nuclear test of 1974, codenamed Smiling Buddha. They drew economic sanctions from several countries, but India soon announced a voluntary moratorium on further testing and later adopted a nuclear doctrine based on credible minimum deterrence and no first use.

The date of the first of these tests is observed every year in India as:

options.A: National Science Day
options.B: National Space Day
options.C: Engineers' Day
options.D: National Technology Day

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The first Pokhran-II tests (Operation Shakti) were conducted on 11 May 1998, and 11 May is observed as National Technology Day (PIB/DST). Two further devices were tested on 13 May 1998.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): National Science Day (28 February) marks C.V. Raman's discovery of the Raman Effect. | Trap (B): National Space Day (23 August) marks the Chandrayaan-3 landing. | Trap (C): Engineers' Day (15 September) marks the birth anniversary of M. Visvesvaraya.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Science & tech – Pokhran-II / National Technology Day

questions.question_text:
In December 2024, an eighteen-year-old Indian grandmaster became the youngest undisputed World Chess Champion in history. He defeated the reigning champion, Ding Liren of China, by 7.5 to 6.5 in a fourteen-game match held in Singapore, winning the decisive final classical game after his opponent erred in a drawish endgame. He had earned the right to challenge for the title by winning the Candidates Tournament in Toronto in April 2024, becoming the youngest player ever to win that event. A few months before the title match, he was also part of the Indian men's team that won its first-ever gold medal at the Chess Olympiad in Budapest, where he also won an individual gold medal on the top board. His victory made him only the second Indian to hold the classical world title, and it was celebrated as a landmark for the rapidly growing chess culture in the country.

Who is the player described in the passage?

options.A: R. Praggnanandhaa
options.B: Arjun Erigaisi
options.C: D. Gukesh
options.D: Viswanathan Anand

questions.pedagogical_explanation: On 12 December 2024, D. Gukesh beat Ding Liren 7.5–6.5 in Singapore to become, at 18, the youngest undisputed World Chess Champion (FIDE). He had won the Candidates Tournament in Toronto in April 2024 and an individual board-one gold at the Budapest Chess Olympiad in September 2024.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Praggnanandhaa was runner-up at the 2023 FIDE World Cup, the other young Indian star. | Trap (B): Erigaisi was also on the 2024 Olympiad gold team, but he did not play the world title match. | Trap (D): Anand is the five-time world champion and the first Indian to hold the title, not the 2024 winner.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Sports – World Chess Championship 2024
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Title defence vs Javokhir Sindarov, Geneva, 24 Nov–12 Dec 2026. The question is about Dec 2024, so the key stays correct, but re-check any 'reigning champion' wording after 12 Dec 2026 (valid until 2026-12-12)

questions.question_text: The World Trade Organization (WTO) is headquartered in:

options.A: New York
options.B: Washington, D.C.
options.C: Vienna
options.D: Geneva

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The WTO, set up on 1 January 1995 under the Marrakesh Agreement to succeed GATT, is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland (WTO official site).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): New York hosts the UN headquarters, not the WTO. | Trap (B): Washington, D.C. hosts the IMF and World Bank, the other Bretton Woods-linked economic bodies. | Trap (C): Vienna hosts the IAEA, UNIDO and OPEC, other economic or technical bodies.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – International organisations – WTO headquarters

questions.question_text:
The Tropic of Cancer, located at about 23.5 degrees North latitude, marks the northernmost line on Earth where the Sun can appear directly overhead at noon, which happens around the June solstice. In India, the line divides the country into almost two equal parts: the region to its south lies in the tropical zone, while the region to its north falls in the subtropical or warm temperate zone. The line enters India from the west in the Rann of Kutch and runs eastward across the central part of the country, passing near cities such as Gandhinagar, Ujjain and Bhopal, before crossing into Bangladesh. It then re-enters India in the north-east and finally passes into Myanmar. Altogether, the Tropic passes through eight Indian States, a fact that frequently appears in competitive examinations because candidates tend to confuse States lying just north or south of the line.

The Tropic of Cancer does NOT pass through which of the following States?

options.A: Odisha
options.B: Tripura
options.C: Chhattisgarh
options.D: Mizoram

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight States: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram (NCERT Geography). Odisha lies entirely south of it.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Tropic does pass through Tripura in the north-east. | Trap (C): The Tropic does pass through northern Chhattisgarh, between Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand. | Trap (D): The Tropic does pass through Mizoram before entering Myanmar.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Geography – Tropic of Cancer

questions.question_text: The Finance Commission, which recommends how tax revenues are shared between the Union and the States, is constituted under which Article?

options.A: Article 263
options.B: Article 279A
options.C: Article 280
options.D: Article 270

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 280 of the Constitution (Constitution text) requires the President to constitute a Finance Commission every five years or earlier. It has a chairman and four other members and recommends how the net proceeds of shareable taxes are divided.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 263 provides for the Inter-State Council, another Union–State coordination body. | Trap (B): Article 279A provides for the GST Council, which also deals with Union–State fiscal matters. | Trap (D): Article 270 provides for taxes levied and distributed between the Union and States, but it does not set up the Commission.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Constitutional body – Finance Commission

questions.question_text: The Battle of Plassey, which laid the foundation of British political power in Bengal, was fought in:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 between Robert Clive's East India Company forces and Siraj-ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal, whose commander Mir Jafar defected (NCERT history).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 1764 is the Battle of Buxar, which consolidated British power and led to the Diwani of 1765. | Trap (B): 1761 is the Third Battle of Panipat between the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali. | Trap (D): 1857 is the Revolt; it happened exactly a hundred years after Plassey.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – History – Battle of Plassey

questions.question_text: The Indian Penal Code, 1860 had 511 sections. How many sections does the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced it, contain?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 as enacted has 358 sections (Gazette of India, Act No. 45 of 2023), against 511 in the IPC. The BNSS has 531 sections and the BSA has 170.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): 531 is the number of sections in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (replacing the CrPC). | Trap (C): 170 is the number of sections in the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (replacing the Evidence Act). | Trap (D): 356 was the section count of the original BNS Bill introduced in August 2023; the Bill was withdrawn and reintroduced in December 2023, and the enacted BNS has 358 sections.

questions.question_text: NITI Aayog, which replaced the Planning Commission, came into existence on:

options.A: 15 March 1950
options.B: 1 January 2015
options.D: 1 April 2017

questions.pedagogical_explanation: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was constituted by a Union Cabinet resolution and came into existence on 1 January 2015, with the Prime Minister as chairperson (PIB/NITI Aayog official site).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 15 March 1950 is when the Planning Commission was set up. | Trap (C): 26 May 2014 is when the new Union government took office, before NITI Aayog was created. | Trap (D): 1 April 2017 came just after the 12th Five-Year Plan ended; this date is confused with the end of plan-era planning.

questions.question_text:
The Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025 received Presidential assent on 4 April 2025 and came into force on 1 September 2025. It gives a single statutory framework for passports and travel documents of persons entering India, visas, registration of foreigners, and the duties of carriers such as airlines and ships, and of hotels, universities and hospitals that host foreign nationals. The Bureau of Immigration is placed on a statutory footing. In doing so, Parliament consolidated four older laws, three of them enacted before Independence, into one Act and repealed them.

Which of the following laws was NOT repealed by the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025?

options.A: The Immigration (Carriers' Liability) Act, 2000
options.B: The Foreigners Act, 1946
options.C: The Citizenship Act, 1955
options.D: The Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Section 36 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025 repeals the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920, the Registration of Foreigners Act, 1939, the Foreigners Act, 1946 and the Immigration (Carriers' Liability) Act, 2000 (India Code; MHA notification S.O. 3981(E) of 31 Aug 2025). The Citizenship Act, 1955 deals with acquiring and losing citizenship and remains in force.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): It was repealed; it is the one post-Independence law among the four, so it looks safe but is not. | Trap (B): It was repealed; it was the main pre-Independence law on the powers over foreigners. | Trap (D): It was repealed; registration of foreigners is now covered by the 2025 Act.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Law – Immigration and Foreigners Act 2025

questions.question_text: In November 2025, the Commonwealth Sport General Assembly confirmed which Indian city as the host of the centenary Commonwealth Games in 2030?

options.A: Bhubaneswar
options.B: Ahmedabad (Amdavad)
options.C: New Delhi
options.D: Abuja

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Delegates of the 74 Commonwealth nations and territories ratified Amdavad (Ahmedabad), Gujarat, as host of the 2030 Centenary Games at the General Assembly in Glasgow on 26 Nov 2025 (PIB, 26 Nov 2025; Commonwealth Sport). The 2030 Games mark 100 years since the first Games at Hamilton, Canada, in 1930.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Bhubaneswar has hosted hockey events but was not the 2030 bid city. | Trap (C): New Delhi hosted the 2010 Commonwealth Games, not the 2030 edition. | Trap (D): Abuja (Nigeria) was the rival bid that Ahmedabad was preferred over.

questions.question_text: Gyanesh Kumar, who took charge as Chief Election Commissioner on 19 February 2025, was the first CEC appointed under the 2023 law on the appointment of Election Commissioners. Under that law, the selection committee that recommends names to the President consists of:
