options.A: The Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister
options.B: The Prime Minister, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha
options.C: The President, the Vice-President and the Chief Justice of India, acting on the advice of the Cabinet Secretary
options.D: The Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 sets up a committee of the PM, the Leader of Opposition (or leader of the largest opposition party) in the Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM. Gyanesh Kumar became the 26th CEC on 19 Feb 2025 (ECI press note, 19 Feb 2025).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Speaker sits on the panel for the NHRC and Lokpal-type bodies, not on the panel for Election Commissioners. | Trap (C): No such panel exists; the President appoints on the committee's recommendation. | Trap (D): This was the interim panel ordered by the Supreme Court in Anoop Baranwal (March 2023) until Parliament made a law.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Polity – Selection of the Chief Election Commissioner
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: CEC Gyanesh Kumar (from 19 Feb 2025, term to Jan 2029); 2023 Act selection panel is under challenge in the Supreme Court. (recheck: if the SC rules on the 2023 Act)

questions.question_text:
In April 2025, in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu, a two-judge Bench of the Supreme Court fixed time limits for Governors and the President to act on State Bills and treated ten pending Bills as having received assent. In May 2025, the President referred fourteen questions on Articles 200 and 201 to the Supreme Court. On 20 November 2025, a five-judge Constitution Bench gave its unanimous opinion.

Consider the following statements:
1. The President made the reference under Article 143(1) of the Constitution.
2. The Constitution Bench held that courts may prescribe uniform time limits within which a Governor must act on a Bill.
3. The Constitution Bench held that the concept of 'deemed assent' by a court order is alien to the Constitution.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

options.A: 2 and 3 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 1 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Special Reference No. 1 of 2025 was made under Article 143(1) on 13 May 2025. On 20 Nov 2025 the Bench led by CJI B.R. Gavai held that courts cannot impose timelines on the Governor or President under Articles 200/201 and that deemed assent is alien to the Constitution, though prolonged, unexplained inaction may invite a limited mandamus (SC opinion, 20 Nov 2025; The Hindu; SC Observer).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Statement 2 is wrong: the Bench refused to impose judicial timelines. | Trap (C): Misses statement 3: the Bench expressly rejected deemed assent. | Trap (D): Statement 2 is the April 2025 two-judge view, which the Constitution Bench said was erroneous.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Judiciary – Presidential Reference on assent to Bills (2025)

questions.question_text: The 2025 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was awarded 'for having explained innovation-driven economic growth'. Who were the laureates?

options.A: Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt
options.B: Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer
options.C: Ben Bernanke, Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig
options.D: Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James A. Robinson

questions.pedagogical_explanation: One half went to Joel Mokyr (prerequisites for sustained growth through technological progress) and the other half jointly to Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt (theory of sustained growth through creative destruction) (nobelprize.org, 2025).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): They won in 2019, for the experimental approach to reducing poverty. | Trap (C): They won in 2022, for research on banks and financial crises. | Trap (D): They won in 2024, for work on how institutions affect prosperity.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Awards – Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences 2025

questions.question_text: The Nobel Peace Prize 2025 was awarded to María Corina Machado for her work promoting democratic rights in which country?

options.A: Colombia
options.B: Iran
options.C: Venezuela
options.D: Belarus

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 2025 Peace Prize went to María Corina Machado 'for her tireless work promoting democratic rights for the people of Venezuela and for her struggle to achieve a just and peaceful transition from dictatorship to democracy' (nobelprize.org, 2025).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Colombia's Juan Manuel Santos won in 2016 for the peace process with FARC. | Trap (B): Narges Mohammadi of Iran won the Peace Prize in 2023. | Trap (D): Ales Bialiatski of Belarus shared the Peace Prize in 2022.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Awards – Nobel Peace Prize 2025

questions.question_text: László Krasznahorkai, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature 2025, is a novelist from which country?

options.A: Poland
options.B: South Korea
options.C: Hungary
options.D: Norway

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Krasznahorkai, born in 1954 in Gyula, Hungary, was honoured 'for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art' (nobelprize.org, 2025).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Olga Tokarczuk of Poland won the delayed 2018 Literature Prize. | Trap (B): Han Kang of South Korea won the Literature Prize in 2024. | Trap (D): Jon Fosse of Norway won the Literature Prize in 2023.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Awards – Nobel Prize in Literature 2025

questions.question_text:
The Government of India has notified that the next Population Census will be held in two phases, with caste enumeration included in the population-enumeration phase. Houselisting is the first phase; population enumeration is the second. For Ladakh and the snow-bound, non-synchronous areas of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, the reference date is 00:00 hours of 1 October 2026.

What is the reference date for the rest of the country?

options.A: 00:00 hours of 1 October 2027
options.B: 00:00 hours of 1 March 2027
options.C: 00:00 hours of 1 January 2027
options.D: 00:00 hours of 1 March 2021

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The gazette notification of June 2025 fixes 00:00 hours of 1 March 2027 as the reference date, and 1 October 2026 for Ladakh and snow-bound areas of J&K, HP and Uttarakhand (PIB; The Hindu). Caste enumeration is part of Phase II.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Confuses the month: 1 October is the date only for the snow-bound areas, and in 2026. | Trap (C): Not a notified reference date for any part of the country. | Trap (D): This was the reference date planned for the 2021 Census, which was postponed.
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Census 2027 reference dates as notified June 2025. (recheck: if re-notified)

questions.question_text:
In July 2025, at Batumi, Georgia, two Indian players met in the final of the FIDE Women's World Cup. After both classical games were drawn, the 19-year-old from Nagpur won the rapid tiebreak 1.5–0.5. With the title she also earned the Grandmaster title automatically, becoming India's 88th Grandmaster and only its fourth woman Grandmaster.

Who won the FIDE Women's World Cup 2025?

options.A: Harika Dronavalli
options.B: Divya Deshmukh
options.C: Koneru Humpy
options.D: R. Vaishali

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Divya Deshmukh beat Koneru Humpy 1.5–0.5 in the rapid tiebreak on 28 Jul 2025, becoming the first Indian woman to win the Women's World Cup and India's 88th GM (FIDE; The Hindu, Jul 2025).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Harika is a woman Grandmaster from earlier years; she did not reach the 2025 final. | Trap (C): Humpy was the losing finalist; she is already a Grandmaster. | Trap (D): Vaishali became India's third woman Grandmaster in 2023; she did not win this event.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Sports – FIDE Women's World Cup 2025

questions.question_text: Which team won the ICC World Test Championship final played at Lord's in June 2025?

options.A: South Africa
options.B: Australia
options.C: New Zealand
options.D: India

questions.pedagogical_explanation: South Africa beat Australia by five wickets at Lord's (11–14 Jun 2025) to win the third WTC final, their first ICC title since 1998 (ICC).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Australia won the 2023 final and lost the 2025 final. | Trap (C): New Zealand won the first final in 2021. | Trap (D): India lost the 2021 and 2023 finals and did not play in 2025.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Sports – World Test Championship final 2025

questions.question_text:
NISAR, an Earth-observation satellite, was launched from Sriharikota on 30 July 2025. It is the first satellite to carry synthetic aperture radars in two frequency bands, allowing it to map changes in land, ice and vegetation through clouds and at night. It was placed in a sun-synchronous polar orbit.

Which of the following correctly describes NISAR?

options.A: A joint NASA–ISRO mission launched on PSLV-C60; ISRO provided the L-band radar and NASA the S-band radar
options.B: A joint ESA–ISRO mission launched on GSLV-F16; ESA provided the L-band radar and ISRO the S-band radar
options.C: An ISRO-only mission launched on LVM3; it carries both L-band and S-band radars built in Bengaluru
options.D: A joint NASA–ISRO mission launched on GSLV-F16; NASA provided the L-band radar and ISRO the S-band radar

questions.pedagogical_explanation: NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) lifted off on GSLV-F16 on 30 Jul 2025. NASA built the L-band SAR and ISRO the S-band SAR (ISRO mission page; NASA news release, 30 Jul 2025).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): PSLV-C60 launched SpaDeX in December 2024, and the bands are swapped. | Trap (B): The partner was NASA, not the European Space Agency. | Trap (C): It is a joint mission; LVM3 carried Chandrayaan-3, not NISAR.

questions.question_text: The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025, which received Presidential assent on 22 August 2025, prohibits which of the following?

options.A: Offering online games of pure chance only, while leaving games of skill free
options.B: Offering online money games, whether based on skill, chance or both
options.C: Online social and educational games that are played by users below 18
options.D: Organising e-sports tournaments without prior licence from a State Government

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Act prohibits offering, advertising and facilitating payments for online money games, 'irrespective of whether such game is based on skill, chance, or both', and promotes e-sports and online social games (Gazette, 22 Aug 2025; MeitY).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Act's ban does not depend on the skill-versus-chance distinction. | Trap (C): Social and educational games are promoted under the Act, not prohibited. | Trap (D): The Act seeks to promote e-sports and recognises them; it does not ban them.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Law – Online Gaming Act 2025
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Online Gaming Act 2025 is under challenge before the Supreme Court. (recheck: if struck down or amended)

questions.question_text:
In August 2025, the Union Government introduced the Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill in the Lok Sabha. It proposes that a Minister, including the Prime Minister or a Chief Minister, who is arrested and detained for thirty consecutive days on a charge of an offence punishable with imprisonment of five years or more, shall be removed or cease to hold office. The Bill was referred to a Joint Committee of Parliament.

Consider the following statements:
1. The Bill proposes to amend Articles 75 and 164 of the Constitution.
2. The Bill also covers Ministers in the National Capital Territory of Delhi through Article 239AA.
3. Removal under the Bill requires a conviction by a trial court.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

options.A: 2 and 3 only
options.B: 1, 2 and 3
options.C: 1 only
options.D: 1 and 2 only

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Bill amends Article 75 (Union), Article 164 (States) and Article 239AA (Delhi). The trigger is arrest and detention for 30 consecutive days for an offence punishable with 5 years or more; no conviction is needed (PRS Bill track; Indian Express). It was referred to a Joint Committee and has not been passed.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Statement 3 is wrong, and statement 1 is correct. | Trap (B): Statement 3 is wrong: the trigger is 30 days of detention on a charge, not a conviction. | Trap (C): Misses statement 2: Article 239AA (Delhi) is also amended.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Polity – Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill 2025
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Constitution (130th Amendment) Bill 2025 is with a Joint Committee (deadline extended to Winter Session 2026). If passed or lapsed, update stem and explanation. (recheck: after Winter Session 2026)

questions.question_text: Under which Article of the Constitution of India can the President seek the opinion of the Supreme Court on a question of law or fact of public importance?

options.A: Article 142
options.B: Article 141
options.C: Article 143
options.D: Article 137

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 143 gives the Supreme Court advisory jurisdiction. The opinion is not binding on the President in the way a judgment binds parties (Constitution text).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass orders for complete justice. | Trap (B): Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts. | Trap (D): Article 137 deals with the Supreme Court's power to review its own judgments.

questions.question_text: An Ordinance promulgated by the President under Article 123, unless approved earlier, ceases to operate:

options.A: at the end of six weeks from the date it was promulgated
options.B: at the end of fourteen days from the reassembly of Parliament
options.C: at the end of six months from the date it was promulgated
options.D: at the end of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 123(2)(a): an Ordinance must be laid before both Houses and ceases to operate six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, unless disapproved earlier. So its maximum life is about six months and six weeks (Constitution text).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Counts six weeks from promulgation instead of from reassembly. | Trap (B): Fourteen days is the Rajya Sabha's limit for returning a Money Bill. | Trap (C): Six months is the maximum gap allowed between two sessions, not the life of an Ordinance.

questions.question_text: The guidelines laid down by the Supreme Court in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) dealt with:

options.A: compulsory registration of FIRs in cognizable offences
options.B: the validity of instant triple talaq among Muslims
options.C: safeguards to be followed by police during arrest and detention
options.D: sexual harassment of women at the workplace

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Vishaka (1997) used CEDAW and Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 to frame guidelines on sexual harassment at work. They were replaced by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): That is Lalita Kumari v. Government of U.P. (2013). | Trap (B): That is Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017). | Trap (C): That is D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997).

questions.question_text: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court struck down which provision as violating free speech?

options.A: Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000
options.B: Section 124A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
options.C: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000
options.D: Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Court held Section 66A (offensive messages) vague and overbroad and not saved by Article 19(2). It upheld Section 69A and read down Section 79.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Section 79 (intermediary safe harbour) was read down, not struck down. | Trap (B): Sedition was kept in abeyance in 2022 (S.G. Vombatkere), not struck down in 2015. | Trap (D): The Court upheld Section 69A (website blocking) with its procedural safeguards.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – Shreya Singhal (2015)

questions.question_text: In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018), a Constitution Bench struck down which provision of the Indian Penal Code?

options.A: Section 497 (adultery)
options.B: Section 498A (cruelty by husband or relatives)
options.C: Section 309 (attempt to commit suicide)
options.D: Section 377, as applied to consensual adult relations

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The five-judge Bench held Section 497 IPC unconstitutional under Articles 14, 15 and 21, as it treated a woman as her husband's property. Adultery remains a civil ground for divorce. The BNS has no adultery offence.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Section 498A was upheld and remains in force, now as Section 85–86 BNS. | Trap (C): Section 309 was not struck down; the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 limited its use. | Trap (D): That was read down in Navtej Singh Johar (2018), a different case in the same year.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – Joseph Shine (2018)

questions.question_text:
On 1 August 2024, a seven-judge Bench of the Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh ruled on whether States may create sub-categories within the Scheduled Castes so that the more backward groups get a separate share of the reserved seats. The majority reasoned that the Scheduled Castes are not a homogeneous class and that States may sub-classify on the basis of quantifiable, empirical data.

Consider the following statements:
1. The decision was by a majority of 6:1.
2. The decision overruled E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2004).
3. The decision held, as binding law, that the creamy-layer exclusion must apply to the Scheduled Castes.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 1, 2 and 3
options.D: 2 only

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Bench led by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud held 6:1 (Justice Trivedi dissenting) that sub-classification of SCs is permissible, overruling E.V. Chinnaiah (2004). Justice B.R. Gavai and some others suggested a creamy layer for SCs, but this was not part of the binding majority holding (SC judgment, 1 Aug 2024).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Statement 2 is correct, and statement 3 is wrong. | Trap (C): Statement 3 is wrong: the creamy-layer remarks were in separate concurring opinions, not the binding majority holding. | Trap (D): Misses statement 1: Justice Bela M. Trivedi dissented, so it was 6:1.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – Sub-classification of SCs (2024)
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: Creamy layer for SCs was in concurring opinions only; statement 3 deliberately false.

questions.question_text:
In July 2024, a nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court decided Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India. The dispute was whether the royalty paid by mining lessees is itself a tax, and therefore whether the States can levy their own taxes on mineral rights and mineral-bearing land. An earlier seven-judge decision of 1989, India Cement Ltd., had been read as saying that royalty is a tax. Justice B.V. Nagarathna dissented.

What did the majority hold?

options.A: Royalty is a tax, so only Parliament can tax mineral rights under the Union List
options.B: Royalty is not a tax, but States cannot tax mineral rights at all under the Constitution
options.C: Royalty is a tax, but States may still levy it with the President's prior assent
options.D: Royalty is not a tax, and States can tax mineral rights and mineral-bearing land

questions.pedagogical_explanation: By 8:1 on 25 Jul 2024, the Bench held that royalty is a contractual payment, not a tax; that the MMDR Act does not limit the States' power to tax mineral rights under Entry 50, List II; and that India Cement (1989) was wrong to that extent.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): This is the India Cement reading that the majority rejected. | Trap (B): Gets the first half right but denies the States' power that the majority upheld. | Trap (C): Mixes up the holding with the Article 304(b) procedure for trade restrictions.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – Mineral royalty (2024)

questions.question_text:
On 8 November 2024, a seven-judge Bench of the Supreme Court considered the test for deciding whether an educational institution was 'established' by a minority and so enjoys the right to administer it. By a 4:3 majority, it overruled a 1967 Constitution Bench decision which had held that the Aligarh Muslim University was not established by the Muslim minority because it was created by a central statute. The question of AMU's own status was left to a regular Bench.

Which 1967 decision was overruled?

options.A: St. Stephen's College v. University of Delhi
options.B: S. Azeez Basha v. Union of India
options.C: In re Kerala Education Bill
options.D: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (8 Nov 2024), the majority led by CJI Chandrachud overruled S. Azeez Basha (1967): creation by statute does not by itself defeat minority character under Article 30(1).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): St. Stephen's (1992) dealt with admissions in minority colleges, not this point. | Trap (C): The Kerala Education Bill reference (1958) was an early Article 30 opinion, not overruled here. | Trap (D): T.M.A. Pai (2002) is the 11-judge case on minority institutions; it was not overruled.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – AMU minority status (2024)
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: All minority-education cases; only Azeez Basha is from 1967.

questions.question_text:
In November 2024, a nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court, in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, examined whether every privately owned resource is a 'material resource of the community' that the State can acquire and distribute under a Directive Principle. By majority, it held that not every private resource falls within the phrase, and it disagreed with a broad view expressed by Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer in a minority opinion of 1977.

Which Directive Principle was interpreted, and in which earlier case did Justice Krishna Iyer express the broad view?

options.A: Article 39(b); Minerva Mills v. Union of India
options.B: Article 38; Sanjeev Coke Manufacturing v. Bharat Coking Coal
options.C: Article 39(b); State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy
options.D: Article 39(c); State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy

questions.pedagogical_explanation: On 5 Nov 2024 the majority led by CJI Chandrachud held that private resources are not automatically 'material resources of the community' under Article 39(b), departing from Justice Krishna Iyer's view in Ranganatha Reddy (1977), later followed in Sanjeev Coke (1983).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Minerva Mills (1980) dealt with Article 31C and basic structure, not this view. | Trap (B): Article 38 is the general welfare principle; Sanjeev Coke followed Krishna Iyer's view later. | Trap (D): Article 39(c) is about concentration of wealth; the phrase 'material resources of the community' is in 39(b).

questions.question_text: After the Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978, the right to property in India is:

options.A: a Fundamental Right under Article 31
options.B: a Directive Principle under Article 39(b)
options.C: a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(f)
options.D: a constitutional right under Article 300A

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 44th Amendment deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 and inserted Article 300A: no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 31 was repealed by the 44th Amendment. | Trap (B): Article 39(b) is about distribution of resources, not a right to property. | Trap (C): Article 19(1)(f) was deleted by the same amendment.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Constitution – Right to property

questions.question_text: Which ground for a National Emergency under Article 352 was substituted by the Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978?

options.A: 'Armed rebellion' was replaced by 'internal disturbance'
options.B: 'External aggression' was replaced by 'war'
options.C: 'Failure of constitutional machinery' was replaced by 'armed rebellion'
options.D: 'Internal disturbance' was replaced by 'armed rebellion'

questions.pedagogical_explanation: After the 1975 Emergency on the ground of internal disturbance, the 44th Amendment replaced it with 'armed rebellion' and required written advice of the Cabinet.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Reverses the change: the 1975 Emergency used 'internal disturbance'. | Trap (B): Both 'war' and 'external aggression' remain grounds. | Trap (C): Failure of constitutional machinery is the Article 356 ground.

questions.question_text: Which type of emergency provided for in the Constitution of India has never been proclaimed so far?

options.A: President's Rule under Article 356
options.B: Financial Emergency under Article 360
options.C: National Emergency under Article 352
options.D: National Emergency on the ground of external aggression

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 360 lets the President proclaim a Financial Emergency if the financial stability or credit of India is threatened. It has never been used.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): It has been imposed well over a hundred times in the States. | Trap (C): It has been proclaimed three times: 1962, 1971 and 1975. | Trap (D): This ground was used in 1962 and 1971.

questions.question_text: The writ that is issued to inquire into the legality of a person's claim to a public office is:

options.A: Mandamus
options.B: Certiorari
options.C: Habeas corpus
options.D: Quo warranto

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Quo warranto ('by what authority') lets the court ask on what authority a person holds a substantive public office (Articles 32 and 226).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Mandamus commands a public authority to perform a public duty. | Trap (B): Certiorari quashes an order already passed by a lower court or tribunal. | Trap (C): Habeas corpus asks for a detained person to be produced before the court.

questions.question_text:
Match the writs in List I with their purpose in List II.

List I: (P) Habeas corpus (Q) Mandamus (R) Prohibition (S) Certiorari

List II: (1) directs a public authority to perform a public duty it has failed to perform (2) stops a lower court from continuing a case beyond its jurisdiction while it is pending (3) quashes an order already passed by a lower court or tribunal without jurisdiction (4) requires a detaining authority to produce the detained person and justify the detention
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Habeas corpus: produce the body. Mandamus: perform a public duty. Prohibition: preventive, issued while proceedings are pending. Certiorari: corrective, quashes an order already made. All are available under Articles 32 and 226.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Swaps Prohibition and Certiorari: Prohibition acts while the case is pending, Certiorari after the order. | Trap (C): Swaps Habeas corpus and Mandamus. | Trap (D): Swaps Mandamus and Prohibition.

questions.question_text: If a question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill, whose decision is final?

options.A: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
options.B: The President of India
options.C: The Union Finance Minister
options.D: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 110(3): if any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill, the decision of the Speaker of the House of the People is final. The Speaker's certificate is endorsed on the Bill.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes to a Money Bill. | Trap (B): The President gives prior recommendation for introducing a Money Bill, but does not decide this question. | Trap (C): The Finance Minister introduces the Budget but does not certify Money Bills.

questions.question_text: Under Article 312, Parliament may create a new All India Service only if:

options.A: the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting
options.B: the Inter-State Council recommends it, followed by an order of the President
options.C: the Lok Sabha passes a resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting
options.D: a majority of State Legislatures ratify a Bill passed by Parliament

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 312(1): if the Council of States declares by a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of members present and voting that it is necessary in the national interest, Parliament may by law create one or more All India Services.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Inter-State Council (Article 263) has no such role. | Trap (C): The power is given to the Rajya Sabha, which represents the States. | Trap (D): Ratification by States applies to certain constitutional amendments under Article 368(2).
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Constitution – All India Services (Article 312)

questions.question_text: Who was appointed as the first Chairperson of the Lokpal of India, in 2019?

options.A: Justice A.M. Khanwilkar
options.B: Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai
options.C: Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose
options.D: Justice H.L. Dattu

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Lokpal was set up under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. Justice P.C. Ghose, a former Supreme Court judge, took oath as its first Chairperson in March 2019.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): He became Lokpal Chairperson later, in 2024. | Trap (B): She chaired the J&K Delimitation Commission and Uttarakhand's Uniform Civil Code panel. | Trap (D): He was a former CJI who later chaired the NHRC.
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Trap mentions Justice A.M. Khanwilkar as Lokpal Chairperson since 2024. (recheck: yearly)

questions.question_text: Which of the following offices is NOT created by the Constitution of India?

options.A: Solicitor General of India
options.B: Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
options.C: Advocate General for a State
options.D: Attorney General for India

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General are law officers appointed by the Government under the Law Officers (Conditions of Service) Rules, 1987, not under any Article of the Constitution.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Created by Article 148. | Trap (C): Created by Article 165. | Trap (D): Created by Article 76.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Constitutional posts – Solicitor General

questions.question_text: The National Green Tribunal was set up under the National Green Tribunal Act of which year?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The NGT Act, 2010 set up the Tribunal for speedy disposal of environmental cases. Its principal bench is in New Delhi.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 1986 is the year of the Environment (Protection) Act. | Trap (B): 1972 is the year of the Wild Life (Protection) Act. | Trap (D): 2002 is the year of the Biological Diversity Act.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Statutory body – National Green Tribunal

questions.question_text:
In the Oleum gas leak case, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), the Supreme Court laid down that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous activity is liable for harm caused by an accident in that activity, without any of the usual exceptions. A few years earlier, the Court noted, English law had developed a rule from Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) that allowed defences such as act of God and act of a third party. The Court said that this rule was not suited to an industrialising country.

What is the principle laid down in the M.C. Mehta case called?

options.A: Strict liability
options.B: Polluter pays
options.C: Absolute liability
options.D: Vicarious liability

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Court held that a hazardous enterprise owes an absolute, non-delegable duty and cannot claim the Rylands v. Fletcher exceptions. Compensation should also reflect the enterprise's size and capacity.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Strict liability is the Rylands v. Fletcher rule, which allows exceptions. | Trap (B): Polluter pays was adopted later, in Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996). | Trap (D): Vicarious liability makes one person liable for another's wrong, like an employer for an employee.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – Absolute liability (M.C. Mehta)

questions.question_text: The Supreme Court's guidelines in D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) are best known for setting safeguards relating to:

options.A: the conditions for imposing the death penalty
options.B: arrest and custodial detention by the police
options.C: protection of women from sexual harassment at the workplace
options.D: the right to a speedy trial for undertrial prisoners

questions.pedagogical_explanation: D.K. Basu laid down 11 requirements on arrest, such as identification of arresting officers, an arrest memo and informing a relative, to prevent custodial violence. Many were later written into the CrPC and now the BNSS.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): That is Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980). | Trap (C): That is Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997). | Trap (D): That is Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979).
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgment – D.K. Basu (1997)

questions.question_text: In Lalita Kumari v. Government of U.P. (2013), the Supreme Court held that registration of an FIR is mandatory when information discloses a cognizable offence. Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which section now deals with information in cognizable cases?

options.A: Section 154
options.B: Section 156
options.C: Section 35
options.D: Section 173

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Section 173 BNSS replaces Section 154 CrPC. It recognises Zero FIR and e-FIR, and permits a preliminary enquiry for offences punishable with 3 to under 7 years (BNSS text).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Section 154 was the FIR provision in the old CrPC, 1973. | Trap (B): Section 156 CrPC dealt with the police's power to investigate. | Trap (C): Section 35 BNSS deals with when the police may arrest without warrant.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023:
1. Information about a cognizable offence may be given electronically, and an FIR can be registered irrespective of where the offence was committed.
2. For offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven years, the police may hold a preliminary enquiry within fourteen days, with prior permission of a senior officer.
3. It abolished plea bargaining, which had been introduced into the CrPC in 2005.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Section 173(1) BNSS allows information by electronic communication and registration regardless of where the offence occurred. Section 173(3) allows a preliminary enquiry within 14 days for offences punishable with 3 to under 7 years, with permission of an officer not below DSP. Plea bargaining continues in Chapter XXIII (Sections 289–300).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Misses statement 2: Section 173(3) allows the 14-day preliminary enquiry. | Trap (C): Statement 1 is correct (e-FIR and Zero FIR), and statement 3 is wrong. | Trap (D): Statement 3 is wrong: plea bargaining is retained in the BNSS.
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: Relies on BNSS s.173(3) wording (DSP-level permission, 14 days).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the International Criminal Court (ICC) is correct?

options.A: It hears disputes only between States, on matters referred by the Security Council
options.B: It is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations and sits at The Hague
options.C: It was set up under the Rome Statute and sits at The Hague; India is not a party to it
options.D: It was set up under the Rome Statute and sits at Geneva; India is a party to it

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Rome Statute (1998) came into force on 1 Jul 2002. The ICC tries individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression. India, like the USA and China, is not a State Party.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): That mixes up ICJ contentious cases with the ICC, which tries individuals. | Trap (B): That describes the International Court of Justice, not the ICC. | Trap (D): The ICC sits at The Hague, and India has not joined the Rome Statute.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – International law – International Criminal Court

questions.question_text: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), 1982, a coastal State's territorial sea may extend up to:

options.A: 3 nautical miles from the baseline
options.B: 12 nautical miles from the baseline
options.C: 24 nautical miles from the baseline
options.D: 200 nautical miles from the baseline

questions.pedagogical_explanation: UNCLOS Article 3 lets a State fix its territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles. India's Maritime Zones Act, 1976 uses the same limits.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 3 miles was the old 'cannon-shot' rule, not the UNCLOS limit. | Trap (C): 24 nautical miles is the outer limit of the contiguous zone. | Trap (D): 200 nautical miles is the limit of the exclusive economic zone.

questions.question_text: How are the non-permanent members of the UN Security Council chosen?

options.A: Ten members are elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms
options.B: Ten members are elected by the General Assembly for five-year terms
options.C: Six members are elected by the Security Council itself for two-year terms
options.D: Ten members are appointed by the Secretary-General for two-year terms

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Under Article 23 of the UN Charter, the General Assembly elects ten non-permanent members for two-year terms, five each year, by a two-thirds majority. India has served eight terms, most recently 2021–22.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The term is two years, and retiring members are not eligible for immediate re-election. | Trap (C): The number was raised from six to ten in 1965, and the General Assembly elects them. | Trap (D): The Secretary-General has no role in choosing members.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – International law – UN Security Council
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: 'India has served eight UNSC terms, most recently 2021–22' in explanation. (recheck: if India is elected again (next bid 2028–29))

questions.question_text: How many Geneva Conventions were adopted in 1949, forming the core of international humanitarian law?

options.A: Two
options.B: Three
options.C: Five
options.D: Four

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The four Geneva Conventions of 12 Aug 1949 protect wounded soldiers on land, wounded and shipwrecked at sea, prisoners of war, and civilians. India gives effect to them through the Geneva Conventions Act, 1960.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Two Additional Protocols were adopted in 1977; the Conventions are four. | Trap (B): Three is the number of Additional Protocols (1977, 1977 and 2005). | Trap (C): No fifth Convention exists; the 1949 set is four.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – International law – Geneva Conventions

questions.question_text: The repo rate is the rate at which:

options.A: the RBI lends short-term funds to banks against government securities
options.B: the RBI lends to banks for long periods without any collateral
options.C: banks lend to their most creditworthy borrowers
options.D: banks park surplus funds with the RBI against government securities

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Under a repo, the RBI buys government securities from banks with an agreement to sell them back, injecting liquidity. It is the policy rate set by the MPC.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): That loosely describes the bank rate. | Trap (C): That is the bank's prime lending rate. | Trap (D): That describes the reverse repo.

questions.question_text: Since April 2022, which instrument forms the floor of the RBI's liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) corridor?

options.A: The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)
options.B: The bank rate
options.C: The fixed-rate reverse repo
options.D: The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The SDF lets the RBI absorb liquidity without giving collateral. It replaced the fixed-rate reverse repo as the floor, with the policy repo rate in between and the MSF at the top.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The bank rate is aligned with the MSF rate, at the ceiling. | Trap (C): It was the floor before April 2022. | Trap (D): The MSF forms the ceiling of the corridor.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Economy – Standing Deposit Facility

questions.question_text: Provincial autonomy was introduced by which Act?

options.A: Government of India Act, 1935
options.B: Indian Independence Act, 1947
options.C: Indian Councils Act, 1909
options.D: Government of India Act, 1919

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 1935 Act abolished dyarchy in the provinces and gave them autonomy from 1937. It proposed dyarchy at the Centre and a federation that never came into being.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The 1947 Act ended British rule and created two dominions. | Trap (C): The 1909 Act introduced separate electorates for Muslims. | Trap (D): The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – History – Government of India Act 1935

questions.question_text: The Poona Pact of 1932 between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar provided for:

options.A: joint Congress–League demands for reforms and separate electorates for Muslims
options.B: the release of political prisoners and suspension of Civil Disobedience
options.C: reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in a joint electorate, instead of separate electorates
options.D: separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, as in the Communal Award

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Gandhi fasted against separate electorates for the Depressed Classes under the Communal Award. The Poona Pact of 24 Sep 1932 gave 148 reserved seats in provincial legislatures within a joint electorate.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): That is the Lucknow Pact (1916). | Trap (B): That is the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931). | Trap (D): The Pact replaced the Communal Award's separate electorates.

questions.question_text:
In March 1946, the British Government sent three Cabinet Ministers to India to discuss the transfer of power and the making of a Constitution. The Mission proposed a three-tier structure with a weak Union, grouping of provinces, and a Constituent Assembly elected by the provincial assemblies.

Who led this Mission?

options.A: Sir Stafford Cripps
options.B: Lord Pethick-Lawrence
options.C: A.V. Alexander
options.D: Lord Wavell

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Cabinet Mission consisted of Lord Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State for India, leader), Sir Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander. Its plan of 16 May 1946 led to the elections to the Constituent Assembly.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Cripps was a member of the 1946 Mission but led the separate Cripps Mission of 1942. | Trap (C): Alexander was a member but did not lead the Mission. | Trap (D): Wavell was the Viceroy, not a member of the Cabinet Mission.

questions.question_text: Who presided over the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly on 9 December 1946 as its temporary chairman?

options.A: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
options.B: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
options.C: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
options.D: Sir B.N. Rau

questions.pedagogical_explanation: As the oldest member, Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary chairman at the first meeting, following French practice. Rajendra Prasad became President on 11 Dec 1946.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): He was elected permanent President on 11 Dec 1946. | Trap (B): He chaired the Drafting Committee from August 1947. | Trap (D): He was the Constitutional Adviser to the Assembly.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – History – Constituent Assembly first meeting

questions.question_text: Who moved the Objectives Resolution in the Constituent Assembly on 13 December 1946?

options.A: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
options.B: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
options.C: Jawaharlal Nehru
options.D: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 Dec 1946; the Assembly adopted it on 22 Jan 1947. It later became the basis of the Preamble.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): He was the President of the Assembly and presided over the debate. | Trap (B): He chaired the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities. | Trap (D): He chaired the Drafting Committee; he did not move the Objectives Resolution.

questions.question_text: After the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022, how many Schedules does the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 contain?

options.A: Six
options.B: Three
options.C: Five
options.D: Four

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 2022 amendment cut the Schedules from six to four: two for animals (by protection level), one for plants and one for CITES-listed specimens. The vermin schedule was deleted.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Six was the number before the 2022 rationalisation. | Trap (B): Counts only the animal and plant schedules and leaves out the CITES schedule. | Trap (C): Counts the vermin schedule, which the 2022 amendment removed.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Environment law – Wild Life (Protection) Act schedules

questions.question_text:
Match the Constitutional Amendment Acts in List I with their subject in List II.

List I: (P) 73rd (Q) 101st (R) 103rd (S) 104th

List II: (1) Goods and Services Tax (2) Panchayati Raj institutions (3) up to 10% reservation for economically weaker sections (4) extended SC/ST seat reservation in the Lok Sabha and Assemblies and ended Anglo-Indian nomination
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 73rd (1992): Panchayats. 101st (2016): GST. 103rd (2019): EWS reservation, Articles 15(6) and 16(6). 104th (2019/20): extended SC/ST reservation to 2030 and ended nomination of Anglo-Indians.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Swaps the 73rd and the 101st. | Trap (C): Swaps the 103rd and the 104th. | Trap (D): Swaps the 101st and the 103rd.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Polity – Constitutional amendments matching

questions.question_text: The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, also called the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserves what share of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and the State Legislative Assemblies?

options.A: One-half
options.B: One-third
options.C: One-fourth
options.D: One-fifth

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 106th Amendment inserted Articles 330A and 332A (and amended 239AA) to reserve one-third of seats for women, including within SC/ST seats. It applies after the first census and delimitation following the Act and lasts 15 years.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): One-half is the share many States give women in panchayats under their own laws. | Trap (C): No such share is used for women's reservation in legislatures. | Trap (D): No such share appears in the Amendment.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – Polity – 106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan)

questions.question_text: The Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 were brought into force on 21 November 2025. How many existing Central labour laws did these four Codes rationalise?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: PIB (21 Nov 2025): the four Labour Codes became effective on 21 November 2025, rationalising 29 existing Central labour laws.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The number of laws merged into the OSH Code alone. | Trap (C): The number of Codes, not the laws they replaced. | Trap (D): An older, often-quoted count of Central labour laws, not the official figure for the four Codes.
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Labour Codes in force from 21 Nov 2025; rules are still being framed and some old provisions continue during the transition.

questions.question_text: Under the four Labour Codes that took effect on 21 November 2025, the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Trade Unions Act, 1926 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 have been merged into which Code?

options.A: The Code on Wages, 2019
options.B: The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020
options.C: The Code on Social Security, 2020
options.D: The Industrial Relations Code, 2020

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 consolidates the three laws on industrial disputes, trade unions and standing orders.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): It merged the Payment of Wages, Minimum Wages, Payment of Bonus and Equal Remuneration Acts. | Trap (B): It merged the Factories Act, Mines Act, Contract Labour Act and similar safety laws. | Trap (C): It merged the EPF, ESI, Gratuity, Maternity Benefit and similar laws.

questions.question_text:
On the recommendation of the 56th meeting of the GST Council held on 3 September 2025, the structure of GST rates was simplified with effect from 22 September 2025. The earlier four main slabs were replaced to make the tax simpler for households and businesses, while a separate higher rate was kept for a small set of sin and luxury goods.

Which of the following correctly describes the new structure?

options.A: Two main rates of 5% and 18%, with a special rate of 40%
options.B: Three rates of 5%, 12% and 18%, with a special rate of 40%
options.C: A single rate of 18%, with a special rate of 28%
options.D: Two main rates of 12% and 18%, with a special rate of 28%

questions.pedagogical_explanation: PIB (Sept 2025): the four slabs (5%, 12%, 18%, 28%) became two, a 5% merit rate and an 18% standard rate, plus a 40% de-merit rate, effective 22 September 2025.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The 12% slab was folded into 5% or 18%. | Trap (C): There are two main rates, and the special rate is 40%, not 28%. | Trap (D): Keeps 12% and 28%, the slabs that were removed.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Economy – GST rate rationalisation 2025
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Tax rates can change at later GST Council meetings.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the GST changes effective from 22 September 2025:
1. They followed the recommendations of the 56th meeting of the GST Council.
2. Individual life insurance and individual health insurance policies were exempted from GST.
3. Cigarettes, chewing tobacco and beedi moved to the new 40% rate on 22 September 2025.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

options.A: 2 and 3 only
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 1, 2 and 3
options.D: 1 and 2 only

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The GST Council's 56th meeting (3 Sept 2025) recommended the changes. Individual life and health insurance were exempted. The GST Council FAQ says the old GST and compensation-cess rates continue for cigarettes, chewing tobacco, unmanufactured tobacco and beedi until the compensation-cess loans are cleared.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Drops statement 1, which is correct, and keeps the incorrect statement 3. | Trap (B): Misses statement 2: individual life and health insurance policies were exempted. | Trap (C): Statement 3 is wrong: the old rates and cess continued for these tobacco items, with new rates to be notified later.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Economy – GST rate rationalisation 2025
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: GST statement 3 correct only while tobacco rates are pending; recheck before use. | Time-sensitive: The tobacco rates were still pending notification when checked; they may since have moved to 40%.

questions.question_text:
The Income-tax Act, 2025 cut the number of sections from 819 to 536 and the number of chapters from 47 to 23, adding tables and formulas for clarity. It also did away with two terms that had long confused taxpayers because they referred to two different financial years.

Which single term did the new Act introduce in their place?

options.A: Fiscal year
options.B: Assessment period
options.C: Accounting period
options.D: Tax year

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Act replaces 'previous year' and 'assessment year' with a single 'tax year' (Income Tax Department FAQ; Akashvani News, Aug 2025).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Not the statutory term used by the Act. | Trap (B): Sounds similar to 'assessment year', which was the term removed. | Trap (C): A general accounting term, not the one the Act uses.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the Income-tax Act, 2025:
1. It received the President's assent on 21 August 2025.
2. It repeals the Income-tax Act, 1961 with effect from 1 April 2026.
3. Income earned in the financial year 2025–26 is assessed under the new Act.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 2 and 3 only
options.C: 2 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Assent: 21 Aug 2025. Commencement and repeal of the 1961 Act: 1 Apr 2026. Income Tax Department FAQ: income of 1 Apr 2025 – 31 Mar 2026 is governed by the 1961 Act; the 2025 Act applies from tax year 2026–27.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Keeps the incorrect statement 3 and drops the correct statement 1. | Trap (C): Misses statement 1: assent was given on 21 August 2025. | Trap (D): Statement 3 is wrong: income of FY 2025–26 stays under the 1961 Act (AY 2026–27).

questions.question_text: Who was sworn in as the 53rd Chief Justice of India on 24 November 2025?

options.A: Justice Sanjiv Khanna
options.B: Justice Vikram Nath
options.C: Justice B.R. Gavai
options.D: Justice Surya Kant

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Justice Surya Kant took the oath before President Droupadi Murmu on 24 Nov 2025. Per the Supreme Court website he is due to retire on 9 February 2027.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): He was the 51st CJI (Nov 2024 – May 2025). | Trap (B): He is a Supreme Court judge but did not take office as CJI in 2025. | Trap (C): He was the 52nd CJI, whom Justice Surya Kant succeeded.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Judiciary – Chief Justice of India
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Office-holder: valid until 9 Feb 2027.

questions.question_text:
The Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025, which received Presidential assent in April 2025, changed several features of the law governing waqf properties, including the composition of Waqf Boards and the procedure for registering waqfs. It also gave the parent law a new name.

What is the Waqf Act, 1995 now called?

options.A: The Muslim Waqf Validating Act, 1995
options.B: The Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development Act, 1995
options.C: The Waqf Properties (Regulation and Protection) Act, 2025
options.D: The Central Waqf Council Act, 1995

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 2025 amendment renamed the Waqf Act, 1995 as the Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development (UMEED) Act, 1995.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Echoes the old Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913, which is a different law. | Trap (C): Invented title: the Act kept the 1995 year and the new name is different. | Trap (D): The Central Waqf Council is a body under the Act, not its name.

questions.question_text:
In In Re: The Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025, the Supreme Court passed an interim order on 15 September 2025 while hearing challenges to the amended law. Consider the following statements:
1. The Court stayed the entire amended Act until the final hearing.
2. The Court put on hold the condition that a person must have practised Islam for at least five years to create a waqf, until rules are framed to verify it.
3. The Court stayed the provision allowing an officer designated by the Government to decide whether a waqf property is government land.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

options.A: 1, 2 and 3
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 only
options.D: 2 and 3 only

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Supreme Court judgment of 15 Sept 2025 (and LiveLaw's report) declined to stay the Act as a whole. It stayed the five-year practice condition until rules are framed and the provision letting the Collector or a designated officer decide whether waqf property is government land.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Statement 1 is wrong: only certain provisions were stayed. | Trap (B): The Court expressly declined to stay the whole Act. | Trap (C): Misses the stay on the designated officer deciding title disputes.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Judiciary – Waqf Act interim order
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: Waqf interim order paraphrased; check statement 3 against the order. | Time-sensitive: Interim order only; the final judgment may differ.

questions.question_text: In July 2025, India signed a Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) with which country?

options.A: Australia
options.B: The United States
options.C: The European Union
options.D: The United Kingdom

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The India–UK CETA was signed on 24 July 2025 at Chequers, Buckinghamshire, during the Prime Minister's visit (UK Parliament treaty record; Reuters).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): India and Australia signed an interim ECTA in 2022. | Trap (B): India and the US were negotiating a separate trade deal. | Trap (C): The India–EU FTA was negotiated separately.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – International relations – India–UK CETA
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: The UK Government site reports entry into force in 2026; verify the date before using it.

questions.question_text:
On 23 April 2025, the day after the terrorist attack at Pahalgam, India's Cabinet Committee on Security decided to hold a 1960 water-sharing treaty with Pakistan 'in abeyance' until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably abjures support for cross-border terrorism. The treaty allots the eastern rivers to India and most of the waters of the western rivers to Pakistan.

Which institution brokered this treaty and signed it as a party for certain purposes?

options.A: The World Bank
options.B: The United Nations
options.C: The Soviet Union
options.D: The International Monetary Fund

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Indus Waters Treaty (1960) was signed by Nehru and Ayub Khan and brokered by the World Bank, which is also a signatory for limited functions (MEA briefing, 23 Apr 2025; Reuters).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The UN had no role in negotiating it. | Trap (C): The USSR mediated the Tashkent Declaration of 1966, not this treaty. | Trap (D): The IMF was not involved.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – International relations – Indus Waters Treaty
questions.review_note: Time-sensitive: Abeyance status as of the check date; it may change.

questions.question_text: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2025, awarded to John Clarke, Michel H. Devoret and John M. Martinis, recognised the discovery of:

options.A: machine learning with artificial neural networks
options.B: metal–organic frameworks
options.C: macroscopic quantum tunnelling in an electric circuit
options.D: attosecond pulses of light

questions.pedagogical_explanation: nobelprize.org: the 2025 Physics Prize was awarded 'for the discovery of macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit'.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): That was the Physics Prize of 2024 (Hopfield and Hinton). | Trap (B): That was the Chemistry Prize of 2025. | Trap (D): That was the Physics Prize of 2023.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Awards – Nobel Prize in Physics 2025

questions.question_text: India beat New Zealand by 96 runs in the final of the ICC Men's T20 World Cup on 8 March 2026 to retain the title. In which city was the final played?

options.A: Ahmedabad
options.B: Colombo
options.C: Kolkata
options.D: Mumbai

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The final was played at Ahmedabad on 8 March 2026; India scored 255/5 and bowled New Zealand out for 159 (ICC; BBC Sport; ESPNcricinfo).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Sri Lanka co-hosted the tournament, but the final was in India. | Trap (C): Eden Gardens did not host the 2026 final. | Trap (D): Mumbai did not host the final.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Current – Sports – ICC Men's T20 World Cup 2026

questions.question_text: Under which Article of the Constitution of India does the President have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment, including in cases of a death sentence?

options.A: Article 53
options.B: Article 72
options.C: Article 74
options.D: Article 161

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 72 gives the President the power to pardon, including for sentences by court martial and death sentences.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President. | Trap (C): Article 74 deals with the Council of Ministers advising the President. | Trap (D): Article 161 gives the Governor's pardoning power, which does not extend to death sentences.

questions.question_text: Which Article of the Constitution of India directs the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code for citizens throughout the territory of India?

options.A: Article 40
options.B: Article 45
options.C: Article 44
options.D: Article 48A

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 44, a Directive Principle of State Policy, speaks of a Uniform Civil Code.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 40 deals with organising village panchayats. | Trap (B): Article 45 deals with early childhood care and education. | Trap (D): Article 48A deals with protecting the environment and wildlife.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Constitution – Uniform Civil Code

questions.question_text: In Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893), the Court of Appeal held that:

options.A: a general offer is accepted by performing its conditions
options.B: a contract with a minor is void from the beginning
options.C: acceptance must always be communicated to the offeror in writing
options.D: an advertisement can never amount to an offer

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The company promised £100 to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball as directed. Mrs Carlill did so, fell ill and was entitled to the money: a unilateral offer is accepted by performance.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): That is Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903). | Trap (C): For a general offer, performing the conditions is enough. | Trap (D): The Court held this advertisement was an offer, as the £1,000 deposit showed it was serious.

questions.question_text: In National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014), the Supreme Court:

options.A: held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right
options.B: decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults
options.C: allowed passive euthanasia through living wills
options.D: recognised transgender persons as a 'third gender'

questions.pedagogical_explanation: NALSA (2014) upheld the right of transgender persons to self-identify their gender and directed the State to treat them as socially and educationally backward classes for reservations.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): That was K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017). | Trap (B): That was Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018). | Trap (C): That was Common Cause v. Union of India (2018).

questions.question_text: In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court set aside which practice?

options.A: Polygamy among Muslims
options.B: The exclusion of women from the Sabarimala temple
options.C: Instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat)
options.D: Nikah halala

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A five-judge bench, by 3:2, held instant triple talaq invalid. Parliament later made it an offence under the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Court did not decide on polygamy in this case. | Trap (B): That was Indian Young Lawyers Association (2018). | Trap (D): Halala was raised but not decided in this case.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgments – Shayara Bano (2017)

questions.question_text: Which Article of the Constitution of India declares the Supreme Court to be a court of record with all the powers of such a court, including the power to punish for contempt of itself?

options.A: Article 136
options.B: Article 215
options.C: Article 141
options.D: Article 129

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 129: the Supreme Court is a court of record and has the power to punish for contempt of itself.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Article 136 provides for special leave to appeal. | Trap (B): Article 215 makes each High Court a court of record. | Trap (C): Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Constitution – Court of record
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: Subtle 'English' wrong option (Art 343(3) and Official Languages Act).

questions.question_text: Under Article 343 of the Constitution of India, the official language of the Union is:

options.A: all languages in the Eighth Schedule
options.B: Hindi and English equally, in any script
options.C: Hindi in the Devanagari script
options.D: English, until Parliament decides otherwise

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 343(1): the official language of the Union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script, with the international form of Indian numerals.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Eighth Schedule lists languages; it does not make them official languages of the Union. | Trap (B): English continues by law for official purposes, but Article 343 names Hindi in Devanagari. | Trap (D): English was allowed to continue alongside Hindi; it is not named as the official language.

questions.question_text: With Parliament's approval at every stage, what is the maximum period for which President's Rule under Article 356 can remain in force in a State?

options.A: One year
options.B: Six months
options.C: Five years
options.D: Three years

questions.pedagogical_explanation: A proclamation lasts six months at a time with Parliament's approval, up to three years. Going beyond one year needs a National Emergency in operation and an Election Commission certificate (Article 356(4)–(5)).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Beyond one year it can continue only if the conditions in Article 356(5) are met, up to three years. | Trap (B): Six months is the period of each approval, not the maximum. | Trap (C): There is no five-year limit; the ceiling is three years.

questions.question_text: Under Article 22, a law providing for preventive detention cannot authorise detention for longer than a certain period unless an Advisory Board reports that there is sufficient cause. What is that period?

options.A: One month
options.B: 24 hours
options.C: Six months
options.D: Three months

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 22(4): detention beyond three months needs an Advisory Board's opinion that there is sufficient cause.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Not the constitutional limit. | Trap (B): 24 hours is the time within which an arrested person must be produced before a magistrate under Article 22(2). | Trap (C): Not the constitutional limit.

questions.question_text:
A State investigating agency wanted to subject an accused person, against his will, to a narco-analysis test, a polygraph test and a brain-mapping test, hoping that the results would lead to evidence. The accused challenged this before the Supreme Court.

In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that the involuntary administration of these tests:

options.A: violates only Article 14, because such tests are applied selectively to some accused
options.B: violates Articles 20(3) and 21
options.C: is valid, because the results are scientific evidence and not testimony
options.D: is valid if a magistrate has approved it in advance

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Selvi held that compelling these tests violates Article 20(3) and the right to privacy and mental liberty under Article 21. Voluntary tests are allowed, with safeguards.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The judgment rested on Articles 20(3) and 21, not Article 14. | Trap (C): The Court treated the results as testimonial compulsion. | Trap (D): Prior approval does not cure the lack of consent.

questions.question_text: In I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court held that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights. Which constitutional amendment was enacted to undo the effect of this ruling?

options.A: The 44th Amendment, 1978
options.B: The 24th Amendment, 1971
options.C: The 42nd Amendment, 1976
options.D: The 1st Amendment, 1951

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The 24th Amendment (1971) affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Part III, and made Presidential assent to amendment Bills obligatory.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): It dealt with emergency safeguards and the right to property. | Trap (C): The 42nd Amendment came later and inserted Article 368(4)–(5). | Trap (D): It came before Golaknath; it added the Ninth Schedule.

questions.question_text: In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court:

options.A: read down Section 377 of the IPC for consenting adults
options.B: struck down Section 66A of the IT Act
options.C: recognised a right of same-sex couples to marry
options.D: struck down Section 497 of the IPC on adultery

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Navtej (2018) overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013) and held Section 377 unconstitutional so far as it criminalised consensual acts between adults.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): That was Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015). | Trap (C): The Court declined to do so in Supriyo Chakraborty (2023). | Trap (D): That was Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018).
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgments – Navtej Singh Johar (2018)

questions.question_text: In Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018), the Supreme Court, by a 4:1 majority, held that:

options.A: excluding women aged 10 to 50 years from the Sabarimala temple was unconstitutional
options.B: the Sabarimala temple was not a public place of worship
options.C: only the Kerala High Court could decide on temple entry
options.D: the exclusion was an essential religious practice protected by Article 25

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The majority struck down Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship Rules, 1965. Review petitions led to a larger-bench reference in 2019.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Court treated it as a public temple. | Trap (C): The Supreme Court decided the matter itself. | Trap (D): That was the dissent of Justice Indu Malhotra, not the majority.

questions.question_text:
Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 allowed a sitting MP or MLA who was convicted to stay in office if an appeal was filed within three months. Other persons were disqualified at once on conviction.

What did the Supreme Court hold in Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013)?

options.A: Section 8(4) was unconstitutional, so sitting legislators are disqualified on conviction
options.B: Only Parliament, not courts, can decide questions of disqualification
options.C: Section 8(4) was valid, because sitting legislators need protection from political cases
options.D: Disqualification takes effect only after the final appeal is decided

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Court held that Parliament lacked competence under Articles 102(1)(e) and 191(1)(e) to make a separate rule for sitting members. Disqualification follows conviction directly.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The Court tested the provision against the Constitution itself. | Trap (C): The Court struck the provision down. | Trap (D): The Court held disqualification takes effect from the date of conviction.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgments – Lily Thomas (2013)

questions.question_text: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), brought by pavement dwellers facing eviction, is best known for holding that:

options.A: municipal bodies cannot be sued
options.B: the right to shelter is a fundamental right that bars every eviction
options.C: the right to livelihood is part of the right to life under Article 21
options.D: Directive Principles override Fundamental Rights

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Court held that the right to livelihood is part of Article 21. Evictions must follow a fair, just and reasonable procedure.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The case was against the Corporation itself. | Trap (B): The Court allowed eviction with fair procedure, not a bar on eviction. | Trap (D): That was not the holding.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgments – Olga Tellis (1985)

questions.question_text: In Common Cause v. Union of India (2018), a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court:

options.A: struck down Section 309 of the IPC on attempted suicide
options.B: permitted active euthanasia by a doctor's lethal injection
options.C: permitted passive euthanasia and living wills
options.D: held that the right to life includes the right to die by suicide

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Building on Aruna Shanbaug (2011), the Court held that dying with dignity is part of Article 21. It allowed withdrawing life support and set safeguards for living wills, which were simplified in 2023.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Court did not decide that question. | Trap (B): Active euthanasia remains illegal. | Trap (D): The Court rejected such a reading of Article 21.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgments – Common Cause (2018)

questions.question_text:
Several couples asked the Supreme Court to interpret the Special Marriage Act, 1954 so that it would also apply to same-sex couples. A five-judge Constitution Bench delivered its verdict in October 2023.

What did the Court hold in Supriyo Chakraborty v. Union of India?

options.A: Same-sex couples may marry under the Special Marriage Act with immediate effect
options.B: The Special Marriage Act, 1954 is unconstitutional as a whole
options.C: Recognising same-sex marriage is for Parliament, not the Court
options.D: Section 377 of the IPC is unconstitutional

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The bench unanimously held that the Constitution does not guarantee a fundamental right to marry and that changing the Special Marriage Act is for Parliament. It noted the Union's offer to set up a committee on the rights of queer couples.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Court declined to read the Act in this way. | Trap (B): No part of the Act was struck down. | Trap (D): That was Navtej Singh Johar (2018).
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgments – Supriyo Chakraborty (2023)

questions.question_text: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar (1979), a case on undertrial prisoners held in jail for years, is known for establishing:

options.A: the right to a speedy trial as part of Article 21
options.B: the right to privacy as a fundamental right
options.C: guidelines on custodial arrest
options.D: the rule of absolute liability for hazardous industries

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Thousands of undertrials had been jailed longer than their possible sentences. The Court held that a speedy trial is part of Article 21 and stressed free legal aid.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): That was Puttaswamy (2017). | Trap (C): That was D.K. Basu (1997). | Trap (D): That was M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987).
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgments – Hussainara Khatoon (1979)

questions.question_text: In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020), decided after communication restrictions in Jammu and Kashmir, the Supreme Court held that:

options.A: access to the internet is an absolute right that can never be restricted
options.B: an indefinite suspension of the internet is impermissible
options.C: Article 370 could not be abrogated
options.D: orders suspending the internet need not be published

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Court held that free speech and trade through the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g). Restrictions must be necessary, proportionate and open to review.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The Court allowed restrictions that are proportionate and time-bound. | Trap (C): That issue was decided in 2023 in In Re Article 370. | Trap (D): The Court required such orders to be published.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgments – Anuradha Bhasin (2020)

questions.question_text: In Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903), the Privy Council held that an agreement with a minor is:

options.A: void from the beginning (void ab initio)
options.B: valid once the minor's guardian approves it
options.C: valid if the minor misrepresented his age
options.D: voidable at the option of the minor

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The minor had mortgaged property to a moneylender. The Privy Council held that, under Sections 10 and 11 of the Indian Contract Act, a minor cannot contract, so the agreement is void.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): A guardian's later approval cannot validate it. | Trap (C): Misrepresentation does not make it valid; estoppel does not apply against a minor. | Trap (D): That was the view rejected by the Privy Council.

questions.question_text: Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932), the 'snail in the ginger beer' case, is famous for laying down:

options.A: the rule of strict liability for escape of dangerous things
options.B: the 'neighbour principle' of duty of care
options.C: the rule of absolute liability for hazardous industries
options.D: that a general offer can be accepted by performance

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Lord Atkin held that one must take reasonable care to avoid harming one's 'neighbours', people closely and directly affected. This founded the modern law of negligence.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): That is Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). | Trap (C): That is M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987). | Trap (D): That is Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893).

questions.question_text: Under the Right to Information Act, 2005, ordinary requests must be answered within 30 days. Within what time must information be provided if it concerns the life or liberty of a person?

options.A: 24 hours
options.B: 7 days
options.C: 48 hours
options.D: 15 days

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The proviso to Section 7(1) of the RTI Act requires information concerning life or liberty to be supplied within 48 hours.
