questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Too short; the Act says 48 hours. | Trap (B): Not the statutory limit. | Trap (D): Not the statutory limit.

questions.question_text: Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which body decides complaints about breaches and can impose penalties?

options.A: CERT-In
options.B: The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India
options.C: The Data Protection Board of India
options.D: The Central Information Commission

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The DPDP Act sets up the Data Protection Board of India to inquire into breaches and impose penalties. Appeals go to TDSAT.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): CERT-In handles cybersecurity incidents under the IT Act. | Trap (B): TRAI regulates telecom, not data protection. | Trap (D): The CIC hears RTI appeals.

questions.question_text:
In December 2023, a five-judge Constitution Bench decided challenges to the 2019 Presidential Orders and the law that reorganised Jammu and Kashmir. Consider the following statements about In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution:
1. The Court upheld the Presidential Orders that made all provisions of the Constitution applicable to Jammu and Kashmir.
2. The Court held that Jammu and Kashmir had retained internal sovereignty after its accession to India.
3. The Court directed the Election Commission to hold elections to the Legislative Assembly by 30 September 2024.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1, 2 and 3

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Court held Article 370 was a temporary provision, upheld the 2019 orders, rejected the claim of internal sovereignty, and directed elections by 30 September 2024 and the early restoration of statehood.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Misses statement 3: the Court set the 30 September 2024 deadline. | Trap (C): Keeps the incorrect statement 2. | Trap (D): Statement 2 is wrong: the Court held that J&K did not retain any element of sovereignty.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgments – In Re Article 370 (2023)
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: 'Internal sovereignty' statement is a paraphrase.

questions.question_text:
A member of a State Legislative Assembly was accused of taking a bribe to vote in a particular way in a Rajya Sabha election. She claimed immunity because the Constitution protects legislators for anything said or any vote given in the House. In March 2024, a seven-judge bench decided the case.

Which of the following correctly states what Sita Soren v. Union of India held?

options.A: It upheld P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998), holding that legislators are immune if they vote as agreed
options.B: It overruled Kesavananda Bharati (1973), holding that legislative privileges are part of the basic structure
options.C: It overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998), holding that Articles 105 and 194 do not protect legislators who take bribes
options.D: It held that Articles 14 and 21 protect legislators from prosecution for votes in the House

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The bench unanimously held that bribery is not protected by parliamentary privilege: the offence is complete when the bribe is accepted, whatever the vote. P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (1998) was overruled.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The 1998 view was overruled, not upheld. | Trap (B): Kesavananda was not involved. | Trap (D): Articles 105(2) and 194(2) were in issue, and the Court denied immunity.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Landmark judgments – Sita Soren (2024)

questions.question_text:
Match the following Acts with their main subject.

(P) Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
(Q) Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015
(R) Consumer Protection Act, 2019
(S) Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

(1) children in conflict with law and children in need of care and protection
(2) time-bound resolution of the insolvency of companies and individuals
(3) sexual offences against children, with special courts
(4) a Central Consumer Protection Authority for class action and recalls
questions.pedagogical_explanation: POCSO 2012 deals with sexual offences against children. The JJ Act 2015 deals with children in conflict with law or in need of care. The CPA 2019 created the CCPA. The IBC 2016 provides time-bound insolvency resolution.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Swaps the Juvenile Justice Act and the Consumer Protection Act. | Trap (B): Swaps POCSO and the Juvenile Justice Act. | Trap (C): Swaps the Consumer Protection Act and the IBC.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Legal – Statutes – Match the Acts

questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the procedure for amending the Constitution under Article 368:
1. A Bill to amend the Constitution can be introduced in either House of Parliament.
2. If the two Houses disagree, there is no provision for a joint sitting to pass the Bill.
3. The President may withhold assent to a constitutional amendment Bill passed by the required majority.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1, 2 and 3
options.C: 2 and 3 only
options.D: 1 only

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Article 368(2): an amendment Bill may be introduced in either House and must pass each House separately by a special majority; Article 108's joint sitting does not apply. The 24th Amendment made assent obligatory.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Statement 3 is wrong: after the 24th Amendment the President shall give assent. | Trap (C): Drops the correct statement 1 and keeps statement 3. | Trap (D): Misses statement 2: joint sittings do not apply to amendment Bills.

questions.question_text: Mahatma Gandhi's Champaran Satyagraha of 1917, his first satyagraha in India, was launched in support of:

options.A: indigo cultivators in Bihar
options.B: peasants in Kheda seeking remission of land revenue
options.C: textile mill workers in Ahmedabad who were demanding higher wages
options.D: salt workers protesting the salt tax

questions.pedagogical_explanation: In Champaran, European planters forced peasants to grow indigo on 3/20 of their land (the tinkathia system). Gandhi's inquiry led to its abolition.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): That was the Kheda Satyagraha of 1918. | Trap (C): That was the Ahmedabad Mill Strike of 1918. | Trap (D): That was the Salt Satyagraha of 1930.

questions.question_text: Project Tiger, India's flagship tiger conservation programme, was launched in which year?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Project Tiger was launched on 1 April 1973, beginning with nine tiger reserves.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The National Tiger Conservation Authority was recommended in 2005 and set up in 2006. | Trap (B): The Wild Life (Protection) Act was passed in 1972. | Trap (D): The Environment (Protection) Act was passed in 1986.

questions.question_text: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was established in:
questions.pedagogical_explanation: ISRO was formed on 15 August 1969, succeeding INCOSPAR (1962) under Vikram Sarabhai.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Aryabhata, India's first satellite, was launched in 1975. | Trap (B): Rohini, the first satellite launched by an Indian rocket (SLV-3), went up in 1980. | Trap (D): INCOSPAR, ISRO's forerunner, was formed in 1962.

questions.question_text: The Paris Agreement on climate change was adopted at which Conference of the Parties (COP) to the UNFCCC?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21 in December 2015. It aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): COP26 at Glasgow produced the Glasgow Climate Pact. | Trap (C): COP3 adopted the Kyoto Protocol. | Trap (D): COP15 at Copenhagen produced the Copenhagen Accord.

questions.question_text: The Chipko movement of the 1970s, in which villagers hugged trees to stop them being felled, began in the region that now forms which State?

options.A: Odisha
options.B: Uttarakhand
options.C: Rajasthan
options.D: Karnataka

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Chipko began in 1973 in the Garhwal Himalayas (then Uttar Pradesh, now Uttarakhand), with Gaura Devi, Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Sunderlal Bahuguna.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Not where the movement began. | Trap (C): Rajasthan is linked with the earlier Bishnoi sacrifice at Khejarli (1730). | Trap (D): Karnataka saw the later Appiko movement, inspired by Chipko.

questions.question_text: The Sun Temple at Konark in Odisha was built in the 13th century by:

options.A: Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty
options.B: Anantavarman Chodaganga
options.C: Rajaraja Chola I
options.D: Krishna I of the Rashtrakuta dynasty

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Konark Sun Temple, built like a chariot with 24 wheels, was commissioned by Narasimhadeva I (c. 1250). It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): He was an earlier Eastern Ganga king, linked with the Jagannath Temple at Puri. | Trap (C): He built the Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur. | Trap (D): He built the Kailasa temple at Ellora.
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – History – Konark Sun Temple

questions.question_text: In which year were the Western Ghats inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Western Ghats were inscribed in 2012 as a serial natural site of 39 components across Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): In 2016 Khangchendzonga National Park was inscribed. | Trap (C): Not the year of inscription. | Trap (D): Kaziranga and Manas were inscribed in 1985.

questions.question_text: Dyarchy in the provinces, under which subjects were divided into 'reserved' and 'transferred', was introduced by:

options.A: the Government of India Act, 1935
options.B: the Indian Councils Act, 1892
options.C: the Indian Councils Act, 1909
options.D: the Government of India Act, 1919

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The Montagu–Chelmsford reforms, enacted as the GoI Act, 1919, introduced dyarchy. Transferred subjects went to ministers answerable to the legislature; reserved subjects stayed with the Governor.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): It ended provincial dyarchy and introduced provincial autonomy. | Trap (B): It expanded legislative councils and allowed indirect election. | Trap (C): It introduced separate electorates (Morley–Minto reforms).
questions.concept_tag: GK – Static – History – Government of India Act 1919

questions.question_text: The Kyoto Protocol (1997) is best described as a treaty that:

options.A: controls trade in endangered species
options.B: set binding emission targets for developed countries
options.C: set nationally determined contributions for all countries
options.D: phased out ozone-depleting substances

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Kyoto put binding targets only on industrialised countries, following 'common but differentiated responsibilities'. Its first commitment period was 2008–2012.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): That is CITES (1973). | Trap (C): That is the Paris Agreement's approach (2015). | Trap (D): That is the Montreal Protocol (1987).

questions.question_text:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(1) Founding of the All-India Muslim League at Dacca
(2) Split in the Indian National Congress at Surat
(3) Partition of Bengal coming into effect
(4) Annulment of the Partition of Bengal announced at the Delhi Durbar
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Partition of Bengal: 16 Oct 1905. Muslim League: Dec 1906. Surat split: Dec 1907. Annulment at the Delhi Durbar: Dec 1911.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Places the Surat split (1907) before the Muslim League (1906). | Trap (B): Places the annulment (1911) before the Surat split (1907). | Trap (D): Places the Muslim League (Dec 1906) before the Partition (Oct 1905).

questions.question_text: What is the remainder when 7^100 is divided by 5?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 7 ≡ 2 (mod 5). Powers of 2 mod 5 repeat in a cycle of 4: 2, 4, 3, 1. Since 100 is a multiple of 4, 2^100 ≡ 1 (mod 5).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Takes the cycle position as 2 (2^2 = 4) instead of 0, since 100 is a multiple of 4. | Trap (B): Takes the cycle position as 3 (2^3 = 8 ≡ 3). | Trap (D): Uses 7 ≡ 2 (mod 5) but stops at 2^1 instead of reducing the exponent.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'C' if pow(7,100,5)==1 else 'X'

questions.question_text: How many prime numbers are there between 50 and 100?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The primes are 53, 59, 61, 67, 71, 73, 79, 83, 89 and 97: ten in all.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Misses one prime, usually 97 or 53. | Trap (C): Counts 91 as prime, but 91 = 7 × 13. | Trap (D): Misses 53 and 59 by starting the count at 60.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'A' if len([n for n in range(51,100) if all(n%k for k in range(2,n))])==10 else 'X'

questions.question_text: What is the units digit of 3^2026 + 7^2026?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Units digits of powers of 3 and of 7 repeat every 4. 2026 = 4 × 506 + 2, so 3^2026 ends in 9 and 7^2026 ends in 9. 9 + 9 = 18, so the units digit is 8.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Treats 2026 as a multiple of 4, giving 1 + 1. | Trap (C): Uses the pattern for exponents of the form 4k+1 or 4k+3, where the units digits add to 10. | Trap (D): Multiplies the units digits (9 × 9 = 81) instead of adding them.

questions.question_text: How many positive divisors of 540 are perfect squares?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 540 = 2^2 × 3^3 × 5. A square divisor needs even exponents: 2 has {0, 2}, 3 has {0, 2} and 5 has {0}. So 2 × 2 × 1 = 4: namely 1, 4, 9, 36.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Forgets that 1 is a perfect-square divisor. | Trap (C): Adds the number of even-exponent choices (2 + 2 + 1) instead of multiplying them. | Trap (D): Counts all divisors of 540, not only the perfect squares.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'B' if len([d for d in range(1,541) if 540%d==0 and int(pow(d,0.5)+0.5)*int(pow(d,0.5)+0.5)==d])==4 else 'X'

questions.question_text: What is the smallest positive integer that leaves remainders 2, 3 and 4 when divided by 3, 4 and 5 respectively, and is also divisible by 7?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Each remainder is one less than the divisor, so N + 1 is a multiple of LCM(3, 4, 5) = 60, giving N = 60k − 1: 59, 119, 179, ... The first that is divisible by 7 is 119 = 7 × 17.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Satisfies the three remainders but is not divisible by 7. | Trap (B): Multiplies the LCM by 7 and adds 1; 421 is not divisible by 7. | Trap (C): Uses N ≡ +1 (mod 60) instead of N ≡ −1 (mod 60).
questions.verify_code: answer = 'D' if min(n for n in range(1,1000) if n%3==2 and n%4==3 and n%5==4 and n%7==0)==119 else 'X'

questions.question_text: How many ordered pairs (a, b) of positive integers have LCM(a, b) = 72?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: 72 = 2^3 × 3^2. For a prime p with exponent e, the larger exponent of p in a and b must equal e, which allows 2e + 1 ordered choices. So (2·3 + 1)(2·2 + 1) = 7 × 5 = 35.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Counts all ordered pairs of divisors of 72 (12 × 12), not only those with LCM 72. | Trap (B): Counts unordered pairs {a, b} instead of ordered pairs. | Trap (C): Counts the divisors of 72 instead of the ordered pairs.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'D' if len([1 for a in range(1,73) for b in range(1,73) if a*b//(lambda f,x,y: f(f,x,y))(lambda f,x,y: x if y==0 else f(f,y,x%y),a,b)==72])==35 else 'X'

questions.question_text: If x + y = 10 and xy = 21, what is x^2 + y^2?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Adds xy to (x + y)^2. | Trap (C): Adds 2xy instead of subtracting it. | Trap (D): Subtracts xy once instead of 2xy.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'A' if 3*3+7*7==58 and 3+7==10 and 3*7==21 else 'X'

questions.question_text: For what value of k does the system 2x + 3y = 5, 4x + ky = 10 have infinitely many solutions?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Infinitely many solutions need 2/4 = 3/k = 5/10, so k = 6.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Gets the sign wrong in the ratio condition. | Trap (B): Divides 3 by 2 instead of multiplying. | Trap (C): Halves 3 instead of doubling it to match the ratio 4/2.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'D' if 2*6==4*3 and 2*10==4*5 else 'X'

questions.question_text: If α and β are the roots of x^2 − 7x + 10 = 0, what is α^3 + β^3?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: α + β = 7 and αβ = 10. α^3 + β^3 = (α + β)^3 − 3αβ(α + β) = 343 − 210 = 133. Check: the roots are 2 and 5, and 8 + 125 = 133.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Gives (α + β)^3 and forgets to subtract 3αβ(α + β). | Trap (C): Subtracts 3αβ but forgets the factor (α + β). | Trap (D): Multiplies the sum of roots by the product.

questions.question_text: How many integers x satisfy |x − 3| + |x + 2| = 5?

options.C: Infinitely many

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The sum of distances from x to 3 and to −2 equals 5, the distance between them, exactly when −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. That gives 6 integers: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Drops one endpoint of the interval −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. | Trap (C): Forgets the sum exceeds 5 outside −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. | Trap (D): Counts only the endpoints x = −2 and x = 3.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'B' if len([x for x in range(-50,51) if abs(x-3)+abs(x+2)==5])==6 else 'X'

questions.question_text: If a + b + c = 0 and a, b, c are non-zero, what is the value of a^2/(bc) + b^2/(ca) + c^2/(ab)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The expression equals (a^3 + b^3 + c^3)/(abc). When a + b + c = 0, a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc, so the value is 3. Check with a = 1, b = 2, c = −3: 1/(−6) + 4/(−3) + 9/2 = 3.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Assumes each term is 1/3, as if a = b = c, which is impossible when a + b + c = 0. | Trap (C): Assumes the expression vanishes because a + b + c = 0. | Trap (D): Gets the sign wrong in a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc.

questions.question_text: A non-zero real number x satisfies x^2 − 3x + 1 = 0. What is the value of x^5 + 1/x^5?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Multiplies (x + 1/x)(x^4 + 1/x^4) = 3 × 47 and forgets to subtract x^3 + 1/x^3. | Trap (C): Multiplies (x^2 + 1/x^2)(x^3 + 1/x^3) and forgets to subtract (x + 1/x). | Trap (D): Raises 3 to the fifth power, as if x^5 + 1/x^5 = (x + 1/x)^5.

questions.question_text: What is the sum of all two-digit multiples of 7?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The multiples are 14, 21, ..., 98, a total of 13 terms. Sum = 13 × (14 + 98)/2 = 13 × 56 = 728.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Counts 14 to 98 as 14 terms, giving 14 × 56. | Trap (B): Leaves out the first term, 14. | Trap (D): Includes 7 itself, which is a one-digit number.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'C' if sum(n for n in range(10,100) if n%7==0)==728 else 'X'

questions.question_text: In a geometric progression, the 3rd term is 12 and the 6th term is 96. What is the first term?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Gives the 4th term (12 × 2) instead of the first term. | Trap (C): Divides 12 by r^3 = 8 instead of by r^2 = 4. | Trap (D): Gives the second term, not the first.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'A' if 3*2*2==12 and 3*pow(2,5)==96 else 'X'

questions.question_text: What is the value of 1·2 + 2·3 + 3·4 + ... + 20·21?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Divides 20 × 21 × 22 by 6 instead of by 3. | Trap (B): Forgets to divide 20·21·22 by 3, halving it instead. | Trap (C): Sums only 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + 20^2 and leaves out the sum of n.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'D' if sum(k*(k+1) for k in range(1,21))==3080 else 'X'

questions.question_text: The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic progression is 3n^2 + 5n. What is its 15th term?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Gives S15, the sum of 15 terms, instead of the 15th term. | Trap (C): Uses t(n) = 6n + 8 by slipping on S(n − 1). | Trap (D): Gives the 14th term (off by one).

questions.question_text: How many terms of the arithmetic progression 25, 22, 19, ... must be added to get a sum of 116?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: S(n) = n/2 × [50 − 3(n − 1)] = 116, which gives 3n^2 − 53n + 232 = 0, so n = 8 or n = 29/3. Only n = 8 is a whole number. Check: S8 = 4 × (25 + 4) = 116.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Stops one term short; S7 = 112. | Trap (B): Keeps the non-integer root of the quadratic; a number of terms must be a whole number. | Trap (D): Rounds the non-integer root 29/3 up to 9.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'C' if [n for n in range(1,40) if n*(53-3*n)==232]==[8] else 'X'

questions.question_text: If f(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 1), what is f(f(3))?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Computes f(4) instead of f(2) by feeding x + 1 into f. | Trap (C): Inverts the fraction at the second step. | Trap (D): Stops at f(3) = 2 and does not apply f again.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'B' if (lambda f: f(f(3)))(lambda x:(x+1)/(x-1))==3 else 'X'

questions.question_text: What is the domain of f(x) = √(x^2 − 5x + 6) over the real numbers?

options.A: x ≥ 3 only
options.B: All real x
options.D: x ≤ 2 or x ≥ 3

questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Keeps only one branch of the solution. | Trap (B): Forgets that the expression under a square root must be non-negative. | Trap (C): Gives the interval where the quadratic is negative, which is the region to exclude.

questions.question_text: A function f satisfies f(x) + 2f(1 − x) = x for all real x. What is f(0)?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: x = 0 gives f(0) + 2f(1) = 0, and x = 1 gives f(1) + 2f(0) = 1. Solving: f(1) = −1/3 and f(0) = 2/3.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Gives f(1) instead of f(0). | Trap (B): Substitutes x = 0 and ignores the f(1 − x) term. | Trap (D): Drops the factor 2 when solving the two equations.

questions.question_text: For what value of k does the equation |x^2 − 4| = k have exactly three real solutions?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The graph of |x^2 − 4| touches 0 at x = ±2 and has a local peak of 4 at x = 0. The line y = k meets it in exactly three points only at the peak, k = 4: x = 0 and x = ±2√2.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): k = 0 gives only two solutions, x = ±2. | Trap (C): k = 8 gives only two solutions, x = ±√12. | Trap (D): k = 2 gives four solutions.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'B' if len(set([round(s*pow(v,0.5),9) for v in (4+4,4-4) if v>=0 for s in (1,-1)]))==3 else 'X'

questions.question_text: What is the value of log₂ 32 + log₃ 81 − log₅ 125?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: log₂ 32 = 5, log₃ 81 = 4 and log₅ 125 = 3, so 5 + 4 − 3 = 6.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Subtracts both the second and third terms (5 − 4 − 3). | Trap (C): Adds all three logarithms instead of subtracting the last. | Trap (D): Uses log₅ 125 = 5 by mistake.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'B' if pow(2,5)==32 and pow(3,4)==81 and pow(5,3)==125 and 5+4-3==6 else 'X'

questions.question_text: If 9^x = 27^(x − 1), what is x?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Writes 27^(x − 1) as 3^(3x − 1), forgetting to multiply the −1 by 3. | Trap (B): Makes a sign error when moving 3x to one side. | Trap (D): Gives the value of 3^(x − 1) at the solution instead of x.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'C' if pow(9,3)==pow(27,2) else 'X'

questions.question_text: Given log₁₀ 2 = 0.3010, how many digits does 2^50 have?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: log₁₀ 2^50 = 50 × 0.3010 = 15.05. The number of digits is the integer part plus 1, so 16.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Confuses the exponent with the number of digits. | Trap (B): Rounds 15.05 up to 16 and then adds 1 again. | Trap (C): Takes the integer part of 50 × 0.3010 = 15.05 without adding 1.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'D' if len(str(pow(2,50)))==16 else 'X'

questions.question_text: What is the sum of all real solutions of x^(log₁₀ x) = 100x?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Take log₁₀ of both sides with t = log₁₀ x: t^2 = 2 + t, so t = 2 or t = −1. That gives x = 100 or x = 0.1, and the sum is 100.1.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Factors t^2 − t − 2 wrongly as (t + 2)(t − 1), giving x = 0.01 and x = 10. | Trap (C): Keeps only the root x = 100 and drops x = 1/10. | Trap (D): Takes the second root as −1/10, which is outside the domain.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'A' if all(t*t==2+t for t in (2,-1)) and abs(100+0.1-100.1)<1e-9 else 'X'

questions.question_text: How many 3-letter arrangements can be made from the letters of MOTHER if no letter is repeated?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Allows repetition (6^3). | Trap (C): Counts selections (6C3), not arrangements. | Trap (D): Arranges all six letters (6!).
questions.verify_code: answer = 'B' if 6*5*4==120 else 'X'

questions.question_text: In how many ways can 5 boys and 3 girls sit in a row so that no two girls sit next to each other?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Arrange the boys: 5! = 120. They make 6 gaps; choose 3 for the girls and arrange them: 6C3 × 3! = 120. Total = 120 × 120 = 14400.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Arranges all 8 without the restriction (8!). | Trap (B): Counts the arrangements with all three girls together (6! × 3!) instead. | Trap (C): Chooses the 3 gaps (6C3) but does not arrange the girls within them.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'D' if 120*20*6==14400 else 'X'

questions.question_text: In how many ways can 10 identical chocolates be shared among 4 children if each child gets at least 2?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Give 2 to each child first; 2 chocolates remain. Sharing 2 identical items among 4 children: (2 + 3)C3 = 5C3 = 10.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Counts only the ways in which one child gets both remaining chocolates. | Trap (C): Ignores the minimum completely (13C3). | Trap (D): Uses 'at least 1' instead of 'at least 2' (9C3).
questions.verify_code: answer = 'A' if len([1 for a in range(2,11) for b in range(2,11) for c in range(2,11) if 10-a-b-c>=2])==10 else 'X'

questions.question_text: How many triangles can be formed using the vertices of a regular decagon such that no side of the triangle is a side of the decagon?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Total 10C3 = 120. Triangles with two decagon sides: 10. With exactly one side: 10 × (10 − 4) = 60. So 120 − 10 − 60 = 50.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Counts all triangles (10C3). | Trap (C): Subtracts only the 10 triangles that share two sides with the decagon. | Trap (D): Subtracts only the 60 triangles that share exactly one side with the decagon.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'B' if len([1 for a in range(10) for b in range(a+1,10) for c in range(b+1,10) if all((y-x)%10 not in (1,9) for x,y in ((a,b),(b,c),(a,c)))])==50 else 'X'

questions.question_text: How many 4-digit numbers divisible by 5 can be formed from the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 5 if no digit is repeated?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Ending in 0: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. Ending in 5: first digit from {1, 2, 3} gives 3 choices, then 3 × 2 for the middle two places = 18. Total 42.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Counts only the numbers ending in 5. | Trap (B): Counts only the numbers ending in 0. | Trap (D): Allows 0 as the first digit when the last digit is 5.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'C' if len([1 for a in (0,1,2,3,5) for b in (0,1,2,3,5) for c in (0,1,2,3,5) for d in (0,5) if len({a,b,c,d})==4 and a!=0])==42 else 'X'

questions.question_text: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 8?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Favourable outcomes: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2), which is 5 of 36.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Counts 4 favourable outcomes instead of 5. | Trap (B): Gives the probability of a sum of 7, the most likely total. | Trap (D): Uses 7 as the count of outcomes for a total of 8.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'C' if len([1 for a in range(1,7) for b in range(1,7) if a+b==8])==5 else 'X'

questions.question_text: Three fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting at least two heads?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: Exactly two heads: 3 outcomes; three heads: 1 outcome. 4/8 = 1/2.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Counts three heads only. | Trap (C): Gives the probability of at least one head. | Trap (D): Counts exactly two heads only.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'A' if len([1 for a in (0,1) for b in (0,1) for c in (0,1) if a+b+c>=2])*2==8 else 'X'

questions.question_text: A bag holds 4 red and 6 green balls. Three balls are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that exactly two are red?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Gives the probability that all three balls are green (20/120). | Trap (B): Gives the probability of exactly one red. | Trap (D): Uses with-replacement probabilities: 3 × (0.4)^2 × 0.6.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'C' if 6*6*10==120*3 else 'X'

questions.question_text: A number is chosen at random from 1 to 1000. What is the probability that it is divisible by none of 2, 3 and 5?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: By inclusion-exclusion, divisible by at least one: 500 + 333 + 200 − 166 − 100 − 66 + 33 = 734. None: 1000 − 734 = 266, so the probability is 0.266.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Gives the probability of being divisible by at least one of them. | Trap (C): Uses 1000 × (1/2)(2/3)(4/5) = 266.67 and rounds up, which is not exact for 1000. | Trap (D): Forgets to add back the 33 multiples of 30.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'B' if len([n for n in range(1,1001) if n%2 and n%3 and n%5])==266 else 'X'

questions.question_text: A fair die is rolled repeatedly until a six appears. What is the probability that this takes an even number of rolls?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Assumes odd and even are equally likely. | Trap (B): Gives the probability of an odd number of rolls. | Trap (D): Gives only the probability of the six coming on exactly the second roll.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'C' if abs(sum(pow(5/6,k-1)/6 for k in range(2,400,2))-5/11)<1e-9 else 'X'

questions.question_text: What is the determinant of the matrix [[2, 3], [4, 5]]?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Adds and then changes the sign. | Trap (C): Subtracts in the wrong order (12 − 10). | Trap (D): Adds the two products instead of subtracting.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'A' if 2*5-3*4==-2 else 'X'

questions.question_text: For what value of k is the matrix [[1, 2, 3], [2, k, 4], [3, 5, 7]] singular?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Makes a sign slip in the cofactor expansion. | Trap (C): Assumes a zero entry makes the matrix singular. | Trap (D): Solves −2k + 6 = 0 as k = 6.

questions.question_text: If A = [[1, 2], [0, 1]], what is the sum of all entries of A + A^2 + A^3 + ... + A^10?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: A^n = [[1, 2n], [0, 1]], so its entries add to 2 + 2n. Summing for n = 1 to 10 gives 20 + 2 × 55 = 130.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Takes the top-right entry of A^n as 2^n instead of 2n. | Trap (B): Adds only the diagonal entries. | Trap (D): Adds only the top-right entries.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'C' if sum(sum(sum(r) for r in m) for m in (lambda f: [f(f,n) for n in range(1,11)])(lambda f,n: [[1,0],[0,1]] if n==0 else (lambda p: [[p[0][0], p[0][0]*2+p[0][1]],[p[1][0], p[1][0]*2+p[1][1]]])(f(f,n-1))))==130 else 'X'

questions.question_text: The circumference of a circle is 44 cm. Taking π = 22/7, what is its area?

options.A: 616 cm²
options.B: 88 cm²
options.C: 77 cm²
options.D: 154 cm²

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 2πr = 44 gives r = 7. Area = (22/7) × 49 = 154 cm².
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Uses the diameter 14 as the radius. | Trap (B): Doubles the circumference instead of finding the area. | Trap (C): Halves the correct area.

questions.question_text: A right triangle has legs 9 cm and 12 cm. What is the length of the altitude drawn to the hypotenuse?

options.A: 7.2 cm
options.B: 7.5 cm
options.D: 6 cm

questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Takes half the hypotenuse, which is the median, not the altitude. | Trap (C): Divides 9 × 12 by 10 instead of 15. | Trap (D): Takes half the longer leg.

questions.question_text: A solid metal sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and recast into cones of base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. How many cones are made?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Uses the cone formula without the 1/3, i.e. treats the cones as cylinders. | Trap (B): Drops the 4/3 in the sphere's volume. | Trap (D): Swaps the cone's radius and height, using (1/3)π × 16 × 3 = 16π.

questions.question_text: A triangle has sides 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. What is the radius of its inscribed circle?

options.A: 2 cm
options.B: 6.5 cm
options.D: 4 cm

questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Divides the area by the full perimeter 42 instead of the semi-perimeter. | Trap (B): Takes half the shortest side. | Trap (C): Gives the circumradius abc/(4 × area) instead.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'D' if abs(pow(21*8*7*6,0.5)/21-4)<1e-9 else 'X'

questions.question_text: From a point P, two tangents are drawn to a circle of radius 5 cm with centre O, where OP = 13 cm. What is the length of the chord joining the two points of contact?

options.A: 12 cm
options.D: 24 cm

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Tangent length = √(169 − 25) = 12. Half the chord = (5 × 12)/13 = 60/13, the altitude from the point of contact to OP. Chord = 120/13 cm.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Gives the tangent length, not the chord. | Trap (C): Gives half the chord. | Trap (D): Doubles the tangent length.

questions.question_text: What is the distance between the points (1, −2) and (7, 6)?
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Forgets to take the square root. | Trap (B): Adds the differences 6 + 8 instead of using Pythagoras. | Trap (D): Uses only the vertical difference.

questions.question_text: Which line passes through (2, 3) and is perpendicular to 2x − y + 4 = 0?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The given line has slope 2, so the perpendicular slope is −1/2. y − 3 = −(1/2)(x − 2) gives x + 2y − 8 = 0.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Correct slope, but the line does not pass through (2, 3). | Trap (C): Uses slope +1/2 instead of −1/2. | Trap (D): Parallel to the given line, not perpendicular.

questions.question_text: What is the reflection of the point (3, 1) in the line x + y = 2?
questions.pedagogical_explanation: The foot of the perpendicular from (3, 1) is (2, 0). The image is 2(2, 0) − (3, 1) = (1, −1). Check: the midpoint (2, 0) lies on x + y = 2, and the segment joining the two points has slope 1, perpendicular to the line.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Swaps and negates the coordinates as if reflecting in the line y = −x. | Trap (B): Reflects in the origin. | Trap (C): Moves only the x-coordinate.

questions.question_text: The price of an item is raised by 20% and then the new price is cut by 20%. What is the net change?

options.A: A 4% increase
options.B: No change
options.C: A 2% decrease
options.D: A 4% decrease

questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Gets the sign of the net effect wrong. | Trap (B): Assumes equal percentage rises and falls cancel out. | Trap (C): Halves the correct net change.
questions.verify_code: answer = 'D' if abs(1.2*0.8-0.96)<1e-12 else 'X'

questions.question_text: A train 240 m long passes a 360 m long platform completely in 30 seconds. What is its speed?

options.C: 20 km/h
options.D: 72 km/h

questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Uses only the platform length. | Trap (B): Uses only the train's length. | Trap (C): Gives the speed in m/s but labels it km/h.

questions.question_text: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 15 hours, and pipe C can empty the full tank in 20 hours. All three are opened together; after 2 hours, C is closed. How long does it take in all to fill the tank?

options.A: 6 hours 40 minutes
options.B: 6 hours
options.C: 7 hours 20 minutes
options.D: 5 hours 20 minutes

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Together: 1/12 + 1/15 − 1/20 = 1/10 per hour, so 2 hours fills 1/5. A and B fill 9/60 = 3/20 per hour, so the remaining 4/5 takes 16/3 hours. Total = 2 + 16/3 = 22/3 hours = 7 h 20 min.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Ignores pipe C altogether (A and B alone take 60/9 hours). | Trap (B): Treats C as a filling pipe for the first 2 hours. | Trap (D): Gives only the time after C is closed and forgets the first 2 hours.

questions.question_text: A shopkeeper marks goods 40% above cost and then allows two successive discounts of 10% and x%. If he still makes a profit of 13.4%, what is x?
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Uses the profit percentage as the discount. | Trap (C): Treats the two discounts as additive: 1.4 × (1 − 0.10 − x) = 1.134. | Trap (D): Takes the total discount 1 − 1.134/1.4 = 19% as x, ignoring the first 10%.

questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to BENEVOLENT.

options.A: Hostile
options.B: Kind and generous
options.C: Cautious
options.D: Wealthy

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Benevolent (Latin bene, 'well' + volens, 'wishing') means well-meaning and kindly.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Close to the opposite of benevolent. | Trap (C): Unrelated quality. | Trap (D): A benevolent person may give money, but the word means goodwill, not riches.

questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to FRUGAL.

options.A: Extravagant
options.B: Careful
options.C: Thrifty
options.D: Modest

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Frugal means sparing with money; its opposite is extravagant, spending freely.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Close in sense to frugal. | Trap (C): A synonym of frugal, not an antonym. | Trap (D): Near-synonym in the sense of simple living.

questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to OBDURATE.

options.A: Obedient
options.B: Obscure
options.C: Stubbornly refusing to change one's mind
options.D: Hard-working

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Obdurate means stubbornly persisting in an opinion or course of action, unmoved by persuasion.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Sound-alike trap (ob-); obedient is close to the opposite. | Trap (B): Sound-alike trap; obscure means unclear. | Trap (D): Confuses 'durate' with endurance or effort.

questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to EPHEMERAL.

options.A: Spiritual
options.B: Delicate
options.C: Transient
options.D: Enduring

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time; enduring means lasting a long time.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Confuses ephemeral with ethereal. | Trap (B): Often linked with short-lived things, but not an antonym. | Trap (C): A synonym of ephemeral.

questions.question_text: Choose the word that completes the analogy. LOQUACIOUS : TACITURN :: PROFLIGATE : ?

options.A: Reckless
options.B: Garrulous
options.C: Parsimonious
options.D: Wasteful

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Loquacious (talkative) and taciturn (silent) are antonyms. The antonym of profligate (wastefully extravagant) is parsimonious (excessively sparing).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Near-synonym of profligate. | Trap (B): A synonym of loquacious, carried over from the first pair. | Trap (D): A synonym of profligate; the analogy needs an antonym.

questions.question_text: Choose the word closest in meaning to PERSPICACIOUS.

options.A: Having sharp insight and understanding
options.B: Clearly expressed
options.C: Persistent
options.D: Suspicious

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Perspicacious describes a person who quickly notices and understands things. Perspicuous, a different word, means clearly expressed.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Confuses it with perspicuous, which describes clear writing, not a sharp mind. | Trap (C): Sound-alike trap from the shared 'pers-' start. | Trap (D): Sound-alike ending (-picious).

questions.question_text: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to SANGUINE.

options.A: Cheerful
options.B: Bloodthirsty
options.C: Confident
options.D: Pessimistic

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Sanguine means optimistic, especially in a difficult situation. The opposite is pessimistic.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): A synonym, not an antonym. | Trap (B): Confuses sanguine with sanguinary; both come from Latin sanguis, 'blood'. | Trap (C): A near-synonym.

questions.question_text: What does the idiom 'to bite the bullet' mean?

options.A: To be wounded in battle
options.B: To face a painful situation bravely
options.C: To make a hasty decision
options.D: To speak rudely to someone

questions.pedagogical_explanation: To bite the bullet is to accept something unpleasant that cannot be avoided and face it with courage.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): A literal reading of the words. | Trap (C): Unrelated sense; the idiom is about endurance, not haste. | Trap (D): Confuses it with idioms about harsh speech.

questions.question_text: Which word does NOT belong with the others?

options.A: Fawning
options.B: Obsequious
options.C: Truculent
options.D: Sycophantic

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Obsequious, sycophantic and fawning all describe excessive flattery or servility. Truculent means aggressively defiant, the odd one out.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Belongs to the group: servile flattery. | Trap (B): Belongs to the group: excessively eager to please. | Trap (D): Belongs to the group: flattering to gain favour.

questions.question_text: In the sentence 'The lecture was so recondite that most of the audience left confused', the word 'recondite' most nearly means:

options.A: Brought into agreement
options.B: Obscure and hard to understand
options.C: Repetitive
options.D: Reckless

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Recondite means little known or abstruse, dealing with obscure subject matter.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Confuses it with reconciled. | Trap (C): Fits 'left confused' loosely, but is not the meaning. | Trap (D): Sound-alike trap (rec-).

questions.question_text: Despite the heavy rain, the match was not ________; play resumed after a short break.

options.A: abandoned
options.B: watched
options.C: played
options.D: won

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Not abandoned' fits the second clause: play resumed after the break.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Fits grammatically but has nothing to do with resuming play. | Trap (C): Contradicts 'play resumed'; the match clearly was played. | Trap (D): Irrelevant to whether play continued.

questions.question_text: The committee's report was so ________ that even a non-expert could follow every step of its reasoning.

options.A: technical
options.B: lucid
options.C: opaque
options.D: lengthy

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'So ... that even a non-expert could follow' needs a word meaning clear: lucid.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Technical writing would be harder for a non-expert. | Trap (C): The opposite: opaque writing is hard to follow. | Trap (D): Length does not explain why a non-expert could follow it.

questions.question_text: Far from being ________, the new rules were welcomed by most traders, who had long complained about the old system.

options.A: popular
options.B: lenient
options.C: complex
options.D: resented

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Far from being X, they were welcomed' needs X to be the opposite of welcomed: resented.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Reverses the contrast set up by 'far from'; the rules were popular. | Trap (B): Not opposed to 'welcomed'; 'far from being lenient' does not contrast with the rest. | Trap (C): Complexity is not the opposite of being welcomed.

questions.question_text: The scientist was ________ about her findings, refusing to announce them until they had been ________ by an independent laboratory.

options.A: circumspect … replicated
options.B: careless … ignored
options.C: boastful … rejected
options.D: candid … published

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Refusing to announce until results are confirmed shows caution (circumspect). Confirmation by another lab means the results were replicated.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Contradicts her careful refusal to announce early. | Trap (C): A boastful person would not hold back; waiting for rejection makes no sense. | Trap (D): Candid (open) clashes with refusing to announce.

questions.question_text: He has been living in Pune ________ 2019.

options.A: by
options.B: for
options.C: since
options.D: from

questions.pedagogical_explanation: With the present perfect continuous, a point in time takes 'since'.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 'By 2019' marks a deadline, not the start of a continuing action. | Trap (B): 'For' takes a length of time (for six years), not a starting point. | Trap (D): 'From' needs a matching end point and does not fit the present perfect continuous here.
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: 'living in Pune from 2019' is common in Indian English; key is 'since'.

questions.question_text: The reforms were ________ rather than radical: they adjusted procedures while leaving the underlying structure ________.

options.A: sweeping … unchanged
options.B: gradual … overhauled
options.C: incremental … intact
options.D: cosmetic … transformed

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Rather than radical' needs incremental, and 'adjusted procedures while leaving the structure ...' needs intact.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 'Sweeping' is close to radical, which the sentence rejects. | Trap (B): An overhauled structure contradicts the idea of non-radical reform. | Trap (D): Contradictory: cosmetic changes do not transform structure.

questions.question_text: Her apology seemed less an expression of ________ than a calculated move to ________ the growing criticism.

options.A: pride … invite
options.B: anger … intensify
options.C: contrition … defuse
options.D: regret … ignore

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The contrast is between genuine remorse (contrition) and a tactic to calm the criticism (defuse).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Pride is the opposite of what an apology expresses, and no one apologises to invite criticism. | Trap (B): An apology does not express anger, and a calculated move would not intensify criticism. | Trap (D): First word fits, but apologising is a response, not a way to ignore criticism.

questions.question_text: Although the evidence was largely ________, the jury found it persuasive because each piece was ________ by the others.

options.A: direct … undermined
options.B: anecdotal … isolated
options.C: circumstantial … corroborated
options.D: conclusive … contradicted

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Although' signals weakness: circumstantial evidence. It persuades because the pieces support (corroborate) one another.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Direct evidence is not a reason for 'although', and undermined evidence is weak. | Trap (B): Isolated pieces would not support one another. | Trap (D): 'Although ... conclusive' gives no contrast, and contradicted evidence would not persuade.

questions.question_text: The new manager's ________ style, in which she rarely raised her voice and always explained her decisions, won the team's trust.

options.A: measured
options.B: erratic
options.C: autocratic
options.D: abrasive

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Calm and reasoned behaviour is a measured style.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Explaining every decision is consistent, not erratic. | Trap (C): Explaining decisions is the opposite of autocratic command. | Trap (D): Contradicts 'rarely raised her voice'.

questions.question_text: The data are ________ with two different explanations, so further experiments are needed to decide between them.

options.A: inconsistent
options.B: consistent
options.C: identical
options.D: incompatible

questions.pedagogical_explanation: If the data fit (are consistent with) both explanations, more experiments are needed to tell them apart.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): If the data ruled out both explanations, there would be nothing to decide between. | Trap (C): Data cannot be identical with explanations; wrong collocation. | Trap (D): Same problem as 'inconsistent'.

questions.question_text:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

Each of the students / have submitted / the assignment / before the deadline.

options.A: Each of the students
options.B: have submitted
options.C: the assignment
options.D: before the deadline

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The subject is 'each', which is singular, so the verb must be 'has submitted'.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Correct: 'each of the students' is a normal singular subject. | Trap (C): Correct as written. | Trap (D): Correct as written.

questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: Neither the manager nor the clerks were aware about the change.
options.B: Neither the manager or the clerks were aware of the change.
options.C: Neither the manager nor the clerks was aware of the change.
options.D: Neither the manager nor the clerks were aware of the change.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Neither ... nor takes the verb of the nearer subject (clerks, so 'were'), and 'aware' takes 'of'.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The idiom is 'aware of', not 'aware about'. | Trap (B): 'Neither' pairs with 'nor', not 'or'. | Trap (C): With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'clerks', so it must be plural.

questions.question_text:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

He is one of those leaders who / never admits / a mistake / in public.

options.A: He is one of those leaders who
options.B: never admits
options.C: a mistake
options.D: in public

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Who' refers to 'leaders' (plural), not 'one', so the verb must be 'admit'.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Correct: the relative clause properly refers back to 'leaders'. | Trap (C): Correct as written. | Trap (D): Correct as written.
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: Traditional plural agreement ('one of those leaders who never admit').

questions.question_text:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

The furniture / in these rooms / are / quite old.

options.A: The furniture
options.B: in these rooms
options.C: are
options.D: quite old

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable and takes a singular verb: 'is'.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 'Furniture' is correct as an uncountable noun. | Trap (B): The plural 'rooms' is inside a phrase and does not decide the verb. | Trap (D): Correct as written.

questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: Had I known about the delay, I would take the earlier train.
options.B: Had I knew about the delay, I would have taken the earlier train.
options.C: Had I known about the delay, I would have taken the earlier train.
options.D: If I would have known about the delay, I would have taken the earlier train.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Third conditional: Had I + past participle, ... would have + past participle.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The result clause must be 'would have taken' for a past event. | Trap (B): After 'had', the past participle 'known' is needed. | Trap (D): 'Would have' does not go in the if-clause of a third conditional.

questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: The number of applicants have risen sharply this year.
options.B: A number of applicants has risen sharply this year.
options.C: The number of applicants has risen sharply this year.
options.D: The number of applicants has rose sharply this year.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'The number of ...' is singular (has), and the participle of rise is risen.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 'The number of' is singular and takes 'has'. | Trap (B): 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb; it also changes the meaning. | Trap (D): The past participle is 'risen', not 'rose'.

questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: No sooner had the bell rung when the students rushed out.
options.B: Scarcely had the bell rung when the students rushed out.
options.C: Scarcely had the bell rung than the students rushed out.
options.D: Scarcely the bell had rung when the students rushed out.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'Scarcely/Hardly ... when' and 'No sooner ... than', each with inversion after the opening word.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): 'No sooner' must pair with 'than'. | Trap (C): 'Than' pairs with 'no sooner', not 'scarcely'. | Trap (D): After an opening 'scarcely', the subject and auxiliary must be inverted.

questions.question_text:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains a grammatical error.

Being a rainy day, / the match / was postponed / by the organisers.

options.A: Being a rainy day,
options.B: the match
options.C: was postponed
options.D: by the organisers

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The participle phrase 'being a rainy day' has no proper subject, so it seems to say the match was a rainy day. It should read 'It being a rainy day,' or 'As it was a rainy day,'.
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): The subject is fine in itself; the problem is the participle that seems to describe it. | Trap (C): The passive is correct. | Trap (D): The agent phrase is correct.

questions.question_text: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.

options.A: She prefers reading novels to watching television.
options.B: She prefers to read novels than watching television.
options.C: She prefers reading novels than watching television.
options.D: She prefers reading novels rather to watching television.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Prefer + gerund + to + gerund (or prefer to read ... rather than watch).
questions.trap_type: Trap (B): Mixes an infinitive with a gerund and uses 'than' without 'rather'. | Trap (C): 'Prefer' takes 'to' when comparing two gerunds, not 'than'. | Trap (D): 'Rather to' is not idiomatic.

questions.question_text: Choose the sentence with correct parallel structure.

options.A: The course teaches students how to analyse data, writing reports and the presentation of findings.
options.B: The course teaches students how to analyse data, write reports and present their findings.
options.C: The course teaches students how analysing data, writing reports and to present their findings.
options.D: The course teaches students how to analyse data, to write reports and presenting their findings.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Items in a list should share one form: analyse, write, present.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Mixes a verb, a gerund and a noun phrase. | Trap (C): 'How' followed by gerunds is ungrammatical, and the list mixes forms. | Trap (D): Mixes infinitives with a gerund.

questions.question_text:
The sentences below, labelled P, Q, R and S, form a paragraph when arranged in the right order. Choose the most logical order.

P. She hurried to the station, only to find the platform empty.
Q. Maya's alarm failed to ring on the morning of her interview.
R. The train she needed had left five minutes earlier.
S. Waking up late, she skipped breakfast and grabbed her documents.

options.A: QPSR
options.B: QSPR
options.C: QSRP
options.D: SQPR

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Cause (Q) → waking late (S) → reaching the station (P) → explanation of the empty platform (R).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): She cannot reach the station (P) before waking up (S). | Trap (C): R explains why the platform was empty, so it must follow P. | Trap (D): S ('waking up late') presupposes Q, the alarm failing.

questions.question_text:
The sentences below, labelled P, Q, R and S, form a paragraph when arranged in the right order. Choose the most logical order.

P. Travel time to the city fell from five hours to ninety minutes.
Q. Within a few years, vegetable farming had replaced wheat as the main crop.
R. A new highway connected the small town to the city in 2015.
S. As a result, the town's farmers began to grow vegetables for the city market.

options.A: RPQS
options.B: RSPQ
options.C: PRSQ
options.D: RPSQ

questions.pedagogical_explanation: Event (R) → effect on travel time (P) → farmers' response (S) → long-term outcome (Q).
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Q, the outcome after a few years, cannot come before the farmers start growing vegetables (S). | Trap (B): 'As a result' in S needs the shorter travel time (P) before it. | Trap (C): P's falling travel time needs the highway (R) to be introduced first.

questions.question_text:
The sentences below, labelled P, Q, R and S, form a paragraph when arranged in the right order. Choose the most logical order.

P. Reading a chapter a second time makes the material feel familiar.
Q. Feeling familiar with a text is not the same as being able to recall it without help.
R. This familiarity is pleasant and creates a sense of mastery.
S. Yet the same ease can mislead us when we judge what we actually know.

options.A: PRQS
options.B: PSRQ
options.C: PRSQ
options.D: RPSQ

questions.pedagogical_explanation: P introduces familiarity, R describes its pleasant effect, S warns that it misleads, and Q explains why.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Q explains why the warning in S holds, so it must follow S; placed before S, the 'Yet' in S would have nothing to contrast with. | Trap (B): 'The same ease' in S needs R's description of the pleasant familiarity first. | Trap (D): 'This familiarity' in R needs P to introduce familiarity.
questions.review_note: Faculty flag: 'the same ease' in S refers back to P and R; needs a careful read.

questions.question_text:
The sentences below, labelled P, Q, R and S, form a paragraph when arranged in the right order. Choose the most logical order.

P. Mangroves, for instance, absorb the force of waves before they reach the shore.
Q. Coastal communities have long relied on natural barriers for protection from storms.
R. When these forests are cleared for shrimp farms, villages behind them become far more exposed.
S. This is why some governments now pay villagers to replant them.

options.A: QPSR
options.B: QPRS
options.C: QRPS
options.D: PQRS

Passage 1:

On a still summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the farmland around it. This difference, known as the urban heat island effect, has three main causes. First, the materials that cities are built from, such as asphalt, concrete and brick, absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly after dark, so city nights cool far less than rural ones. Second, cities have replaced trees, grass and open soil, which cool the air by evaporating water, with sealed surfaces that stay dry. Third, the engines, air conditioners and factories of a city release waste heat directly into the streets.

The consequences are not merely a matter of discomfort. During heatwaves, the warmest neighbourhoods record markedly higher numbers of hospital admissions and deaths, especially among elderly people living alone. Warm nights matter most, because the body depends on cooler hours to recover from the heat of the day. There is a cruel loop as well: as temperatures rise, households that can afford it install more air conditioners, which push more heat outside and make the streets hotter still for those who cannot.

Responses fall into two broad groups. Some aim to change surfaces: painting roofs white so that they reflect sunlight, laying paving that lets rainwater soak in, or planting street trees whose shade can keep pavements more than ten degrees cooler at noon. Others aim to change how cities are planned, keeping corridors of open land that let cooler air flow in from the countryside at night. Each response has limits. White roofs cool the buildings beneath them but do little for people walking in the street below, and trees need years to grow, water to survive and space that dense neighbourhoods often lack.

What the evidence suggests, then, is not that any single measure will cool a city, but that the right mix depends on the neighbourhood. A crowded old quarter with narrow lanes may gain most from reflective roofs and shaded walkways, while a new suburb still being laid out has the rare chance to plan for green corridors from the start.

Question: According to the passage, why do city nights cool less than rural nights?

options.A: Cities have more cloud cover, which traps heat.
options.B: Cooler country air is blocked by tall buildings.
options.C: Air conditioners are switched off at night.
options.D: Building materials release the heat they absorbed during the day slowly after dark.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: The first paragraph says materials 'release the stored heat slowly after dark, so city nights cool far less than rural ones'.
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): Cloud cover is never mentioned. | Trap (B): The passage mentions corridors that let cool air in, but does not give blocking as the cause of warm nights. | Trap (C): Not stated; the passage says air conditioners add waste heat.

Passage 2:

Until the middle of the nineteenth century, almost every town kept its own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over that particular place, so a town a few hundred kilometres to the west kept clocks several minutes behind its eastern neighbour. For most people this caused no difficulty. A farmer rarely travelled far, and a difference of ten minutes between his village and the next was of no practical importance.

The railways changed this. A train that left one city at a scheduled hour and arrived at another needed a timetable that both cities could read in the same way, and a company running dozens of trains across a region could not publish its timetable in dozens of local times. Railway companies therefore began to keep a single 'railway time' along their lines, usually the time of their headquarters city. Some station clocks carried two minute hands, one for local time and one for railway time, and travellers learned to check which hand they were reading.

The confusion that followed eventually pushed governments to act. In 1884, delegates from twenty-five countries met in Washington and agreed to use the meridian through Greenwich, near London, as the starting point for measuring longitude. This laid the groundwork for a worldwide system of time zones, each roughly fifteen degrees of longitude wide and differing from its neighbours by an hour. Adoption was neither quick nor uniform. Some countries took decades to accept the system, and several chose offsets of half an hour so that a single zone could cover their whole territory.

The story is often told as a triumph of reason over local habit, but it can also be read differently. Local time was tied to something every person could observe: the sun overhead. Standard time replaced this with an agreement among distant authorities, accurate to the minute but no longer visible in the sky. Those who resisted were not always clinging to superstition; some were objecting to the idea that the rhythm of their day should be set by a timetable drawn up elsewhere.

Question: According to the passage, why did local time cause little difficulty before the railways?

options.A: The differences between towns were always less than a minute.
options.B: All towns already set their clocks to the same time.
options.C: Governments had already standardised time.
options.D: Most people rarely travelled far enough for small time differences to matter.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'A farmer rarely travelled far, and a difference of ten minutes ... was of no practical importance.'
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The passage gives an example of ten minutes. | Trap (B): Contradicts the opening: almost every town kept its own time. | Trap (C): Standardisation came later, after railway confusion.

questions.question_text:
Passage 3:

When the last fluent speaker of a language dies, linguists often describe the event as the loss of a library. The comparison is apt in one respect: a language stores knowledge that may exist nowhere else, from the names of medicinal plants to ways of describing kinship, direction or time that other languages do not make easy. Some languages, for example, describe position not as left or right of the speaker but as uphill or downhill, or towards the sea, so that their speakers keep track of compass directions throughout the day without conscious effort.

Yet the comparison can mislead. A library is a store of finished texts; a language is a living practice, constantly remade by the people who use it. A dictionary and a set of recordings, however complete, preserve a language rather as a pressed flower preserves a plant: the form survives, but not the growth. This is why many communities working to revive their languages put less emphasis on archives than on creating situations in which the language is needed, in nursery schools, in family kitchens and on local radio, so that children hear it used for ordinary purposes.

It is tempting to assume that languages decline because their speakers stop valuing them. More often the causes are practical. When jobs, schooling and government services are available only in a dominant language, parents may decide, with real affection for their own tongue, that their children's prospects depend on switching. Decline is therefore usually a matter of economic and political pressure rather than indifference, and attempts at revival that ignore this pressure tend to produce enthusiastic adult learners but few native speakers.

None of this means that revival is impossible. Several languages once spoken mainly at home or in ritual have been brought back into daily use, but in each case the change depended on giving the language a role in schools, work and public life, not merely on recording it. The lesson is that a language survives where it is useful, and that usefulness is something a society can choose to create.

Question: According to the passage, in what respect is it apt to compare a language to a library?

options.A: Both can be fully preserved by recordings.
options.B: Libraries, like languages, are constantly remade by their users.
options.C: A language stores knowledge that may exist nowhere else.
options.D: A language, like a library, is a store of finished texts.

questions.pedagogical_explanation: 'The comparison is apt in one respect: a language stores knowledge that may exist nowhere else.'
questions.trap_type: Trap (A): The passage says recordings preserve form but not growth. | Trap (B): Reverses the passage's contrast. | Trap (D): The author uses this point to show where the comparison misleads.
